cards.title: Four pillars of ecommerce security mapped to store controls
cards.summary: Frame storefront security work around privacy, integrity, authentication and non-repudiation, and translate each pillar into concrete store controls.
cards.use_when: Auditing or planning your store's security program and deciding which controls to add next across PDP, account, checkout and order records.
steps: Treat Privacy as keeping customer personal and payment data away from unauthorized parties: require encryption in transit and at rest, restrict admin/data access by role, and limit which apps and integrations can read customer records.

Treat Integrity as ensuring customer-submitted data is not altered in transit or storage: use TLS, validate and re-confirm order, address and payment details server-side, and keep tamper-evident change logs on orders and customer profiles.

Treat Authentication as proving both buyer and seller are real: require email verification or magic links for accounts, offer PIN or card verification at checkout, and publish verifiable business identity and contact details so buyers can confirm you are genuine.

Treat Non-repudiation as making transactions undeniable: retain signed order confirmations, timestamped payment authorizations, consent records and email/confirmation logs so a disputed purchase or chargeback can be evidenced by both sides.

Assign each control to an owner and review the four pillars quarterly, since gaps usually appear at new touchpoints (subscriptions, B2B portals, additional payment methods) rather than at the original checkout.
caveats: The four-pillar framing is a conceptual model, not a certification. Meeting it does not by itself make you PCI DSS compliant.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Layered defense: block malicious traffic before it reaches origin
cards.summary: Combine a CDN and WAF in front of the origin, plus MFA on admin/account access, so no single control is the only barrier.
cards.use_when: Designing the network and access architecture of a self-hosted or heavily customized storefront that must absorb bots, DDoS and random malicious traffic.
steps: Put a CDN or edge proxy in front of the origin server so volumetric DDoS traffic and obvious bot floods are absorbed or filtered at the edge; the source notes CDNs use machine learning to block malicious incoming traffic before it reaches your server.

Layer a Web Application Firewall in front of the application to filter spam, bad bots and common web attack classes such as XSS and SQLi; configure it in front of the store rather than only on the origin host.
Add multi-factor authentication to admin panels, hosting, payment dashboards and customer accounts that store payment or address data, so a stolen password alone is not sufficient.
Apply the same layering to non-web surfaces: DNS, email (for staff and customer-facing sending), and any API or integration endpoint that can trigger orders or refunds.
Monitor edge and WAF logs for attack patterns and adjust rules; treat the first layer as disposable filtering, not as proof the origin is safe.
Verify each layer actually passes legitimate checkout and login traffic end to end after any rule change, since over-blocking converts directly into lost orders.
caveats: The source (quoting Roger Grimes, 2018) states most companies using MFA are still hacked, so MFA is a layer, not a guarantee.
CDN, WAF and MFA capability and configuration differ by provider; verify current features and defaults in your own platform before relying on them.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: SSL/TLS: encrypt data in transit across every hop
cards.summary: Deploy TLS certificates so customer data is unreadable to intermediaries between buyer and server, and treat missing encryption as exposed credentials and card data.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing transport security for a storefront, checkout, account area or admin interface, especially after migrating hosts or adding a custom domain.
steps: Install and maintain SSL/TLS certificates for every customer-facing domain and subdomain, including checkout and account pages, so data is encrypted on each hop between the buyer's device and your server.

Explain the principle to stakeholders: without encryption, any device between sender and server can read passwords, usernames and card numbers, because data passes through multiple computers before reaching the destination.
Enforce HTTPS across the whole site and redirect or block plain-HTTP requests; a partially secure checkout does not protect the session.
Automate certificate issuance and renewal, and monitor expiry, so an expired certificate does not silently break checkout.
Extend the same transport discipline to integrations: webhooks, payment provider callbacks and fulfillment APIs should be encrypted and authenticated as well.
caveats: HTTPS protects data in transit only; it does not by itself make you PCI compliant, prevent malware, or secure stored card data.
Certificate setup and renewal workflows vary by host and platform; verify the current interface, and note that hosted platforms may manage this for you.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: PCI DSS scope: who owns what across hosted vs self-hosted
cards.summary: Treat PCI DSS as applying to any business handling card transactions, and decide card-data handling based on whether you are hosted, self-hosted or using redirect/iframe payments.
cards.use_when: Deciding your payment integration architecture, evaluating a hosted platform like Shopify, or assessing how much cardholder-data responsibility your team actually carries.
steps: Accept the baseline rule from the source: PCI DSS applies to all businesses that handle credit card transactions, and it enforces strict protection of credit card data.
Reduce scope by not storing or transmitting raw card numbers yourself: use your payment provider's hosted fields, redirect or tokenized checkout so card data never touches your servers.
If self-hosted, map where cardholder data flows through your infrastructure, apply the standard's requirements to that environment, and keep evidence for audits.

If on a hosted platform, apply the shared responsibility model: the platform secures its own infrastructure, but you still own your admin account security, app/permission choices, refund and order handling, and any custom code or integrations you add.
Review annually and whenever you add a payment method, market, or integration, because each addition can change your PCI scope.
Keep card data out of logs, order notes, support tickets and exported CSVs; storing it there re-expands scope unintentionally.
caveats: This source describes PCI DSS at a high level only; the actual requirements and current version must be checked against the PCI Security Standards Council and your acquirer.
Shared responsibility boundaries vary by platform and plan; verify your specific agreement rather than assuming the platform covers everything.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Protect against counterfeit sites and brand abuse
cards.summary: Counterfeit lookalike sites and content tampering damage trust and valuation; use packaging authentication and monitoring to fight them.
cards.use_when: Planning brand-protection work for a store selling branded or high-demand physical goods that phishing and counterfeit sites might imitate.
steps: Monitor for fake versions of your store: the source notes attackers can create counterfeit sites cheaply, harming reputation and valuations, so set up periodic searches, typosquat monitoring and takedown requests for lookalike domains.
Add QR code authentication to product packaging so customers can verify authenticity from a smartphone, giving buyers an independent way to distinguish genuine goods from counterfeits.
Watch for malicious alterations to your own site content designed to divert traffic to competitors or damage reputation; use integrity monitoring and a change log on published content.
Treat customer data theft as a brand event, not only an IT event: notify affected customers, document what was exposed, and prepare a response plan before an incident.
Keep robust backups with ransomware protection so a worm, virus or defacement can be rolled back quickly and downtime minimized.
caveats: QR packaging authentication applies to physical products you control; pure-digital or dropshipped catalogs need different verification methods.
The source's framing of counterfeit-site risk is qualitative; no specific detection thresholds or measurement methods are provided.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Handle the fraud, dispute and delivery moment of uncertainty
cards.summary: Online buyers face uncertainty at payment, dispute resolution and delivery, so make these stages transparent and accountable to reduce fraud exposure and abandonment.
cards.use_when: Reviewing checkout, post-purchase communication and dispute handling to reduce buyer uncertainty and the fraud that exploits it.
steps: Identify the three high-uncertainty moments the source names: payment, dispute resolution and delivery. These are the points where buyers are most exposed to fraudsters.
At payment, show recognizable payment controls (card verification, secure-payment indicators) and keep the checkout on a trusted, encrypted domain.
At dispute resolution, give a clear point of contact for problems and a documented process, so customers do not have to rely on unofficial channels where impersonation happens.
At delivery, provide tracking and a verifiable record of what was ordered and shipped; this also supports non-repudiation if a chargeback is filed later.

Be explicit about data collection and usage, not just problem-contact transparency. The source notes many businesses disclose contact points but fail to disclose how personal data is collected and used.
caveats: The source's suggestion to embed third-party reviews for transparency is promotional and outside this section's defensive scope; treat reviews as a separate trust decision.
No specific abandonment or fraud-reduction figures are given for these measures.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Anti-malware scanning and scheduled detection for storefront files
cards.summary: Malware such as card skimmers, spam injectors and redirects hides in store files; use continuous scanning plus scheduled scans to detect and clean it.
cards.use_when: Operating a self-hosted or plugin-heavy store and needing a routine for detecting malicious code injected into the site.
steps: Deploy anti-malware software that scans both your web system and supporting devices; the source's requirement is that it renders hidden malware on your website visible and resolvable.
Enable scheduled scans (daily, weekly, fortnightly or monthly) rather than relying on manual checks, so the routine survives busy periods.
Turn on file-change notifications so you learn immediately when store files are modified, which is the typical signature of an injection.
Prioritize known storefront malware families the source names: credit-card skimming scripts, spam injections, pharma-injection pages, pub2srv and malicious redirects.
After any detection, treat it as a breach until proven otherwise: rotate admin and integration credentials, check for unauthorized admin users or payment-route changes, and review checkout code.
Keep backups with ransomware protection so a clean restore is possible if cleaning fails.
caveats: The source promotes specific third-party scanner and firewall products; the durable practice is scheduled scanning, file-change alerts and credential rotation, not any one vendor.
Anti-malware does not replace a WAF, access control or transport encryption; it is one layer.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Defend against digital skimming and payment-page tampering
cards.summary: Card skimming (Magecart-style attacks) injects code into checkout to steal card data; protect by minimizing third-party scripts and monitoring checkout code.
cards.use_when: Managing checkout page scripts, tags and third-party apps, or investigating an incident where card data may have been captured from your site.
steps: Inventory every script and app that loads on checkout and payment pages, including analytics, chat, A/B testing and tag managers, and remove anything that does not need to run at the payment step.

Restrict who can edit checkout templates and scripts, and require review for checkout code changes, since injected skimming code typically arrives through a compromised admin account or third-party dependency.
Use hosted payment fields or redirect flows so raw card numbers never enter your page's DOM where injected script could read them.
Monitor checkout code and script sources for unexpected changes, and route alerts to a named owner who can act quickly.
Include checkout integrity checks in your regular security review, alongside malware scans, so tampering is detected even if the script is served from a legitimate-looking domain.
If skimming is suspected, treat it as a card-data breach: isolate, rotate credentials, notify your payment provider and follow your incident process.
caveats: The source names Magecart as a category but provides no technical detection recipe; methods vary by platform and should be validated on systems you own.
No control fully eliminates skimming risk while third-party scripts run on checkout.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Bot, spam and OWASP-class application defense with a WAF
cards.summary: A Web Application Firewall filters spam, bad bots and common web attacks like XSS and SQL injection before they reach your store application.
cards.use_when: Configuring application-layer protection for a storefront and deciding what the WAF should block versus allow.
steps: Place a WAF in front of the store application to filter bad bots, spam and the OWASP top 10 threat classes the source names, including cross-site scripting (XSS) and SQL injection (SQLi).

Verify your platform path: WAF configurations differ for WordPress, Magento, Opencart, Prestashop, Drupal, Joomla and custom PHP sites, so confirm a supported setup rather than assuming one configuration fits.
Test the WAF against legitimate checkout, login and account flows after any rule change; false positives block real customers and directly cost orders.
Combine WAF filtering with rate limiting and bot challenges on high-abuse endpoints such as login, account creation, password reset and checkout submission.
Review WAF logs regularly to tune rules and identify patterns, and keep a documented bypass path for emergencies so a bad rule does not take the store down.
caveats: The source names the Astra firewall and its feature claims; treat vendor capability lists as claims to verify in your environment, not guarantees.
A WAF does not fix vulnerable application code; it filters traffic in front of it.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Layer passwords, PINs and magic links for buyer authentication
cards.summary: Verify buyers with login credentials, card PINs, magic links or email verification so accounts and orders belong to real identities.
cards.use_when: Designing customer account login, guest checkout verification, or account-recovery flows for the store.
steps: Require authentication that proves identity for account access, using recognized methods such as client login credentials and card PINs at the point of verification.
For friction-averse buyers, use email-based magic links or one-time codes so verification does not require remembering a password.
Apply MFA or step-up verification to sensitive account actions: changing email or shipping address, viewing stored payment data, and issuing refunds or store credit.
Verify on the seller side too: publish enough business identity and contact information that buyers can confirm the store is genuine.
Align verification strength with the action: browsing can stay open, but saved-payment access and address changes should require re-verification.
Watch for account-takeover patterns in support channels, such as sudden email or address changes before an order, and add manual review triggers.
caveats: The source notes authentication solutions can require expert help if you cannot implement them yourself.
Stronger authentication adds checkout friction; the source does not provide a benchmark for how much friction is acceptable.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Non-repudiation: keep evidence that orders and consents happened
cards.summary: Digital signatures and retained records let neither buyer nor seller deny a transaction, which matters in ecommerce where no live video exists.
cards.use_when: Setting up order records, consent capture and chargeback evidence for the store, especially for high-value or subscription orders.
steps: Accept the principle: non-repudiation is a legal and security layer confirming that communication reached the recipient, so a party cannot deny a signature, email or purchase.
Retain timestamped records of the order confirmation, payment authorization, terms acceptance and delivery confirmation for each transaction.
Use digital signatures or authenticated confirmations where available, and store them alongside the order record rather than in a separate system that may not be searchable during a dispute.
Capture marketing and data consent separately from purchase consent, since the source notes businesses often disclose contact points but not how personal data is collected and used.
Make the evidence retrievable by support staff before a chargeback deadline so disputes can be answered quickly.
Review retention periods and access controls so the evidence store itself does not become a privacy or breach liability.
caveats: Non-repudiation is described as a legal principle; specific admissibility of digital records varies by jurisdiction and should be checked with counsel.
The source gives no specific retention period or tooling recommendation.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Treat security failures as a survival risk, not an IT line item
cards.summary: Cybercrime causes financial, market-share and reputation losses, and the source reports most small stores that suffer attacks do not survive six months.
cards.use_when: Making the business case for security investment, or deciding how much budget and staffing to allocate to storefront protection.
steps: Quantify the business exposure in the terms the source uses: losses in finances, market share and reputation, plus the possibility of criminal charges against the company.
Present the survival framing to decision-makers: the source reports that almost 60% of small ecommerce stores that experience cybercrimes do not survive more than six months.
Identify the specific loss mechanisms you face: diverted traffic, stolen customer and inventory data, denied service reducing store functionality, and stolen or altered intellectual property.
Convert the risk into operational requirements: staffing or expert support for security, backups with ransomware protection, and monitoring that runs continuously rather than annually.
Revisit the assessment when you add markets, payment methods or integrations, since those increase attack surface and change which losses are plausible.
caveats: The statistics cited (32.4% of attacks, 29% malicious traffic, 85.6% purchase rate, 60% survival) are dated around 2018 and presented loosely; use them as source-stated framing, not current benchmarks.
Survival statistics describe a correlation in the cited reporting, not a causal guarantee for any individual store.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Harden store networks against worms, Trojans and destructive payloads
cards.summary: Malware delivered via worms, viruses and fake software can hijack systems, erase or block data, and propagate malicious links through your network.
cards.use_when: Establishing endpoint and store-adjacent device protection, especially for teams running order management, warehouse or admin workstations.
steps: Install and maintain anti-virus and anti-malware protection on the devices and systems that touch the store, admin panels and order data; the source lists this as a necessary minimum alongside firewalls and encryption.
Recognize the delivery vector: the source notes attackers hide Trojans in fake software, so restrict software installation to approved sources for staff who access store systems.
Plan for the damage types named: hijacked systems, erased data, blocked data access, and the spread of malicious links to clients and other computers on the network.
Segment admin and operational networks from general browsing where feasible, so a single infected workstation cannot reach store infrastructure.
Keep an offline or immutable backup with ransomware protection, and test restoration so recovery is a rehearsed process rather than an untested assumption.
Educate staff who open order emails, supplier files and attachments, since malicious links can be forwarded onward through your network.
caveats: Anti-virus and firewalls reduce but do not eliminate infection risk; the source presents them as a minimum, not a guarantee.
No specific product or detection rate is endorsed here beyond the source's vendor examples.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Route traffic through selective-permeability firewalls
cards.summary: Firewalls regulate inbound and outbound store traffic with selective permeability, allowing only trusted traffic through.
cards.use_when: Choosing and configuring firewall or plugin protection for a self-hosted ecommerce site.
steps: Deploy firewall protection using ecommerce-appropriate software or plugins that bar untrusted networks and regulate both inbound and outbound traffic.
Configure for selective permeability: the rule is to permit trusted traffic only, rather than blocking individual known-bad sources.
Verify outbound rules too, since compromised store code often needs an outbound channel to exfiltrate card or customer data.
Combine the firewall with the WAF and malware scanning layers so network filtering, application filtering and file integrity are covered separately.
Test the rules against real checkout, login and webhook traffic after changes, and log blocked events for review.
caveats: The source promotes a specific vendor firewall; vendor feature lists are claims to verify, and results vary by site architecture.
A firewall in front of a vulnerable plugin does not fix the underlying vulnerability.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Automate high-risk order handling on hosted platforms
cards.summary: Hosted platforms leave platform infrastructure to the provider but you still own order-risk decisions, so automate high-risk order review and actions.
cards.use_when: Operating on a hosted platform like Shopify and needing a repeatable process for suspicious orders, refunds or account changes.
steps: Clarify the shared responsibility split: the hosted platform secures its own infrastructure, while you remain responsible for your admin accounts, apps, data access and order-level decisions.

Define what counts as a high-risk order for your store (for example mismatched billing and shipping, unusually large first orders, or rapid repeat orders from one buyer) and make the criteria explicit rather than leaving it to staff judgment alone.
Automate the response on hosted platforms using workflow tooling such as Shopify Flow: tag or hold high-risk orders, notify a named reviewer, and release or cancel based on a documented rule.
Restrict admin permissions so only authorized staff can refund, export customer data or edit payment settings.
Log every automated and manual risk decision so patterns can be reviewed and rules adjusted over time.
Re-verify the current interface and available triggers before building workflows, since platform automation features change.
caveats: The source names Shopify Flow and hosted-platform handling in this section's header, but the body does not detail the workflow configuration; treat platform specifics as needing verification.
Automated rules can produce false positives that delay legitimate orders, so include a review path.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Map payment-fraud controls: verification checks at checkout
cards.summary: Address verification, card verification and 3D Secure shift some fraud risk decisions to the checkout step, alongside PCI compliance for card data.
cards.use_when: Choosing and configuring payment verification settings for checkout, or deciding how much friction to add to reduce card-not-present fraud.
steps: Distinguish the mechanisms rather than treating them as one control: address verification checks the billing address against issuer records, card verification value checks the printed code, and 3D Secure adds an issuer-side buyer authentication step.
Enable these checks on your payment provider's settings and confirm they apply to the payment methods and regions you sell into.
Accept that requiring 3D Secure or strict address matching can convert some legitimate buyers away, so weigh fraud reduction against checkout completion for your own catalog and markets.
Keep these verification steps separate from transport encryption and compliance work; verification is a fraud signal, not a substitute for PCI DSS or TLS.
Record which checks fired on each order so disputes and rule tuning have evidence.
Review chargeback and decline patterns periodically and adjust thresholds rather than setting rules once and leaving them.
caveats: This source's body mentions 3DS, AVS and CVV only in the section header; it gives no configuration detail, so verify current provider options and rules.
None of these checks guarantees fraud prevention, and none replaces PCI DSS obligations.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Defend against denial-of-service and keep the store selling
cards.summary: Hackers can prevent legitimate users from using the store, reducing functionality; DDoS filtering and preparedness keep orders flowing.
cards.use_when: Preparing for or responding to traffic floods, slow checkout, or downtime during a peak sales period.
steps: Assume downtime is a revenue event: the source frames denial of service as preventing legitimate users from using the store and causing a reduction in its functioning.
Absorb volumetric attacks at the edge with a CDN or DDoS-protection layer, so the origin server is not the first thing hit.
Rate-limit and challenge high-cost endpoints such as search, cart, login and checkout submission, which bots often target to exhaust server capacity.
Maintain current backups with ransomware protection so a destructive event can be restored quickly and downtime minimized.
Prepare a response plan with named owners, customer communication templates, and a decision rule for when to enable stricter mitigation that may inconvenience some buyers.
Review capacity and mitigation settings before major sale events rather than during them.
caveats: The source describes CDN machine learning as blocking DDoS threats but gives no capacity figures or thresholds.
Strict mitigation can block real customers during high traffic; plan the trade-off in advance.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Integrity: keep customer data unaltered to preserve trust
cards.summary: Integrity means using customer information as given, without changing any part of it, because alterations erode buyer confidence.
cards.use_when: Reviewing how order, address and profile data is edited and stored across the store, especially where staff or integrations can modify customer records.
steps: Adopt the principle: the business uses customer information as provided, without changing anything, and altering any part of the data causes the buyer to lose confidence in the enterprise's security.
Prevent silent edits: make changes to shipping addresses, order contents and contact details deliberate and logged rather than overwritten by tooling.
Validate customer-submitted data on receipt and flag discrepancies instead of auto-correcting them without notice.
Restrict write access so only the roles and integrations that need to change customer records can do so.
Show customers what was recorded, via order confirmation and account views, so discrepancies surface early rather than at delivery or dispute time.
Treat unexplained changes in records as a security signal, since unauthorized alteration may indicate compromise rather than a data-entry issue.
caveats: Integrity in this source is a conceptual principle; it names no specific validation library or logging standard.
Some normalization (address formatting, phone formatting) is operationally necessary; the principle is to avoid altering meaning without the customer's knowledge.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Privacy: prevent unauthorized access to customer data
cards.summary: Privacy means no party other than the seller the customer chose should access their personal information and account details.
cards.use_when: Reviewing app permissions, data exports, staff access and vendor sharing for the store's customer database.
steps: Define the baseline: a breach of confidentiality occurs when sellers let others access customer information, so the standard is that only the chosen seller accesses personal information and account details.
Audit every app, integration and agency that can read customer records, and remove or scope down access that is not required for its function.
Apply a minimum protective stack as the source describes: anti-virus, firewall, encryption and other data protection to safeguard credit card and bank details.
Limit data exports, and avoid keeping card or bank details in spreadsheets, support tickets or marketing tools.
Document what personal data you collect and how it is used, since the source notes businesses often disclose a problem contact point but not their data collection and usage practices.
Review access when staff leave or agency relationships end, since retained credentials are a common confidentiality gap.
caveats: The source gives the privacy principle and a minimum control list, not a full privacy-regulation compliance program; check applicable law separately.
Encryption and firewalls reduce exposure but do not guarantee customer data remains private if access is misconfigured.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Run a continuous security review across store surfaces
cards.summary: Security is ongoing, not a one-time setup; the source's closing recommendation is proactive, continuous protection across the website.
cards.use_when: Setting a recurring security cadence for the store rather than reacting only after an incident.
steps: Accept the source's closing posture: don't stop at basic authentication, SSL and MFA, because attackers keep improving, so implement proactive protection across the website continuously.

Define a recurring review covering the store surfaces named across this section: transport encryption, authentication and MFA, firewall/WAF rules, malware scans, backups, payment verification settings and admin permissions.
Assign an owner and a schedule for each review item, and record the outcome so gaps are visible between cycles.
Include ongoing vulnerability monitoring, which the source names as part of the overall ecommerce-security definition alongside encryption, secure payments, PCI DSS compliance and bot protection.
Re-run the review after significant changes: new market, new payment method, new app, platform migration or staff change.
Keep an incident response plan ready, and rehearse the steps for notifying customers and payment partners.
caveats: The source gives no specific review frequency or checklist depth; set a cadence proportionate to order volume and data sensitivity.
Vendor product claims in the source are promotional illustrations of the tactics, not endorsements or performance guarantees.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Shared responsibility model: what the platform secures vs. what you secure
cards.summary: On hosted ecommerce platforms the platform owns infrastructure, checkout and server-side PCI, while the merchant owns credentials, app permissions and data handling.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest security effort for a store on a hosted platform (e.g., Shopify) versus a self-hosted cart, and scoping what your team is actually accountable for.
steps: Map responsibility: the platform secures servers, payment processing, checkout code and software; the merchant secures login credentials, third-party app permissions, sensitive-customer-data handling, and admin access for team members.
Accept that the platform cannot compensate for weak merchant-side practices — an admin password of 'password123' or a click on a phishing link hands over the store regardless of platform hardening.

On self-hosted setups, budget for the work the platform would otherwise do: sourcing and renewing SSL/TLS certificates, achieving PCI compliance, patching server software, and configuring firewalls. PCI compliance alone is cited as costing small businesses roughly $1,000–$10,000 per year depending on transaction volume.
Prioritize merchant-side gaps first: enable 2FA/passkeys on admin accounts, audit app permissions, and stop storing card data in order notes, emails or spreadsheets.

Recognize that hosted checkout code is not merchant-editable, which the source says significantly reduces Magecart-style skimming exposure versus self-hosted stores where checkout JavaScript can be injected by attackers.
caveats: Cost figures and platform behaviors are vendor-published and can change; verify current terms with your platform and processor.
Hosted platforms reduce skimming exposure but do not eliminate all fraud, ATO or bot risk.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: CNP fraud and card testing: the mechanism to defend against
cards.summary: Card-not-present fraud uses stolen card data validated through small test transactions before larger fraudulent purchases.
cards.use_when: Designing checkout fraud controls, selecting a payment processor configuration, or investigating a spike in small declined/approved orders on your store.
steps: Understand the attack chain: fraudsters obtain card data through breaches, phishing or skimming, then run small transactions to validate the numbers before using them for larger fraud or selling the validated data on dark web markets.
Treat unusual clusters of small orders — especially from new accounts, mismatched geographies or repeated attempts on the same card range — as a likely card-testing signal rather than organic demand.
Use CVV checks so an attacker without physical card access has more difficulty completing a transaction, and AVS to check that the billing address matches the issuer's records.

Note the source's cost framing: each dollar lost to fraud costs store owners an average of about $4.61 once processing fees, lost inventory and operational disruption are counted (source-specific figure, not a benchmark to plan against).
Configure processor fraud analysis and automated rules rather than reviewing every order manually, because card testing runs at machine speed.
caveats: Financial figures are published estimates from the source and its cited research, not guarantees for any single store.
AVS/CVV alone do not stop all CNP fraud; enablers like tokenization and 3DS work with them.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Chargeback thresholds: know your danger zone
cards.summary: Track disputes using the processor's actual definitions and thresholds instead of copying a fixed chargeback percentage.
cards.use_when: Monitoring order-risk and dispute metrics, setting an internal alert threshold, or deciding when to escalate fraud controls before processor action forces it.
steps: Obtain current monitoring definitions, thresholds, periods and consequences from the processor or acquirer.
Calculate the relevant metrics on the correct denominator; different programs can count disputes and transactions differently.
Set internal alerts early enough to investigate fraud, delivery and customer-service causes.
Evaluate authentication, review routing and evidence collection while monitoring legitimate-order declines.
Confirm coverage conditions before relying on any chargeback-protection program.
caveats: The source's 0.9%, 1% and average loss figures are not universal current thresholds or guarantees.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Dynamic 3D Secure and the liability shift
cards.summary: Dynamic 3D Secure adds step-up authentication on higher-risk transactions and can shift fraudulent chargeback liability from the store to the card issuer.
cards.use_when: Configuring checkout authentication to reduce fraudulent chargeback exposure without adding friction to every legitimate order.
steps: Configure the supported 3DS flow according to processor requirements and applicable authentication rules; frictionless and challenge outcomes are not simply low-risk versus high-risk switches.

When a cardholder completes the 3DS verification step (one-time code or biometric), the source states the responsibility for a fraudulent chargeback moves from the store to the card issuer for authenticated Visa and Mastercard disputes — confirm the exact current liability-shift rules with your processor and card networks.

Check whether your payment gateway supports 3DS 2.0 authentication when selecting a processor; this is one of the stated security criteria alongside processor-level PCI DSS certification and tokenization.
Treat 3DS as a liability-shift and verification tool, not as proof that a transaction is legitimate; step-up authentication does not guarantee the buyer is the cardholder.
Monitor approval rates and false declines after enabling dynamic 3DS so authentication friction does not silently suppress legitimate conversions.
caveats: The source cites that only 32.4% of store owners implement 3DS; this figure is a snapshot and may change.
Liability-shift rules, coverage and eligible transaction types vary by network, region and processor — verify before relying on them.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Automated order risk handling with workflow tools
cards.summary: Wire fraud-analysis risk ratings into automated workflows that auto-capture low-risk orders and queue high-risk ones for manual review.
cards.use_when: Setting up order review and capture automation so fraud decisions scale without a human watching every order.
steps: Confirm your platform's fraud analysis scores each order low, medium or high using signals such as AVS checks, CVV verification, IP data, proxy detection and unusual purchase patterns.

Build workflows triggered by order-risk events that: auto-capture low-risk orders, add high-risk orders to a manual review queue, send internal notifications for medium-risk orders, and cancel orders matching specific fraud patterns.
Use pre-built workflow templates from your platform's help center as starting points, then adapt thresholds to your store's order profile and risk tolerance.
Revisit automation as order volume and fraud patterns change; a rule set tuned for one season can create either false declines or un-reviewed high-risk captures later.
Keep a human escalation path for medium- and high-risk queues so automated cancellation rules do not silently reject legitimate high-value customers.
caveats: Fraud scores are model outputs, not verdicts; both false positives and false negatives are possible.
Workflow trigger names and template availability change over time — verify against the current platform interface and help documentation.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: AVS, CVV and 3DS: keep the three verification tools distinct
cards.summary: AVS checks billing address, CVV checks for physical card presence, and 3DS adds step-up authentication on higher-risk transactions.
cards.use_when: Configuring fraud-prevention settings or explaining to your team which control addresses which fraud vector at checkout.
steps: AVS (Address Verification System): checks whether the billing address provided matches the address on file with the card issuer — useful against stolen-card use where the attacker lacks the correct billing address.
CVV: the three- or four-digit code on the card; requiring it makes stolen card numbers harder to use without physical access, but it is not proof of cardholder identity.
3DS: adds a multifactor authentication step (one-time code or biometric) for higher-risk transactions and can shift fraudulent chargeback liability to the issuer when completed.

Configure AVS and CVV requirements and decide how checkout handles mismatched billing addresses under Shopify Payments fraud-prevention settings (path cited: Settings → Payments → Shopify Payments → Manage → Fraud prevention; verify current navigation).

Before enabling AVS, note the source's warning that AVS is deactivated by default in Shopify Payments because fraud analysis handles high-risk transactions separately, and that enabling it alongside fraud analysis can raise false declines on legitimate orders — review your order risk reports first.
Do not treat any single control as sufficient; combine them and monitor outcomes.
caveats: No single control guarantees a transaction is legitimate; AVS, CVV and 3DS catch different failure modes and can all be defeated or produce false declines.
Admin navigation paths and defaults change — verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Confirm merchant PCI scope with the acquirer and payment setup
cards.summary: Determine the store's actual payment-data responsibilities and validation route even on a hosted platform.
cards.use_when: Understanding your compliance obligations as a small store, or checking that store operations do not introduce non-compliant card-data handling.
steps: Map where payment data is captured, processed and stored, including apps and customer support.
Ask the acquirer or payment brand which validation route and SAQ eligibility apply to the actual environment.
Do not infer the required assessment from a universal 20,000-transaction rule.
Confirm the hosted provider's scope and retain responsibility for merchant accounts, integrations and handling practices outside that scope.
Keep payment data out of support messages, order notes and spreadsheets; use approved payment collection flows.
caveats: Platform compliance does not automatically validate every merchant workflow; requirements depend on the actual environment.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Payment gateway selection: what to verify before committing
cards.summary: When choosing a gateway, check processor-level PCI DSS certification, tokenization and 3DS 2.0 support.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a new payment gateway or reviewing whether an existing gateway meets your store's security requirements.
steps: Verify the gateway is PCI DSS-certified at the processor level — certification of your own storefront does not substitute for processor-side compliance.
Confirm tokenization is supported: card data is replaced with a non-sensitive token so raw card numbers are not retained in your environment.
Confirm 3DS 2.0 authentication support so you can apply dynamic step-up verification on higher-risk transactions.

Compare against a built-in option where available: Shopify Payments is described as PCI-compliant by default and includes fraud analysis, 3D Secure and Shopify Protect for eligible stores; third-party gateways can be used but bring their own compliance and security requirements.
Check certifications directly with the provider before you commit rather than relying on marketing pages, and re-verify periodically since provider terms and certifications change.
caveats: Vendor feature claims and program eligibility change; verify with the provider and your own processor.
Adding a third-party gateway may complicate which party handles compliance and chargeback liability.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Account takeover, credential stuffing and phishing defenses
cards.summary: Credential stuffing and phishing feed account takeover, which the source links to customer churn and reputational spread.
cards.use_when: Hardening customer accounts and admin access against takeover, or assessing the retention risk of an account-security incident.
steps: Recognize the attack chain: large-scale breaches expose username/password pairs, which attackers test automatically across other sites (credential stuffing), or use for targeted phishing that impersonates a trusted source to harvest credentials.

Require 2FA on all admin accounts, not just payment-related ones — the source notes 2FA is required to use Shopify Payments but should be enabled everywhere; the setup path cited is profile → Manage account → Security → two-step authentication (verify current navigation).
Add passkeys as an additional authentication layer where supported.

Train the team on generative-AI-crafted phishing: check suspicious sender domains, verify any request for credential changes or payment redirects through a separate channel, and give staff a reporting route for suspicious emails, voice (vishing) and SMS (smishing).

Weigh retention impact: the source cites a survey finding that 75% of consumers say they would stop using a site after an account takeover there and 87% would share the experience with others (survey findings, not a guarantee for your store).
caveats: 2FA, passkeys and training reduce but do not eliminate ATO risk; attackers also target APIs and support channels.
Survey percentages are third-party research snapshots, not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Auditing third-party apps and integrations
cards.summary: Every installed app can access order data, customer information or store settings depending on permissions — audit access regularly and remove unused apps.
cards.use_when: Reviewing app permissions before or after installing storefront, marketing, review or fulfillment apps, or cleaning up an accumulated app stack.
steps: List installed apps and their permissions from the platform admin (the source cites Settings → Apps and sales channels; verify current navigation) and check what each is permitted to access.
Remove any app no longer in use — an unused integration with order or customer-data permissions is standing risk.

When selecting new apps, prioritize those with 'Built for Shopify' status and review scores above 3.75; the source states these have been reviewed against Shopify's technical requirements and are maintained to current platform standards.
Treat installed apps as part of your data-handling surface: an app with broad permissions can undermine your PCI and privacy posture even when your own checkout is clean.
Re-audit after adding apps with checkout, payment or customer-data access, since permission scope at install time determines what data the app can reach.
caveats: Review-score and status thresholds are platform-specific heuristics from the source; verify current app-review criteria.
Neither a badge nor a score guarantees an app is secure.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Digital skimming (Magecart): why hosted checkout reduces exposure
cards.summary: Skimming malware injects malicious JavaScript into checkout pages to capture card data as customers type, and hosted platforms reduce this exposure because merchants cannot modify checkout code.
cards.use_when: Deciding between hosted and self-hosted checkout, or assessing skimming risk from custom checkout scripts and third-party front-end code.
steps: Understand the attack: attackers inject malicious code into the checkout page to capture debit/credit card details as customers enter them; the source describes these as brute-force attacks targeting JavaScript that are hard to spot without regular code audits.

If you run a hosted platform, note that the source says hosted stores are significantly less exposed because merchants cannot alter the underlying checkout code — a structural control, not a guarantee.
If you run self-hosted or heavily customized checkout, add regular code audits and review any third-party JavaScript added to payment pages as a standing practice.
Restrict who can modify checkout templates and injected scripts; every additional script on the payment page is a potential injection point.
Do not treat HTTPS or a padlock icon as protection against skimming — skimming captures data after it is typed, inside a page that may still be encrypted in transit.
caveats: Hosted platforms reduce but do not eliminate skimming or supply-chain script risk from installed apps and tags.
The source does not prescribe a specific audit frequency; treat regular audits as a principle, not a fixed schedule.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Bot attacks, API targeting and DDoS: what to watch
cards.summary: Bots run card testing, price scraping, fake account creation and inventory hoarding, and 44% of advanced bot traffic now targets API endpoints handling checkout, inventory and accounts.
cards.use_when: Investigating suspicious traffic patterns, inventory hoarding, fake account signups or site slowdowns that could be bot-driven.
steps: Treat the API surface as the priority: the source cites a 2025 Imperva report stating 44% of advanced bot traffic targets API endpoints that handle checkout, inventory and customer account data — so review what your APIs expose and who can call them.
Watch for bot-driven commerce behaviors: card-testing transaction patterns, pricing-data scraping, bulk fake-account creation, and stockpiling of high-demand products before real shoppers can buy.

For DDoS, recognize the signature as traffic flooding that locks out real customers; the source does not prescribe a specific mitigation stack, so rely on platform-level protections and your provider's DDoS handling.

Use early bot-detection signal where available: the source cites an example where a platform's Sidekick flagged a major bot attack on Maggy London's storefront before any other monitoring system (a single case example, not a guaranteed detection capability).
Prioritize protections by business impact — checkout and inventory APIs affect revenue directly; scraping affects pricing strategy.
caveats: The 44% API-targeting figure is a third-party report snapshot, not a benchmark for your store.
The Maggy London detection case is an illustrative example; do not assume equivalent detection performance.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Security failures as retention and conversion risk
cards.summary: Account takeover and missing HTTPS drive measurable customer abandonment, and the source ties security to conversion and retention decisions.
cards.use_when: Making the business case for checkout security signals, privacy transparency, or remediating a security incident's customer-facing impact.
steps: Weigh the retention cost of incidents: the source cites a survey finding that 75% of consumers would stop using a site after an account takeover there and 87% would share the experience with others.

Recognize the conversion cost of missing encryption: modern browsers flag any site without HTTPS with a 'Not secure' warning in the address bar, visible at the moment customers decide whether to enter card details.

Use visible trust signals at the right point in the journey: the padlock icon and HTTPS prefix are the most widely recognized security signals for shoppers, Shop Pay stores returning users' shipping and payment details securely to reduce checkout friction, and third-party trust badges can supplement these on checkout pages — particularly for security-conscious categories like health products or high-value goods.

Address privacy transparency as a conversion factor: the source cites a finding that 36% of consumers have stopped using a website due to privacy concerns, and GDPR requires clear information on what data is collected, why and how it is stored for EU/UK customers.

Treat HTTPS and a padlock as baseline hygiene that removes a warning, not as proof of security — the source notes 98% of US web traffic on Google's platforms ran over HTTPS as of June 2026, making encryption an expectation, not a differentiator.
caveats: Consumer survey percentages are third-party research snapshots; results in your store's audience may differ.
Trust badges and privacy copy should not substitute for actual controls; false or outdated signals can worsen trust.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Privacy policy, GDPR exposure and third-party audit signals
cards.summary: GDPR applies to EU/UK customers regardless of store location, with fines up to 4% of global annual revenue, and SOC audits act as third-party trust signals.
cards.use_when: Publishing or updating a privacy policy, supporting an EU/UK customer base, or evaluating what independent security assurance your platform provides.
steps: Confirm scope: if you sell to customers in the EU and UK, GDPR applies regardless of where your store is based.

Publish clear information on what customer data is collected, why it is collected, and how it is stored; for Shopify-hosted stores, automated privacy policy templates cover core requirements and the Customer Privacy API supports cookie-consent banners that meet GDPR standards (verify current feature names and coverage).

Understand the penalty scale: serious GDPR violations carry fines of up to 4% of a company's global annual revenue, with the source citing approximately €1.2 billion in EU supervisory authority fines in 2025 and average breach notifications around 443 per day (published figures, not predictions for your store).

Use independent audits as diligence signals: the source states Shopify undergoes SOC 1 and SOC 2 audits every six months, verifying controls over customer data encryption, access management, incident response and physical infrastructure — check the current status and scope before citing it to customers or partners.
Treat platform audit reports as covering the platform's environment only, not your store's apps, workflows or data handling.
caveats: GDPR requirements and official templates change; verify current obligations with qualified counsel for your markets.
SOC report scope and frequency can change — confirm the latest reports rather than relying on this description.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Guaranteed chargeback coverage programs: eligibility and limits
cards.summary: Shopify Protect (formerly Fraud Protect) covers chargebacks and dispute fees on eligible protected orders for eligible Shopify Payments users in the US.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a guaranteed chargeback-coverage program applies to your store and how it changes your manual fraud-review workload.
steps: Check eligibility first: the source states Shopify Protect is available to eligible Shopify Payments users in the US — eligibility and geography matter, so verify current terms in the platform's help documentation.
Understand what coverage does: orders are marked protected, payment is guaranteed, and if a dispute is filed on a protected order the platform covers the chargeback and the dispute fee.
Use the covered-order marking to reduce manual review for orders that qualify, while keeping review in place for orders outside coverage.

Reallocate the freed review time toward customer experience and high-value account management — the source quotes a merchant who said a staff member previously spent nearly her whole job on fraud and shifted to customer experience after switching to integrated fraud management.
Do not assume all orders are covered; confirm which orders are marked protected in your admin before treating the program as your only fraud control.
caveats: Program availability, eligibility and coverage terms are vendor-specific and subject to change — verify current terms.
Coverage addresses chargeback liability on protected orders, not all fraud losses, false declines or operational costs.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Preventing card data from leaking outside checkout
cards.summary: PCI compliance on a hosted platform is maintained by keeping card handling inside the compliant checkout and never storing card data in notes, emails or spreadsheets.
cards.use_when: Reviewing order-management, support and fulfillment workflows for card-data handling that could break compliance on an otherwise compliant platform.
steps: Instruct all staff never to ask customers for card details outside of checkout — any such request moves card handling into a non-compliant channel.
Ban storing card numbers in order notes, emails, spreadsheets or shared documents used for fulfillment, support or record-keeping.
When a customer sends card details by email or chat, treat the message as exposure: do not process it manually from that channel; direct the customer back to the compliant checkout flow.
Apply the same rule to app and integration data flows: apps with order or customer permissions should not be used to store or relay raw card numbers.

Recognize this is the merchant's practical PCI obligation on a hosted platform — the platform handles processing and storage in a compliant environment, and your role is not to introduce non-compliant handling.
caveats: This guidance addresses card-data handling specifically; other customer data still carries privacy obligations under rules like GDPR.
Individual staff workflows and third-party tools change — re-audit periodically.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Prioritizing fraud controls when resources are limited
cards.summary: When a store cannot implement every control, sequence by direct financial exposure: enable account protection, then automated risk handling, then verification and coverage options.
cards.use_when: Building a fraud and security roadmap for a small store, deciding what to configure first, or allocating limited operational time to security work.
steps: Start with account protection since it gates everything else: enable 2FA on every admin account and add passkeys where supported — the platform can't protect an admin account with a weak or phishable credential.

Then enable the platform's built-in fraud analysis and wire its risk ratings into automated order handling (auto-capture low risk, queue high risk for review) so fraud decisions do not depend on someone watching every order.

Then reduce chargeback exposure financially: apply dynamic 3D Secure so higher-risk transactions carry step-up authentication and liability can shift to the issuer, and check eligibility for guaranteed chargeback-coverage programs.
Then tighten verification settings like AVS and CVV carefully, watching for false declines on legitimate customers before changing defaults.

Layer in organizational controls last but do not skip them: phishing training, app-permission audits, and prohibiting card data outside checkout — these address the human and integration paths that technical controls miss.
caveats: No single control or sequence guarantees protection; each reduces specific risk and some increase false declines.
Platform defaults, thresholds and feature availability change — verify current behavior before relying on any specific setting.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Assessing platform-level security defaults before you rely on them
cards.summary: Hosted platforms supply PCI compliance, TLS/HTTPS and fraud scoring by default, but you should verify what each default actually covers for your store.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a hosting platform's security posture during store setup or migration, or documenting which security obligations remain with your team.
steps: Inventory the platform-provided defaults you can rely on: PCI DSS compliance by default, a free TLS certificate with HTTPS switched on by default, and card readers that are PCI and EMV compliant (per the source's Shopify description).

Confirm fraud scoring exists and what signals it uses: one described implementation scores every order low/medium/high using AVS checks, CVV verification, IP address data, proxy detection and unusual purchase patterns.
Check which optional programs and features you must explicitly enable or qualify for, such as guaranteed chargeback coverage, dynamic 3D Secure, and workflow automation apps.
Document the residual merchant-side obligations — credentials, app permissions, staff access and customer-data handling — so platform defaults are not mistaken for complete coverage.
Re-verify platform features and certifications periodically; vendor security offerings change and published descriptions may lag the interface.
caveats: Platform feature descriptions here reflect a vendor blog source and may be outdated or specific to certain plans and regions.
Default protections reduce risk but do not transfer all responsibility away from the merchant.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Bot and fraud monitoring for inventory and high-demand drops
cards.summary: Bots create fake accounts and stockpile high-demand products before real shoppers can buy, so inventory protection is a bot-mitigation concern, not just a security one.
cards.use_when: Planning a limited-release, high-demand drop, or investigating inventory that sells out unusually fast with suspicious buyer accounts.
steps: Treat inventory APIs as a defended surface: the source notes bots target API endpoints that handle checkout, inventory and customer account data, not only the storefront front end.
Watch for the specific bot behaviors the source lists in ecommerce: card testing, pricing-data scraping, fake account creation, and stockpiling high-demand products before real shoppers can buy.
Add friction proportional to risk on high-demand releases — for example, requiring authenticated accounts, limiting per-account quantities, and reviewing orders from newly created accounts.

Monitor for early warning signs and act on them: the source describes a case where a platform's bot-detection tool flagged a major bot attack on Maggy London's storefront before any other monitoring system, illustrating the value of detection layered ahead of manual review (single case example).
Keep account-creation defenses in place, since fake accounts are the base layer for hoarding and card testing.
caveats: The Maggy London case is illustrative and does not guarantee similar detection performance.
Inventory protection measures can create friction for legitimate customers; balance against conversion impact.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Four Pillars of Ecommerce Security: Privacy, Integrity, Authentication, Non-Repudiation
cards.summary: Frame a storefront's security posture around four named pillars so controls map to distinct failure modes rather than a vague 'be secure' goal.
cards.use_when: Auditing overall storefront security coverage, or deciding which control category a proposed security project belongs to.
steps: Assess coverage against four distinct pillars: Privacy (preventing unauthorized internal and external access to customer data — encryption, firewalls, antivirus), Integrity (accuracy of customer datasets — phone, address, purchase history), Authentication (proving the business is legitimate and customers are who they claim — 2FA or magic links), and Non-repudiation (neither company nor customer can deny a transaction, typically enforced via digital signatures).
Map each existing control to a pillar; note gaps — for example, encryption addresses Privacy but does nothing for Authentication or Non-repudiation.
For Authentication on the customer side, treat it as two-sided: credibility signals (customer quotes, case studies per the source) plus identity verification at transaction time.
For Non-repudiation, plan how transactions are digitally signed so chargeback disputes and order denials have a verifiable record.
Record which pillar each new security investment serves so overlapping projects are consolidated and uncovered pillars get funded.
caveats: Non-repudiation is a concept the source explains generally; implementing digital signatures is a platform/payment-processor capability that should be verified for your stack.
The source's suggestion to use customer quotes and case studies as 'authentication' evidence is a credibility measure, not a technical control — do not treat it as a substitute for account security.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce security — what it means, common threats, and modern best practices.docx

cards.title: Multilayer Security: CDN Plus MFA as Defense in Depth
cards.summary: Stack independent security layers (notably a machine-learning CDN and multifactor authentication) so compromising one control still leaves others to penetrate.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing storefront defense architecture, especially before high-traffic launches or sales events.
steps: Adopt the source's multilayer principle: add secondary and tertiary controls so an attacker who defeats one layer must still penetrate at least one more before reaching data.
Layer 1 recommended by the source: a Content Delivery Network; favor CDNs that use machine learning to block threats and infectious traffic.
Layer 2: multifactor authentication for employees logging into company systems and for customers logging into loyalty accounts — requiring a second code sent via text, email, or authenticator app.

Add firewalls as a further layer: firewall software and plugins allow trusted traffic while keeping untrusted connections off the site, which the source notes also makes anomaly detection easier and helps block XSS, spam, and SQL injection.
Note that no single layer is sufficient; the value comes from combining controls so failures in one do not expose everything.
caveats: The source does not claim any layer — CDN, firewall, or MFA — is individually sufficient; each can be bypassed.
Verify current CDN threat-blocking capabilities and MFA mechanics against the vendor's current documentation, as these change over time.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce security — what it means, common threats, and modern best practices.docx

cards.title: Preventing E-Skimming at Checkout
cards.summary: Reduce digital skimming risk by keeping web servers patched, vetting ad server code, and updating third-party APIs — and know the shutdown response if skimming is detected.
cards.use_when: Hardening the checkout page and payment flow against payment-data theft, or responding to a suspected checkout compromise.
steps: Understand the threat: e-skimming is stealing credit card and personal data from payment processors by gaining access to checkout pages and capturing payment information as customers type it in real time.
Apply the source's three preventive measures: regularly push patches to your web server, vet your ad server code (injected ad scripts are a common skimming vector), and keep third-party APIs updated.
Recognize that e-skimming can result from XSS, phishing, or brute force attacks, so closing those upstream vectors also reduces skimming exposure.
If already impacted, the source advises checking whether cyber insurance covers losses and shutting down the shopping cart page while investigating and eliminating the source of the compromise.
Treat checkout JavaScript and any third-party scripts loaded on the payment page as the highest-risk surface and inventory them regularly.
caveats: The source's insurance and cart-shutdown guidance is a response outline, not an incident-response plan; consult qualified security and legal resources for a real breach.
HTTPS/SSL alone does not stop e-skimming, since skimmers capture data before encryption in many cases — do not rely on SSL as the control.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce security — what it means, common threats, and modern best practices.docx

cards.title: Reducing XSS and SQL Injection Risk Through Untrusted-Data Discipline
cards.summary: Hinder XSS and SQLi by treating every data-table edit and API integration as untrusted and scanning for vulnerabilities before deployment.
cards.use_when: Reviewing custom storefront, theme, plugin, or API integration code for injection vulnerabilities.
steps: Train developers on the source's core rule: treat all edits to data tables as untrusted — SQL servers store data in tables retrieved by queries, and unprotected servers let attackers inject their own queries to view or change any data.
Adopt modern web development technologies and frameworks that reduce raw query construction and unsafe output rendering.

For XSS — where an attacker inserts malicious code into a page that exposes that page's visitors to phishing or malware — scan regularly for vulnerabilities in your website code and API integrations, and patch quickly.
Vet every third-party API and theme/plugin integration as a potential injection path rather than trusting vendor code by default.
Combine with firewalls, which the source notes help protect against XSS and malicious SQL injections by regulating traffic flow.
caveats: Input validation and output encoding are the general defensive principle; the source only outlines this at a high level, so treat framework-specific implementation guidance as outside this note.
No scanning tool guarantees complete coverage — regular scanning reduces, not eliminates, risk.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce security — what it means, common threats, and modern best practices.docx

cards.title: Defending the Storefront Against Pricing and Inventory Scraping Bots
cards.summary: Combat bots that scrape pricing and inventory or hoard popular items by combining reCAPTCHA, API checks, old-browser blocking, and alerting.
cards.use_when: Protecting product pages, pricing data, and limited-inventory drops from scraping and cart-hoarding bots.
steps: Identify the business harm the source describes: bots scrape sites for pricing and inventory data, and attackers use that to hike prices or add the most popular inventory to their own carts, leaving customers unable to buy — leading to sales declines, negative reviews, and bad press.
Deploy reCAPTCHA tools on the site, particularly on forms and entry points.
Check and monitor your API connections, since bots often access inventory and pricing through APIs rather than rendered pages.
Block older browser versions, which the source recommends as a bot countermeasure.
Set up alerts for the three signals the source flags as bot indicators: unusually high web traffic, failed gift card validations, and repeated failed login attempts.
Review whether your product feed or pricing API exposes full inventory levels to unauthenticated callers.
caveats: CAPTCHA systems generate friction and change over time; verify current reCAPTCHA capabilities and consider accessibility impact before deploying broadly.
The source's alert signals are indicators, not proof of bot activity — corroborate before taking blocking action that could affect real customers.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce security — what it means, common threats, and modern best practices.docx

cards.title: Brute Force Protection for Admin Console and Customer Accounts
cards.summary: Protect the storefront admin panel and loyalty accounts from automated password guessing with strong passwords, rotation, and access limits.
cards.use_when: Securing the admin console, staff logins, or customer loyalty accounts against credential-guessing attacks.
steps: Understand the attack pattern: brute force attacks target an online store's administrator console, using automated scripts to guess every combination of letters, numbers, and characters that could form the password once a connection is established.
Choose a complex, strong password for the admin panel and change it regularly.
Ask customers to use complex, strong passwords for any loyalty accounts they create.
Set up alerts for repeated failed login attempts, which the source lists as a sign of brute force attempts.
Combine with multifactor authentication for employee system logins and customer loyalty logins so a guessed password alone is insufficient.
Note the link the source draws: brute force is one of the upstream causes of e-skimming, so hardening login also reduces payment-data exposure.
caveats: Password rotation intervals are a policy choice; verify current guidance, as forced frequent rotation can also encourage weaker passwords.
Alerts only help if monitored and acted on — pair with lockout or rate-limiting controls.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce security — what it means, common threats, and modern best practices.docx

cards.title: Controlling Spam via Comment Cleanup, CAPTCHA, and Root-Cause Analysis
cards.summary: Reduce spam that injects malicious links through blog comments, social posts, or contact forms by combining CAPTCHA, pruning, and tracing its origin.
cards.use_when: Cleaning up spam on storefront blogs, comment sections, contact forms, or review channels that could carry malicious links.
steps: Recognize spam's dual harm per the source: it prompts users to click malicious links and also slows browsing speeds on the site.
Enable reCAPTCHA on forms — the source notes reCAPTCHAs require users to enter a slightly distorted series of characters that spambots cannot read.
Delete spam comments that get through, keeping form response reports clean.
Perform root cause analysis on spam that gets through to determine where it came from, which informs a durable fix rather than repeated cleanup.
Note the source's observation that spam spreads via email as well as infected links left in blog comments, social media posts, and contact forms.
caveats: CAPTCHA alone does not stop all spam, and the source treats deletion and root-cause analysis as complementary, not optional.
Blog comment and review spam affects SEO and trust as well as security — evaluate both impacts.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce security — what it means, common threats, and modern best practices.docx

cards.title: SSL Certificates: What They Do and Do Not Protect
cards.summary: Use SSL certificates to verify site identity and encrypt connections, while recognizing they do not substitute for checkout-specific skimming controls.
cards.use_when: Establishing or reviewing baseline transport security on a storefront, or explaining to stakeholders what SSL does and does not cover.
steps: Deploy an SSL (secure sockets layer) certificate, which per the source verifies a website's identity and serves as an encrypted connection.
Rely on it to protect credit card details and other sensitive transaction data in transit, and to prevent attackers from using your site as part of a phishing attack.
Treat SSL as one layer rather than the whole program — the source positions it alongside CDNs, firewalls, and antivirus/antimalware as separate best practices.
Combine with checkout-page controls (patching, ad-code vetting, API updates) because SSL does not stop code injected into the checkout page from capturing data before transmission.
On hosted platforms, confirm who provisions and renews the certificate under the platform's shared responsibility model.
caveats: The source does not claim SSL alone secures a storefront; treating it as sufficient would leave skimming and account risks unaddressed.
Certificate provisioning, renewal, and configuration specifics differ by host and change over time — verify against your platform's current documentation.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce security — what it means, common threats, and modern best practices.docx

cards.title: Firewalls as Traffic Regulation for Anomaly Detection
cards.summary: Deploy firewall software or plugins to admit trusted traffic, block untrusted connections, and make anomalies easier to detect before they enter the network.
cards.use_when: Selecting or configuring perimeter controls for a self-hosted or platform storefront.
steps: Install firewall software or plugins that allow trusted traffic while keeping untrusted connections off the ecommerce site.
Use the firewall to regulate traffic flow, which the source notes makes detecting anomalies easier and stops them before they enter the network.
Rely on it particularly against the threats the source names: XSS, spam, and malicious SQL injections.
Pair with a CDN layer and antivirus/antimalware scanning so the firewall is one layer in a multilayer approach rather than a standalone defense.
On hosted platforms, check which firewall functions the platform provides versus what you must add — the source frames this under the shared responsibility model.
caveats: Firewalls do not stop e-skimming injected via third-party scripts loaded in the browser, nor phishing aimed at customers.
Misconfigured rules can block legitimate traffic and affect conversion — monitor for false positives after changes.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce security — what it means, common threats, and modern best practices.docx

cards.title: Inventory of Common Storefront Threat Types and Their Countermeasures
cards.summary: Use a threat-to-countermeasure map covering phishing, malware/ransomware, SQLi, XSS, brute force, e-skimming, spam, bots, and Trojan horses to prioritize storefront defenses.
cards.use_when: Building or reviewing a storefront security threat model and assigning owners to each countermeasure.
steps: Phishing — attacks that trick victims into providing confidential information via email, text, or phone, conveying urgency and mimicking trusted companies. Countermeasure the source highlights for merchants: inform customers you will never email or text to ask for personal information.

Malware/ransomware — malicious software that disrupts or gains unauthorized access; ransomware encrypts files until payment. Counter with antivirus and antispyware, updated systems, and secure authentication.
SQL injection and XSS — address through developer training, treating data-table edits as untrusted, vulnerability scanning, and quick patching.
