Keep your own pages from making excessive storage or resource demands, and avoid embedding untrusted third-party frames that could do so.
When a browser API assumes good-faith use of a limit, ask what happens if the limit is bypassed via multiple origins, repeated calls, or nested frames.
Stay current with browser fixes: the source notes the localStorage issue was eventually fixed in major browsers, highlighting that platform behavior changes over time.
caveats: The localStorage exhaustion issue is described as historical and since fixed in major browsers — verify current behavior rather than assuming the technique still works.
Do not reproduce attacks on systems you don't own; use this as a design-review lens.

cards.title: Scope and govern good-faith security testing of your store
cards.summary: Findings should come from controlled, authorized testing that avoids destroying data or attacking third parties.
cards.use_when: Setting up a pentest, bug bounty, or internal security research program for an ecommerce site, or reviewing what staff and contractors are permitted to test.
steps: Define what is in scope: your own storefront, admin, APIs, and integrations — the source emphasizes don't attack anything that will get you (or the business) in trouble, and explicitly disqualifies findings manufactured by having a friend build an insecure site.

Require responsible disclosure rules: don't act in ways that destroy systems or delete data, and ask before taking uncertain actions. The source points to a published bug-bounty process as a rough template for ground rules.

Recognize that a demonstrated attack is not automatically a responsible test: the source's classroom demos (localStorage exhaustion, clickjacking a camera feed) are illustrations, not procedures to run against live sites.
Set rules for handling sensitive findings — real collected data, credentials, or customer information should be reported through a controlled channel, not circulated.
Decide how findings map to remediation urgency using a vulnerability-versus-exploit distinction.
caveats: The source's policy details are specific to a university course and its bug-bounty program; adapt the principles to your own legal and contractual obligations, which are not covered here.
Testing that impacts live shopper data or third-party services can create legal and customer-harm exposure; get explicit authorization first.

cards.title: Map DNS resolution to counter store-domain hijacking
cards.summary: Walk through the recursive DNS resolution chain so you can identify and defend every point where a storefront domain can be rerouted and validate protection with TLS.
cards.use_when: Hardening your storefront domain, or diagnosing why customers report landing on a look-alike checkout or phishing page for your brand, or selecting DNS providers and records.
steps: Model the resolution chain the browser actually follows: client → recursive resolver → root nameserver → TLD nameserver (e.g. .com) → your domain's authoritative nameserver → IP address. Each hop is an attack surface, because classic DNS queries are plain text.

Enumerate the hijack points: malware editing a customer's local hosts file, a compromised recursive resolver (often the ISP-supplied one), a compromised router, a hacked authoritative nameserver, or a registrar account takeover. Any of these can return a malicious IP and send shoppers to an attacker-controlled server posing as your store.
Mitigate on owned systems: lock registrar accounts with strong unique credentials and MFA, restrict who can edit DNS records, and prefer resolvers that support encrypted DNS where available.

Understand the TLS counter and its limit: HTTPS uses signatures so clients detect the wrong server, but if an attacker answers the domain lookup, a free certificate authority that only verifies domain control can be induced to issue them a valid certificate. Confirm current provider behavior before relying on any specific check.
Validate defensively: from your own environment verify records and certificates resolve and match expectations; do not attempt to hijack third-party domains to test.
caveats: Encrypted-DNS support and certificate-issuance rules change; verify current browser and CA behavior rather than assuming a fixed state.
HTTPS alone does not guarantee the request reached your real server if the domain lookup was subverted during issuance.

cards.title: HTTPS, integrity and authenticity for storefront trust
cards.summary: Explain why TLS/HTTPS gives integrity and authenticity, not just confidentiality, so those properties guide how you protect customer data and admin sessions.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to protect checkout pages, login flows and admin panels, or evaluating what HTTPS actually buys you against tampering and impersonation.
steps: Treat HTTPS as three guarantees: confidentiality, integrity (responses cannot be silently modified without the client detecting it) and authenticity (you are talking to the server holding the certificate's private key).

Use integrity to reason about injected content: an intermediary that wants to alter your checkout page or inject a crypto-miner script cannot do so undetected if they lack the private key matching the served certificate.

Use authenticity to reason about impersonation: a wrong-server attack fails because the attacker cannot present a certificate whose private key they control for your domain — this is the core defense against DNS-hijack phishing.

Do not assume a padlock equals a legitimately-operated store: cheaper CAs verify only that the requester controls the domain, so a hijacked domain can still obtain a valid cert. Combine TLS with registrar hardening and account MFA.
caveats: Confidentiality, integrity and authenticity are distinct properties; the source stresses they come as a set for HTTPS but each addresses a different threat.
Certificate-issuance verification practices vary and change; verify current CA policies.

cards.title: Encrypt DNS queries to protect customer browsing privacy
cards.summary: Understand how plain-text DNS leaks a store's and shoppers' domain lookups to ISPs and how DNS-over-HTTPS reduces that exposure.
cards.use_when: Choosing DNS configuration for your organization or advising on privacy of traffic to and from your store, or evaluating whether ISP DNS behavior affects your customers.
steps: Recognize the privacy risk: classic DNS queries are plain text, so the recursive resolver — often the ISP — can log and even sell lists of domains a user looked up, including which stores and services they visit.

Switch to a provider with an explicit privacy policy stating they do not sell DNS queries, as a partial fix. Note that without encryption, an observing ISP can still see queries even if you point them elsewhere.

Prefer DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) where it is available, which tunnels queries over an encrypted connection so observers cannot read them. The source notes Firefox made DoH a default and other browsers were testing it, and that OS-level support was limited — verify current support before relying on it.

Application to the store: enable DoH at the browser/OS or router level where supported so internal admin lookups and vendor tooling traffic are not trivially readable; assess whether your outbound traffic reveals sensitive internal domains.
Recognize that ISPs sometimes DNS-hijack invalid domains to show ad/search pages; this is a behavior to be aware of, not a control you administer.
caveats: Configuring DoH at the router leaves traffic on the local network visible; setting it only in the browser covers just that browser.
DoH support and default settings change over time; verify the current state of browsers and operating systems.

cards.title: Read HTTP request and response structure to audit store traffic
cards.summary: Parse HTTP's textual request/response format and header model so you can inspect and debug what your storefront actually sends and receives.
cards.use_when: Debugging storefront requests in dev tools, understanding method/header usage when integrating an API or CDN, or auditing whether sensitive data leaks into URLs.
steps: Read a request as: a first line naming the method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.), the requested path/resource, and the HTTP version (commonly 1.1), followed by key-value headers. HTTP/1.1 is plain text and human-readable; HTTP/2 and 3 are binary and not directly typeable.

Read a response as: protocol version and a status code with message, followed by headers and the body. Use the status code category to triage: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.

Leverage extensibility: because headers are just keys and values, servers ignore headers they do not understand, so you can add features (caching, range, conditional requests) without a protocol change.

Account for statelessness: two consecutive requests have no inherent relationship, so anything that looks like state — a login that persists across clicks — is layered on top via mechanisms like cookies, not the base protocol.
For the store: audit whether cart tokens, session IDs or customer identifiers are placed in URLs (which get logged and shared) versus headers or cookies.
caveats: HTTP is transport-agnostic (it can run over channels other than TCP), but TCP is the typical transport; do not assume the transport from the protocol version.
Later HTTP versions are not human-readable; use tooling to inspect them.

cards.title: Use HTTP status codes to drive caching and retry logic
cards.summary: Apply the meaningful status codes — 200/206, 301/302, 304, and 4xx/5xx — to caching, redirect and retry behavior in a storefront.
cards.use_when: Tuning caching/CDN rules, redirects and retry behavior for storefront and checkout endpoints, or diagnosing why a cached page or redirect misbehaves.
steps: For content serving: 200 means success with the full resource; 206 means a partial response to a range request. Range requests let a client fetch a byte offset (e.g. seeking into a video) without downloading the whole file; if a server ignores the range header it falls back to 200 with the whole file, so clients must handle both.

For redirects: understand the 301 vs 302 difference. A permanent 301 says the resource is permanently moved, so the browser caches it and stops asking — which breaks any feature that should land on a different page each visit (e.g. a 'random page' link). Use 302 (temporary) when the destination can vary.

For caching: 304 'not modified' supports conditional requests where the browser sends a version (or a since-date) it already holds and the server replies 304 without resending the body when nothing changed, saving bandwidth. If the client does not include that condition, it gets a 200.
For errors: 4xx means the client's request was wrong (bad URL, no permission) while 5xx means the server erred (uncaught exception) — this distinction tells you whether retrying is worthwhile.
For proxy/gateway layers: 502 (bad gateway), 503 (service unavailable/overloaded) and 504 (timeout) reflect failures between a proxy and backend servers.
caveats: Numeric status meanings come from the protocol spec; specific caching durations and validation values are implementation choices, not fixed numbers.
A 301 that varies by request will silently break; confirm your redirect choice matches the intended caching behavior.

cards.title: HTTP methods and range requests in practice
cards.summary: Place the common request methods and partial-content fetching in context so storefront integrations send the correct verb and handle partial media.
cards.use_when: Choosing GET vs POST/PUT/DELETE for a storefront or API integration, or implementing video/audio delivery and seeking on product pages.
steps: Use GET for requests that fetch a resource and POST/PUT/DELETE for operations that change something. The source treats GET as the common default; do not use GET for actions that mutate state (aligning with the general principle that GET requests should be safe and not change data).
Recognize the request line groups the method, the path (the requested resource name) and the protocol version, then headers follow. In modern dynamic servers the path need not map to a literal file.
For media on PDPs, rely on range requests: the client asks for a byte offset and the server can respond 206 with just that slice, enabling seeking into a video before the whole file downloads.
Build clients to tolerate a 200 response when a range was requested, since servers that do not understand the range header return the full file instead of a 206.
caveats: The source lists common methods and notes others exist; consult the HTTP spec for the authoritative method list and their safety/idempotency properties.
Range behavior depends on server/CDN support; test against your actual delivery stack.

cards.title: Use URL parsing to distinguish commands from user input
cards.summary: Break URLs into scheme, host, port, path, query and fragment so you can build safer routing and detect where user input could be interpreted as structure.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing storefront routing, query-parameter handling, search/filter URLs, or debugging why a URL escaped or failed to resolve.
steps: Decompose a URL into its parts: scheme (protocol), host (server domain), port, path (the requested resource — dynamic today, not necessarily a file), query (key=value pairs starting with ? and separated by &), and fragment (a # anchor scrolling to a labeled point in the page).

In query strings, disambiguate delimiter vs data: if a key or value must contain an ampersand, it must be escaped; otherwise it will be read as a separator. This escaping is the core of where user input can be confused with structure.

Treat this confusion — separating the command from user input — as the root issue behind many web attacks; when building search, filters or redirects from user-supplied values, escape and validate so input cannot become structure.

For prompts longer than the standard fragment behavior: standard fragments only scroll to anchors the page author pre-defined; a newer spec (which the source says was under consideration) allows control-F-style text matching after the hash. Verify current browser support before depending on it.
caveats: Path may point to a real file or be fully dynamic; do not assume filesystem semantics.
The text-matching fragment behavior was described as a proposal, not established; verify current support.

cards.title: Relative vs absolute vs fragment URLs in storefront links
cards.summary: Master how relative, absolute and fragment URLs resolve against the current page so navigation, catalog links and anchors behave predictably.
cards.use_when: Building link generation, breadcrumbs, category pagination or deep links so shoppers land on the intended path rather than a 404.
steps: Full URLs embed the entire address; relative URLs resolve against the current page's location, effectively appending to the current 'folder'.

Watch the trailing slash: on a page ending in '/2019/October', a relative link to 'September' resolves to '/2019/September' (the last path segment is replaced), but if the current URL ended with a trailing slash the resolution differs — the source stresses the trailing slash matters.
Absolute URLs beginning with '/' resolve from the site root, replacing the entire path (e.g. a link to '/events' resolves to same-domain.com/events regardless of the current path).

Fragment URLs append a #fragment to the current URL, scrolling to a matching labeled element on the page — useful for linking to a specific section of a PDP or help page without the author pre-defining an anchor only if the newer matching behavior applies.
For the store: standardize link generation (root-relative for internal links) so category, CMS and templated links do not accidentally drop or carry a path segment and produce 404s.
caveats: Relative resolution quirks (especially trailing slashes) are easy to get wrong; test generated links against real nesting levels.
The source notes a fragment text-matching enhancement was under development; do not assume universal behavior.

cards.title: Treat link/style/script tags as the primary attack surface
cards.summary: Focus security review on <link>, <style> and <script> because these tags load external resources and are where the source says attacks concentrate.
cards.use_when: Reviewing how your storefront loads CSS, JavaScript, fonts and third-party scripts, or setting a content-security and dependency-review policy.
steps: Know the loading model: CSS is loaded externally with <link> and inline with <style>; JavaScript is loaded externally via <script src=...> and inline by pasting it inside <script>. The inconsistency (script vs link) is historical.

Because these tags pull in external and inline code, treat every third-party tag manager, analytics, chat, pixel and hosted font as untrusted code that executes in your storefront's context — this is the surface the source says most attacks use.

When auditing: enumerate every link/style/script (including inline) on a checkout or account page, and decide which are truly necessary, since each is a potential tampering or data-exfiltration vector.
Understand that the web cannot break backwards compatibility, so these historical tag decisions persist and you must design controls around them rather than assuming they will change.
caveats: The source presents these tags as where the class's attacks live; that is a strong emphasis, not a claim that only these tags are ever involved.
Specific mitigations (CSP, SRI) are covered in later material; verify current browser support for any control before relying on it.

cards.title: Distinguish JS language, DOM and Node APIs when auditing code
cards.summary: Separate the JavaScript language spec from browser-provided DOM APIs and Node-provided APIs so you correctly attribute behavior and risk.
cards.use_when: Reviewing storefront script code, blaming or debugging unexpected behavior, or deciding whether code belongs in the browser or a server environment.
steps: Classify each API you encounter: features built into the language itself (e.g. arrays) come from the JS spec; document/createElement-style calls come from the browser's Document Object Model; file-reading and networking calls belong to Node.js, not the browser.
Recognize that the browser supplies DOM APIs because the language alone would have no page to manipulate, and the source attributes most 'bad' APIs to the DOM rather than the language.

For the store: keep browser and server responsibilities distinct — file reads and socket connections belong on the server (Node), never in client-side storefront JavaScript, which should only manipulate the DOM.

Note that Node.js added scripting-language capabilities the browser language lacked — filesystem, HTTP, DNS, sockets, a module system for requiring code, and binary data support (before which everything was strings, awkward for media). Modern JS has absorbed some of these needs.
caveats: Node itself is just 'JavaScript on the command line' with added platform APIs; do not confuse Node's APIs with the language spec.
The source notes JS was famously created quickly (Brendan Eich, ~10 days) and its flexibility was a deliberate trade-off; this is historical context, not a security control.

cards.title: Assume the browser can move and resize windows (pop-up risk)
cards.summary: Recognize that browser APIs like window.open, moveTo and resizeTo mean a loaded page can open pop-ups and move windows, so don't treat such behavior as impossible.
cards.use_when: Assessing how your storefront handles third-party or user-generated scripts, or explaining unexpected pop-up/window behavior to stakeholders.
steps: Note the legacy APIs the source flags: window.open opens a new window (the pop-up API), and moveTo/resizeTo let a page reposition and resize a window; the source notes a browser in 2019 could still do this, and students could build demos making a window follow the cursor.

Treat this as an attack and abuse surface: any script you embed (ads, third-party tags, user-generated content) inherits the page's ability to open pop-ups, which is why script-sourcing policy matters for a storefront.

Practical storefront action: control which scripts load on checkout and account pages, and treat pop-up/open-window behavior from embedded third parties as something to constrain rather than assume impossible.
For users, browsers attempt to restrict pop-up behavior in various versions — but do not assume any given trick is blocked; verify current browser behavior rather than trusting a fixed rule.
caveats: These APIs' actual behavior and trigger restrictions (e.g. requiring a user gesture) vary by browser and change over time; verify the current interface.
The source's window-following demo is an educational demonstration, not a description of a storefront attack.

cards.title: Use range and conditional requests to speed storefront media and content
cards.summary: Explain how partial-content (206) and conditional (304) requests cut bandwidth for media and repeat content delivery on a store.
cards.use_when: Delivering product video/audio and large assets, configuring CDN caching, or debugging repeated full downloads of unchanged pages or images.
steps: Implement range requests for media: a client requests a byte offset (e.g. seeking mid-video or mid-song) and the server can return a 206 with only that slice, avoiding a full sequential download before playback.

Handle the fallback: if a server does not understand the range header, it returns 200 with the whole file, so clients must check the status code and adjust (a 200 when a 206 was expected signals a non-range server).

Implement conditional requests for caching: the browser sends the version (or a since-date) of a resource it holds; the server returns 304 'not modified' without a body if nothing changed, saving bandwidth, or a 200 with fresh content if it changed.
Confirm the mechanism requires the client to include the condition header each time; without it, the server always returns 200.
caveats: The source frames 206 as the reason range requests work; specific offsets and caching windows are implementation choices.
CDN and server range/conditional support varies; test your actual delivery path.

cards.title: Design for statelessness and layer state deliberately
cards.summary: Understand that HTTP is stateless and that any persistent behavior — like a logged-in cart — is state you must knowingly layer on and secure.
cards.use_when: Architecting sessions, carts and login persistence, or reasoning about why two requests have no inherent relationship.
steps: Treat the base protocol as stateless: two consecutive requests have no built-in relationship, so nothing is remembered by default.

Recognize that anything that appears stateful in a real storefront — persisting login across clicks, a cart that survives navigation — means the service deliberately layered state on top of HTTP (via mechanisms like cookies, covered in later material).
When adding state for carts or sessions, decide explicitly what is remembered, for how long, and how it is protected, because the base protocol provides none of these guarantees.
The source notes a server can implement per-visitor behavior (e.g. counting requests) — but that is the application building state, not HTTP holding it.
caveats: The source defers the actual state mechanism (cookies) to later material; the mechanism's security details are not covered here.
Do not assume statelessness means requests are isolated in practice; application-layer state can still couple them.

cards.title: Handle proxy/gateway failure codes for resilient checkouts
cards.summary: Use the 502/503/504 family to reason about proxy-to-backend failures and configure sensible timeouts and retries for storefront infrastructure.
cards.use_when: Operating a storefront behind a load balancer or proxy, setting timeouts and retry policy, or debugging intermittent checkout errors.
steps: Understand the architecture: a proxy can sit in front of many backend servers so users see one server, and big web services scale this way. Failures between the proxy and backends produce specific gateway codes rather than client or server errors.
Map the codes: 502 (bad gateway — the backend is down or unreachable), 503 (service unavailable — temporarily down or overloaded), 504 (timeout — the backend took too long).
Configure the proxy's timeout deliberately: a backend may be online but slow, and the proxy should give up after a bounded time rather than tie up a connection on a never-ending request.
Use the code distinction for retry logic: because these indicate a backend/transient problem, a retry may succeed, whereas a 4xx indicates a client mistake that should not be blindly retried.
caveats: The source presents these as examples of proxy failure modes; specific timeout and retry values are configuration choices, not fixed recommendations.
Exact behavior depends on your proxy/load balancer; verify its timeout and retry semantics.

cards.title: HTTP status codes drive retry and error-handling logic
cards.summary: Use distinct status codes to decide whether an automated or manual request should be retried, fixed, or abandoned.
cards.use_when: Designing error handling for an ecommerce integration (inventory sync, payment webhook, catalog feed) or deciding how storefront client code should react to a failed API call.
steps: Read the response status code before deciding what to do. A 404 means the resource is not there; retrying the same request will not help, so surface a real error or fix the URL.
A 500 means the server had an exception. It is reasonable to retry later with backoff because the failure may be transient.
A 503 service unavailable means the server is temporarily down or overloaded; retry after a delay rather than immediately.
A timeout means the request took too long; decide based on your store's needs whether to retry, degrade gracefully, or alert.
A 400 bad request means the client's request was malformed (the source demonstration removes the required Host header and gets a 400) — fix the request, do not retry unchanged.
Codes exist separately from messages so that machines and humans can branch on a stable, standard signal rather than parse free-text error strings.
Build retry policy per code: retry transient (5xx, timeout), do not retry deterministic client errors (4xx) until the request is corrected.
caveats: The specific meaning of any given code should be verified against current HTTP specifications, which can change; the retry advice here is a design heuristic, not a guarantee of the server's behavior.

cards.title: Use the Host header to route multi-tenant or multi-store requests
cards.summary: Servers rely on the Host header to know which domain or store is being requested when one IP serves many sites.
cards.use_when: Setting up, debugging, or securing a storefront server, reverse proxy, or CDN where multiple domains or brand sites share infrastructure.
steps: Always include the Host header in request tooling and custom HTTP clients. Most servers will not respond without it.

Understand that a single IP address commonly hosts many domains (the source notes a server might serve several sites under one IP). Without a Host header, the server may error (400) or return an arbitrary site.
When writing storefront or integration code that calls backends, pass the intended store's hostname explicitly so requests hit the correct tenant.
When building or configuring a reverse proxy, use the Host header to route traffic to the correct backend store.
In security review, treat Host-header handling as a configuration to validate (mis-routing can send one brand's traffic to another); test on your own infrastructure.
caveats: The source describes this behavior in a general teaching context; exact proxy and server behavior varies by vendor and configuration, so verify against your current platform.

cards.title: Treat User-Agent as a weak signal, not an access control
cards.summary: User-Agent headers can identify crawlers and obvious bad bots for monitoring or coarse blocking, but clients control them so they are not a reliable defense.
cards.use_when: Analyzing storefront traffic, deciding whether to allow or block a bot, or setting up analytics to distinguish search crawlers from scrapers.
steps: Read the User-Agent to understand who is visiting: search engines identify themselves (e.g., Googlebot), command-line tools send recognizable strings like curl.
Use this for analytics and monitoring — e.g., seeing which crawlers or startups are hitting your store — rather than for trust decisions.
Optionally block requests from an obviously abusive user-agent string (the source blocks a scraper called Site Slurper that was downloading an entire site).
Do not rely on User-Agent as security: attackers fully control the header and can impersonate a legitimate browser or crawler.
Pair agent-string filtering with other controls (rate limiting, authentication) rather than treating it as sufficient.
caveats: The source explicitly states User-Agent is not a good defense because clients control it; it is only useful against obvious, lazy visitors. Specific bot user-agent strings change over time and should be verified.

cards.title: Use referer data to see inbound traffic sources
cards.summary: The Referer header tells you the page a visitor came from, useful for understanding traffic sources and off-site links.
cards.use_when: Analyzing acquisition channels or investigating where traffic to a product or landing page originates.
steps: Read the Referer request header to learn which page the user was on before requesting your page.
Use it to measure how many visitors arrive from a given external site and to attribute traffic sources.

Recognize that the header is historically misspelled as 'referer' in the HTTP standard and is unlikely to be corrected because changing it would break existing code — this reflects the web's strong preference for backward compatibility over cleaning up old decisions.
Keep in mind the header is client-supplied and can be stripped or spoofed, so treat it as one signal, not a definitive attribution method; supplement with server-side tracking.
When building analytics for a store, log Referer to help identify which partner, ad, or site drove a visit.
caveats: Referer is client-controlled and can be absent or falsified; privacy tools and policies may strip it, so do not treat it as authoritative.

cards.title: Use request headers for content negotiation and language
cards.summary: Accept-Language and compression headers let you return the right localized or compressed response for each visitor.
cards.use_when: Implementing storefront localization, serving translated product pages, or optimizing response size for faster page loads.
steps: Read the Accept-Language header to detect a visitor's preferred language and vary the response (the source demo requests Spanish, then Arabic, and gets back localized content).
Use Accept headers to decide response format — for example return HTML only when the client accepts HTML, and avoid sending a format the client cannot handle.
Advertise and honor compression: a client can indicate it understands compressed (e.g., gzip) responses, so the server can compress to reduce payload size.
Control connection and caching behavior with headers (keep connections open for multiple requests for performance; use conditional requests to fetch only if changed since a date).
Verify your current framework and CDN behavior, since which headers are honored varies by stack.
caveats: Header names and supported values are version- and vendor-dependent; confirm against current specifications and your platform's documentation.

cards.title: Control caching with response headers to avoid stale or wrong content
cards.summary: Response cache-control headers plus Vary prevent one user from receiving another user's cached page.
cards.use_when: Configuring caching for product pages, localized content, or any personalized storefront response served to many visitors.
steps: Use cache-control to say a response may be cached, or to forbid caching entirely for sensitive or personalized content that must not be saved on the user's machine.
Use an Expires value to instruct the client to discard a cached copy after a specific date when you know a new version will be published.

Set the Vary header to list the request headers that affect the response (e.g., language). The client stores those header values with the cached copy and reuses the cache only when the new request's headers match exactly.

Worked example from the source: if a page is cached under a Spanish Accept-Language setting, a later Arabic request for the same URL must not reuse it — Vary on the language header prevents the wrong-language page being served.
Apply the same reasoning to any variable that changes the page (locale, device, logged-in state) and treat those as cache-key dimensions.
caveats: Vary on too many headers degrades cache hit rate; balance correctness against performance. Specific header handling differs across CDNs and frameworks — verify current behavior.

cards.title: Serve large files as streams instead of buffering
cards.summary: Stream files to responses so large product images or downloads don't consume memory and delay delivery.
cards.use_when: Serving large assets (images, videos, downloadable catalogs) from your store's backend or implementing file endpoints.
steps: Instead of reading an entire file into memory and then sending it, open a read stream and pipe it directly to the response object (the source uses createReadStream piped to the HTTP response).
This sends bytes across the socket as they are read, so a very large file (the source cites a 1 GB example) does not require holding the whole thing in RAM before responding.
Use this pattern for any large asset so the first bytes reach the client sooner and memory use stays bounded.

Watch for the stream lifecycle: in raw-socket demos the connection may stay open after the response because the client never closed it or the server didn't signal connection close; explicitly manage connection close where relevant.
Verify your framework's current streaming API, since method names and conventions change between versions.
caveats: The source demonstrates this with Node's file-system streams; the specific API is version-dependent and should be checked against current documentation.

cards.title: Understand a page load as many chained requests
cards.summary: One URL triggers an HTML request followed by many sub-resource requests, and minimizing round trips matters for storefront performance.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing slow product pages, optimizing page load, or explaining why a storefront makes so many network calls.
steps: Recognize the full flow: DNS lookup → open a TCP connection to the IP on the web port → send a GET → receive HTML → parse HTML → build the DOM → render → then request missing sub-resources (CSS, JS, images).
Expect sub-resource responses to potentially generate more requests, repeating until all resources are resolved and the page finishes rendering.
Use the browser's developer tools Network tab to inspect exactly which request and response headers the browser sends and receives on your store pages.
Reduce round trips where you can — fewer requests and earlier requests generally improve perceived load time.
Use this model when auditing a storefront with an agent or performance tool so failures are traced to the right request, not just the page.
caveats: The exact rendering pipeline varies by browser and is described here in simplified teaching form; measure with current tooling rather than assuming a fixed sequence.

cards.title: Never trust client-controlled cookies for identity or authorization
cards.summary: Cookies are client-controlled, so storing a username or role in a plain cookie lets anyone impersonate another user.
cards.use_when: Reviewing authentication or session handling for a storefront, admin panel, or customer account system before shipping.
steps: Recognize the vulnerability: if the server trusts a plain cookie like username=Alice to identify the user, anyone can edit the cookie to username=Bob and be treated as Bob (the source demonstrates this directly).
Treat all cookie content as attacker-controlled input. Do not use a client-set value as proof of identity or authorization.
Apply the principle 'you cannot trust the client': users can modify any client-side state and skip the steps your app expects.
Validate on the server side: check the identity against a server-held session or signed token rather than reading an unverified value.
Be aware that many real sites have stored important data in cookies this way; audit your own session design for the same flaw.
caveats: This is about plain, unsigned cookies; the correct fix (signing or server-side sessions) is covered separately. Cookie attributes and same-site rules also matter and should be verified.

cards.title: Sign cookies so tampering is detectable
cards.summary: Use a signing algorithm and verify the tag server-side so a modified cookie is rejected.
cards.use_when: Designing session cookies for a storefront or agent integration where you need tamper-evident client-held state.
steps: Understand the primer: a signing scheme has a generator producing a public key and a secret key, a signer that takes the secret key and a value and outputs a tag, and a verifier.
When the client returns the value, it also returns the tag. The server verifies the value against the tag using the verification key so it can detect whether the value was changed.
Apply this so the browser can hold, e.g., username=Alice and the server can be confident the value was not edited to username=Bob.
Keep the secret key server-side; never expose it to the client.
Distinguish signing from encryption: signing detects tampering, it does not hide the value.
Verify your framework's current signing API and key management before relying on it.
caveats: The source gives an introductory overview, not a full crypto recipe; correct implementation details (algorithm choice, key storage, rotation) require current, authoritative documentation.

cards.title: Clear a cookie by re-sending it with a past expiry
cards.summary: There is no direct 'delete cookie' call; you clear a cookie by setting the same name with an expiry date in the past.
cards.use_when: Implementing logout or session invalidation on a storefront or customer account system.
steps: To log a user out, send a Set-Cookie with the same cookie name and any value, plus an expiration date in the past (the source uses 1970-01-01).
The browser sees the past date and deletes the cookie. The source notes there is no built-in clear operation — this expiry trick is the mechanism.
The cookie name must match exactly for the clear to work; verify the path/scope also matches so the right cookie is removed.
After clearing, redirect the user back to a sensible page (e.g., home) as the source does.
Remember that logout is only effective if the server does not also honor a still-valid token elsewhere; invalidate server-side session state where you maintain it.
caveats: Cookie attributes (path, domain, secure, same-site) affect whether the clear takes effect; verify against current browser behavior.

cards.title: Sessions exist because HTTP is stateless
cards.summary: Cookies let a server tie a series of requests to one user, enabling login, carts, and preferences.
cards.use_when: Designing cart persistence, login persistence, or any storefront feature that must remember state across page loads.
steps: Understand that HTTP itself is stateless: without a mechanism, the server cannot tell that two requests come from the same user.
Use a session — a set of data the server keeps about a user across requests — to solve this.
Implement it by having the server set a cookie the browser returns on subsequent requests; the server matches those requests to the stored session.
Apply this to real storefront needs: staying logged in while browsing, keeping a shopping cart populated as a visitor moves between pages, and remembering preferences such as dark mode.
Note the same mechanism is used for cross-site tracking by ad servers; be mindful of privacy expectations and rules when you use cookies for identification.
caveats: Cookies are the most common session mechanism but not the only one; server-side sessions and tokens have different tradeoffs. Privacy regulations affect cookie use and should be checked.

cards.title: Recognize ambient authority and its limits
cards.summary: Ambient authority lets a cookie automatically authorize every request, which is convenient but must be scoped and protected.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much access a logged-in customer or an automated agent gets without re-authenticating each action.
steps: Understand ambient authority: access control is based on a global, persistent property of the requester (the cookie sent on every request), so the user is not re-proving identity every time.
This convenience is why you stay logged in while browsing and why a like button doesn't require re-entering a password each time; the alternative (re-authenticating every action) is impractical.
Accept the tradeoff: because the cookie carries the authority, protecting it becomes critical — anyone who obtains or forges the cookie inherits that authority.
Scope authority narrowly so a stolen or misused credential grants the least access needed, and combine with signing and expiration.
Note the alternative ambient-authority mechanisms exist (IP-based, built-in HTTP auth), but cookies are by far the most common on the web.
caveats: Ambient authority is inherently broad; the source treats cookies as the dominant web mechanism but notes IP-based and HTTP-auth approaches exist and are used in narrower cases.

cards.title: Use built-in HTTP authentication and IP checks only in narrow cases
cards.summary: Alternative ambient-authority mechanisms (IP address, built-in browser auth) are limited and often unsuitable for storefronts.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to use IP allow-listing (e.g., for an internal admin tool) or deciding against built-in browser auth for customer login.
steps: IP-based authentication grants access based on the source IP of the request (the source cites libraries allowing access only from campus).
Recognize its weakness: it can be bypassed if a user routes traffic through a machine in the allowed range, and it is hard to make reliable because TCP connections involve a round trip.
Understand built-in HTTP authentication as the old browser username/password prompt: it was envisioned as the original web login but is inflexible in UI and experience, so cookies became the norm.
For a customer-facing storefront, prefer cookie-based sessions with proper signing; reserve IP checks for tightly controlled internal or partner access.
Verify current browser and platform behavior before depending on any of these.
caveats: The source marks built-in HTTP auth and some IP-based approaches as rarely appropriate; specifics vary by environment and should be validated.

cards.title: Parse form bodies and cookies with framework middleware
cards.summary: Use body-parser and cookie-parser so you get clean objects instead of manually parsing raw request text.
cards.use_when: Building a storefront login, checkout form handler, or any endpoint that receives posted form data or reads cookies.
steps: Raw form submissions arrive as URL-encoded key/value text (e.g., username=Alice&password=...), which is tedious to parse by hand.
Add a body parser middleware so the request exposes a clean body object with the submitted keys and values (the source parses username and password).
Add a cookie parser middleware so requests expose a cookies object with all cookies on the request, instead of parsing the Cookie header yourself.
Use these parsed values in your route logic to compare credentials or read session state.
Verify the current middleware package names and setup, since these libraries and their APIs change over time.
caveats: The source uses specific npm packages during a live demo; the exact module names and usage should be confirmed against current documentation.

cards.title: Routes and request/response objects structure a storefront backend
cards.summary: Express-style routes match method plus URL and hand you a request and response object for reading inputs and sending results.
cards.use_when: Implementing storefront endpoints such as login, logout, product pages, or cart actions.
steps: Create a server and have it listen on a chosen port; that makes it an HTTP server.
Define routes as conditional handlers: when the request method and URL match (e.g., POST /login), run the associated function.
Match the method correctly — a login form submits via POST, so the route must be POST, not GET.
Read inputs from the request object (body, headers, cookies) and write outputs through the response object.
Use a development auto-restart tool so the server picks up file changes, speeding iteration on store features.
Verify current framework APIs, since these evolve.
caveats: The source demonstrates with Express and nodemon in a teaching context; API details are version-specific.

cards.title: Session tokens need server-side revocation, not just signatures
cards.summary: Signed cookies can't be invalidated on logout; store session IDs server-side so logout and remote session kill actually work.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing how logged-in customers stay logged in — login, logout, 'log out of all devices', and admin account sessions for your storefront.
steps: Recognize the failure mode: a stateless signed cookie or signed session ID remains valid forever because the server holds no record to delete. A stolen cookie keeps working even after the customer logs out and changes their password.

Issue a random session ID instead of a signed self-contained token when you need revocability. On login, generate the ID and store a mapping from session ID to user (plus anything else you want to track) in server-side storage such as a sessions table or cache.
On each request, look the presented session ID up in that store. If it's missing or unrecognized, treat the visitor as logged out.
On logout, delete that session ID entry from the store. Now the cookie the browser holds no longer matches anything, so it can't be reused.
Store more than a user name in the session record if useful — the mapping can hold an object of arbitrary complexity for real systems.

Enable a 'your active sessions' page by listing the customer's stored sessions and letting them delete individual entries, which supports remotely killing a session left open on a shared or friend's device.
caveats: If malware is persistently on the customer's device watching everything, even revocable sessions can't help — that is out of scope for this defense.
The source presents signing as wrong for session identity specifically, not as useless generally.

cards.title: Session IDs must come from a large cryptographic random space
cards.summary: Sequential or guessable session IDs let attackers enumerate into other customers' accounts; generate 128-bit random values instead.
cards.use_when: Implementing how your store generates session identifiers for customer or admin logins.
steps: Never use sequential counters or low-entropy values for session IDs. If IDs run 0, 1, 2..., an attacker who is issued a low number can simply try nearby values and land in another customer's session.

Generate session IDs from a cryptographically secure random source. In Node, use the crypto module's randomBytes with 16 bytes (128 bits of entropy) and convert the buffer to a string, because cookie values are strings.
Sanity-check by logging in as two different users and confirming the IDs look completely unrelated.
Accept that collision between two randomly generated 128-bit IDs is not a realistic concern, so you don't need elaborate collision handling.
Note the caveat that signing the session ID also blocks guessing, but the source treats signing as a detour here — the simpler fix is a sufficiently large random space plus server-side storage.
caveats: If session IDs are never stored server-side, even strong randomness doesn't give you logout revocation.
Reusing keys across different algorithms or purposes is discouraged — signing is presented as unsuitable for sessions, not as a general pattern to reuse.

cards.title: Use signed cookies only for values users must not alter
cards.summary: Signing proves a value wasn't tampered with; it is the right tool for user-editable-but-trusted data like a discount code, not for sessions.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a value stored in a customer's browser cookie may be trusted by your store — e.g. a promotional discount, a cart attribute, or a preference.
steps: Understand what signing gives you: correctness means a valid value always verifies; security means an attacker who fabricates a value or tag can essentially never pass verification. The signature is not secret — the client can read it — but it prevents modification.

Apply signing when the client knowing the value is fine but changing it is not. Example from the source: set discount=20 in a cookie and sign it, so the server can confirm the customer didn't edit their browser to discount=100.
Reject altering the value: if the customer or their tooling changes the signed value or the tag, verification fails and you should not honor the discount.

Note that signing does not stop sharing — if someone forwards the whole signed cookie to a friend, the friend gets the same discount. The source suggests possibly embedding the user name in the signed blob to bind it, with caveats.
Do not use signing as the mechanism for session identity, because a signed token can't be destroyed and logout can't invalidate it.
caveats: Signing hides nothing; the value stays readable in the browser.
Signed values remain valid indefinitely — combine signed cookies with server-side records when revocation matters.
Framework shortcuts exist (e.g. Express cookie signing via a secret string plus signed-cookie parsing) but the mechanics still reduce to generate keypair, sign, verify.

cards.title: Crawl your own checkout flow for third-party script exposure
cards.summary: Cookies are readable by scripts and the whole security model treats them as a special, weaker case — audit who can touch your session cookies.
cards.use_when: Reviewing which tags, pixels, analytics tools, chat widgets, and third-party scripts run on your storefront's logged-in pages and checkout flow.
steps: Map every third-party script loaded on pages where a logged-in session cookie exists — marketing pixels, chat, analytics, A/B tools. Any of them can read document.cookie in that page context.

Test directly: in your own browser's dev tools on your site, open the console and evaluate document.cookie while logged in. Whatever the script could see, an attacker who lands script on the page could also see.

Remember the source's demonstration: an injected image whose src points at an attacker's URL fires a request that carries the cookie, exfiltrating it. Treat any script-reading capability as equivalent to exfiltration capability.
If a cookie only needs to be sent back to the server (session, auth), add the HttpOnly attribute when setting it so document.cookie can't read it.
Don't use HttpOnly on values your own front-end script must read (e.g. a theme preference) — those are typically not sensitive and don't belong in cookies anyway.
HTTPS prevents the on-path sniffing variant of session hijacking; it does not prevent script-based exfiltration, so do both.
caveats: Historically, unencrypted (HTTP) requests exposed session IDs to anyone watching traffic; a 2010 Firefox monitor-mode extension demonstrated collecting cookies from open Wi-Fi. Treat HTTPS-everywhere as the modern baseline.
HttpOnly does not defend against a server that itself is compromised or against other server-side leaks.
Older 'Path' scoping is a lie: pages under a different path on the same host can reach a cookie if they run code you can reach with same-origin DOM access.

cards.title: Prefer HTTPS and the Secure cookie attribute for every storefront request
cards.summary: Unencrypted requests expose session cookies to on-path observers; HTTPS everywhere removes the vulnerability rather than mitigating it.
cards.use_when: Configuring transport security and cookie attributes for your storefront, especially login and any page where a customer is authenticated.
steps: Serve the whole site over HTTPS, not just the login POST. The source's contrast is instructive: the old pattern encrypted only the password submission, then returned an unencrypted session ID used on all subsequent requests — making the session ID the weak point.

When a site still has mixed HTTP/HTTPS pages (deductible in legacy stacks), mark cookies with the Secure attribute so the browser refuses to send them over unencrypted connections. That means the cookie isn't leaked in the clear; the customer is simply treated as logged out on the insecure page.
Treat HTTPS-everywhere as the real remedy and Secure/EOL HTTP pages as transitional mitigation.

Recognize the failure case the source describes: an attacker on the same network grabs the session ID from plaintext traffic, replays it to the server, and is served the private page as though they were the customer. No amount of good session ID generation prevents this if the token travels in the clear.
caveats: HTTPS does not protect against script-based cookie theft or the cookie's odd same-origin behavior — those need HttpOnly and careful isolation.
Modern browsers increasingly force HTTPS; verify current behavior before relying on mixed-mode assumptions.

cards.title: Scope cookies with Domain and consider subdomain isolation for your store
cards.summary: Cookies are shared across subdomains by default only when you set Domain; treat each host as isolated unless you deliberately widen scope.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether login sessions on your shop subdomain should be visible to other hosts you control (blog, help center, marketing site).
steps: Understand the default: a cookie set by login.yourshop.com is limited to that subdomain unless you add Domain= yourshop.com, which broadens it to all subdomains.
Only set Domain when you genuinely need the cookie across hosts — for example a shared login across shop and support subdomains.
For isolation, rely on the same-origin triple the source describes: protocol + host name + port. Different subdomains count as different hosts, so separate hosts do not automatically share access.
A practical pattern the source notes: use a distinct subdomain to isolate a component that you don't want sharing cookies with the rest of the site.
Re-examine third-party or legacy integrations that set Domain broadly — that widens the blast radius of any script-based cookie theft.
caveats: Never widen scope without understanding what other services share that subdomain.
Host-based isolation depends on all your hosts being served as separate origins (protocol/host/port differ), so don't accidentally flatten them.

cards.title: Treat cookie Path as broken and design defenses without it
cards.summary: Path was meant to limit a cookie to a URL prefix, but a page under another path can read it if you can reach its DOM; do not rely on it for isolation.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether path-scoped cookies protect a store's admin panel, embedded login, or a differently-scoped part of a site.
steps: Know what Path is intended to do: set Path=/blog so a cookie is only sent on requests whose URL begins with /blog, keeping it out of the rest of the site.

Recognize the established failure: if an attacker can reach the other path's DOM, they can read the cookie even though it was meant to be isolated. The source's visual demonstration: on a different site under the same web host, construct an iframe pointing to the target path, append it (optionally hidden), access iframe.contentDocument, and read document.cookie — because the same-origin policy allowed it.
Do not treat Path as a security boundary.
Use genuinely isolating structure instead — separate hosts/subdomains, HttpOnly cookies for server-only values, and server-side session records — rather than URL subtleties.
caveats: The demo worked because the two paths shared protocol, host, and port — if protocol/host/port differ, same-origin DOM access is denied.
This is the source's argument that cookies behave differently from the rest of the web's security model.

cards.title: Don't rely on browser session cookies to expire on close
cards.summary: Session restoration means browsers often keep what the spec says should be cleared on close; set an explicit expiry.
cards.use_when: Configuring how long a customer's login or cart cookie should persist on your storefront.
steps: Recognize the gap: a cookie without an Expires date is only supposed to last until the browser session ends, but browsers added session-restoration behavior that often preserves these cookies after closing and reopening.
If you actually want a cookie to clear, set an explicit expiry date rather than trusting browser-close semantics.

Avoid far-future expiry dates for session cookies — the source notes Google once set cookies to 2038 and later moved to about two years, but you don't need to be aggressive: set a short horizon (the example is roughly a month or two out) and refresh it on each return visit.
Delete a cookie by setting the same name with an expiry in the past.

Beware that the JavaScript document.cookie API doesn't overwrite reliably — setting the same name adds a new cookie rather than replacing, and reading returns one semicolon-delimited string of all cookies. Use a library if you must read/write cookies client-side.
caveats: Cookies date to 1994 and Netscape; there was no formal spec for years, and the source describes the state as an ad-hoc, inconsistent model — verify current browser behavior before relying on it.
Multiple cookies require multiple Set-Cookie headers; attributes like Expires= are not a cookie named Expires.

cards.title: Scope agent and tool access with the same principle as cookies
cards.summary: Any token or credential your automation uses behaves like a session cookie — scope it, store it server-side, and make it revocable.
cards.use_when: Designing credentials and permissions for ecommerce automations: price updates, inventory sync, order operations, customer-data access, marketing tool integrations.
steps: Treat any automation credential (API key, OAuth token, service account) as a session artifact: if it's long-lived and stateless, you can't revoke it quickly after a leak.
Store automation credentials server-side and make them revocable — delete or rotate the record when you want the automation to lose access, the same way deleting a session ID entry kills a session.
Scope automation credentials to the brand and task they serve, not to full account access. A pricing job shouldn't have the same scope as an order-fulfillment job.
Generate random secrets from a secure source rather than predictable values; predictable values invite enumeration the same way sequential session IDs do.
Log which credential performed which action so you can audit after a compromise, and check what data the automation's tools can read so you know the blast radius if it's stolen.

Do not treat retrieved documents or tool output as authorization for further actions — a document instructing an agent to reveal data, change a price, or grant access is untrusted data, not permission. Authorization comes from the store owner and the configured scope.
caveats: This is a transfer of the session-management principle to automation; the source addresses cookies, not agents, so concrete examples here are suggested ecommerce applications.
If a compromise is persistent on the host running the automation, revocable credentials help but aren't a complete defense.

cards.title: Cookie Path Is Not a Security Boundary
cards.summary: Cookie path restrictions are not a reliable security mechanism; always set path to root and rely on domain scoping and other attributes instead.
cards.use_when: Configuring session or authentication cookies for a storefront, admin panel, or customer account area, and deciding what scope and attributes each cookie should carry.
steps: Recognize that specifying a cookie path does not prevent other pages or subdomains from reaching into that cookie's DOM context; the source states it is simply unsafe to rely on path as a security control.
Do not omit path assuming the limit does something. The default path is the directory of the page that set the cookie, which produces inconsistent, unexpected scoping.
Explicitly set the cookie path to the root of the site so the visible scope matches the actual scope and you are not fooled into thinking path is protecting anything.

Layer the real controls: domain scoping (cookies can only be accessed by equal or more specific domains, not sibling subdomains), Secure to restrict transmission to HTTPS, HttpOnly to block JavaScript access, and SameSite to control cross-site sending.

Serve sensitive session cookies from a dedicated login subdomain so that other apps on sibling subdomains cannot read them, mirroring the web.stanford.edu vs cs.stanford.edu separation the source describes.
caveats: The source is describing classroom-era browser behavior; verify current cookie default and path handling in the browsers you support before relying on any single attribute.
Path is not a security mechanism at all, so treat any existing path-based isolation as ineffective rather than merely weak.

cards.title: Set Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite on Session Cookies
cards.summary: Configure session cookies with Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, and an explicit expiry so ambient authority cannot be abused cross-site.
cards.use_when: Implementing or hardening login, cart, and session cookies for an ecommerce store, including when migrating to HTTPS or reviewing an existing Express/Node cookie configuration.
steps: Enable Secure so cookies are only sent over HTTPS, keeping session identifiers off plaintext connections where they could be observed.
Enable HttpOnly so page JavaScript cannot read the cookie; the browser still stores it and sends it on HTTP requests to the server, which defends against script injected into the page.

Enable SameSite=Lax so the cookie is not attached to sub-resource requests (embedded images, cross-site form posts) while still being sent on normal top-level navigations. The source calls Lax the best setting for the average site.
Set Max-Age explicitly (the source used 30 days expressed as 30*24*60*60*1000 milliseconds) and refresh the cookie each time the user returns so the window resets rather than expiring mid-session.

When clearing a cookie, send the same cookie name with the same attributes (HttpOnly, SameSite, path, domain) and an expiry in the past; otherwise the browser treats it as a different cookie and the original remains.
caveats: SameSite=Strict is more aggressive and drops cookies even on top-level links from other sites, so users clicking a link from an email or blog may appear logged out; the source calls this probably too aggressive for the average site but plausible for finance.

SameSite=Lax breaks legitimate embedding use cases such as third-party comment widgets and ad tracking; the source notes Google has proposed defaulting to Lax and requiring Secure on SameSite=None cookies.

In the source's live demo, SameSite did not take effect while the attacker used a raw localhost IP; it behaved correctly once the attacker site used a real-looking hostname, indicating hostname versus IP matters for cross-site classification.

cards.title: Convert Cookie Exfiltration to a Defensive Recognition Checklist
cards.summary: Understanding when a browser will attach a cookie to a request lets you identify which storefront endpoints are vulnerable to ambient-authority abuse.
cards.use_when: Reviewing state-changing storefront or admin endpoints (cart mutations, order creation, address or email changes, refunds, password reset) for cross-site request exposure.
steps: Note the source's key threat: a browser automatically attaches cookies to any request matching the cookie's domain, regardless of which page initiated the request, so a request can carry the user's authority without the user intending it.
Identify which of your endpoints change state using only cookie-based authentication and no per-request secret. These are the candidates for abuse.

Understand the classic cross-site request forgery pattern the source demonstrates: a hidden form on an unrelated page posts to your transfer/checkout endpoint, the browser attaches the victim's session cookie, and the server processes it as a legitimate user action.

Recognize that the source's demo worked even though the request used POST, and worked with the form hidden inside an iframe with a prefilled recipient and amount so the victim never sees it and is not navigated away.

Treat your own ecommerce state-changing endpoints the same way: if a cross-site page can make the browser submit a valid form with the victim's cookies, the endpoint is exploitable. Apply defense in depth rather than assuming POST alone is protection.
caveats: The source explicitly states that switching to POST does not stop the attack; forms can be submitted cross-site, which the presenter calls a legacy exception that flies in the face of the same-origin policy.

The severity scales with the privilege of the logged-in user: the source notes that hijacking an admin session can allow creating new admin users or running server-side commands, so weight admin endpoints accordingly.

cards.title: Prefer Tokens Over Ambient Cookie Authority for State Changes
cards.summary: Reduce reliance on ambient cookie authority for sensitive actions by requiring an explicit per-request token, since browsers attach cookies automatically.
cards.use_when: Designing defensive controls for high-value ecommerce operations such as placing orders, changing stored payment methods, issuing refunds, or editing admin permissions.
steps: Accept the source's framing: ambient authority from cookies is convenient because every request is automatically authorized, but that same automatic behavior is what enables unwanted cross-site actions.

For sensitive endpoints, do not allow authorization to rest on cookies alone. Require an additional value that a cross-site attacker cannot predict or obtain, in the spirit of the CSRF defense the source promises to cover later.
Verify the request's origin context rather than trusting that a valid session cookie means the user intended the request.
Prefer moving the most dangerous operations to server-rendered flows or out-of-band confirmation, and scope authority narrowly so a hijacked session cannot reach operations beyond the task at hand.
Keep the browser's SameSite behavior as one layer, but the source cautions it is not a complete solution, so do not treat it as the only control.
caveats: The source does not provide a full CSRF token recipe in this section; it explicitly notes SameSite is one defense that is not a complete solution and defers the rest.

The source's demo defense appeared to work once the attacker used a hostname rather than a raw IP, so test your specific deployment rather than assuming the browser will classify your attacker surface as cross-site.

cards.title: SameSite Lax versus Strict: Choose by Funnel Impact
cards.summary: Select SameSite policy by weighing cross-site abuse protection against legitimate embedded and referral flows your store depends on.
cards.use_when: Deciding the SameSite setting for storefront session cookies when your site relies on embedded widgets, affiliate links, email campaign links, or third-party checkout embeds.
steps: Use the source's definitions: None always attaches cookies; Lax blocks cookies on sub-resource requests from other sites but sends them on top-level navigations; Strict never sends cookies to a site the user arrived at from elsewhere, including top-level navigations.

For a typical store with email and affiliate traffic, prefer Lax: a user clicking a link from your campaign email should arrive logged in, while hidden cross-site form posts and embedded sub-resource requests should not carry the session cookie.

Reserve Strict for high-assurance contexts such as finance or admin consoles, accepting that a user clicking a link from an external blog or social post will land logged out in that tab even though they are logged in elsewhere.

Audit what breaks under Lax: the source's examples are third-party comment widgets that appear logged out and ad-tracking cookies that want to attach to every request; enumerate your own embeds before switching.

Plan for defaults to change: the source cites a Google proposal to make Lax the default and require Secure on explicit SameSite=None cookies, so review cookie configuration before relying on legacy None behavior.
caveats: The source calls Strict almost too aggressive for the average site and notes it can confuse users who are logged in elsewhere but appear logged out after clicking a link.

The source's demo defense appeared to work once the attacker used a hostname rather than a raw IP, so test your specific deployment rather than assuming the browser will classify your attacker surface as cross-site.

cards.title: Why Cross-Site POSTs Still Reach Your Endpoints
cards.summary: Forms are a legacy exception to the same-origin policy, so a cross-site page can submit a valid form to your server and the browser will attach the victim's cookies.
cards.use_when: Assessing whether a hidden cross-site form could trigger a state change on your order, account, or admin endpoints even though modern fetch requests would be blocked.
steps: Classify your request paths: fetch/XHR calls are governed by the same-origin policy and a cross-site caller cannot read the response, but a plain HTML form submission from another origin is still allowed to reach your server.
For each state-changing endpoint reachable by a simple form post (no custom headers, standard content types), assume a hidden cross-site form can reach it with the victim's cookies attached.
Do not rely on the attacker being unable to read the response. The source stresses that the damage is done when the server processes the request; the attacker does not need to see the result.
Reduce the exposed surface by requiring values a cross-site form cannot supply, by verifying origin context, and by keeping privileged operations off simple form-reachable routes.
Note the source's observation that many sites still use plain HTML forms with JavaScript interception for better UX; the plain-form fallback is what keeps this legacy hole open.
caveats: The source describes this as a backwards-compatibility exception nobody wanted to break, not an intentional feature; it may change in future browser behavior, so verify current handling.

The source's demo defense appeared to work once the attacker used a hostname rather than a raw IP, so test your specific deployment rather than assuming the browser will classify your attacker surface as cross-site.

cards.title: Same-Origin Policy: What It Allows, Blocks and Leaves Open
cards.summary: The same-origin policy blocks cross-origin DOM access and response reading but permits embedding, navigation and resource loading, so map your storefront's cross-origin interactions against that boundary.
cards.use_when: Reviewing storefront widgets, embeds, iframes, third-party scripts, and CDN resource references to understand what cross-origin behavior is expected and what would be a vulnerability.
steps: Define an origin as the tuple of protocol, hostname and port. If any component differs, the two pages are different origins; the browser enforces this consistently and the source notes it is implemented reliably across browsers.

Blocked by policy: reading another origin's response body via fetch (the source shows the CORS error and explains the browser refuses to hand back the result because cookies would be attached), and reaching into an embedded document (contentDocument returns null).

Allowed despite being cross-origin: linking from one site to another, embedding another site in an iframe, navigating an embedded frame to a new destination, and embedding resources such as images or shared JavaScript from a CDN.

Watch for gaps the source flags: form submissions cross origins (which is how the CSRF attack worked), and cookies use a looser domain-only notion of scope than the same-origin policy, which is why the two rules diverge.

When you add a third-party embedded widget or shared CDN script, note that you are deliberately granting a cross-origin resource a position in your page; there is no same-origin protection inside that relationship.
caveats: The source notes the policy is sometimes too narrow (login.stanford.edu cannot share with cs.stanford.edu despite related ownership) and sometimes too broad (two sites from different organizations on the same origin are treated as fully trusted).
The source warns it is not enforced for legacy features like form submission, so knowing which features are exempt is necessary to know where your site is vulnerable.
Historical browser behavior: verify current same-origin and cookie scoping rules rather than assuming the classroom-era behavior still holds.

cards.title: Replace legacy document.domain relaxation with explicit messaging
cards.summary: Treat legacy origin relaxation as migration work rather than a new storefront integration pattern.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a legacy storefront, admin subdomain, or partner integration can rely on document.domain to share cookies or DOM access across subdomains.
steps: Inventory legacy widgets that assign document.domain or depend on sibling-origin DOM access.
Prefer explicit postMessage communication between named origins.
Validate sender origin, expected window and message schema; do not accept wildcard trust for sensitive messages.
Test the migration with actual embedded checkout, account and support flows.
caveats: The lecture describes historical browser behavior; origin relaxation does not itself change cookie Domain rules.

cards.title: Attribute a Hijacked Session to the Right Threat Level
cards.summary: Evaluate what a stolen or forged session can actually do, because the same cross-site request is far more damaging against an admin than against a shopper.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing which ecommerce sessions to protect most tightly and where to require re-authentication, extra confirmation, or a second factor.
steps: For a normal shopper session, the source's example damage is forced actions such as transferring funds, changing an email address, or resetting a password, all performed as the user.
For an admin session over a store or CMS, the source states the request can be far more damaging: creating a new admin user, and in some cases running shell commands on the server as the server user.
Rank your own endpoints by blast radius: customer-facing actions versus admin actions like user creation, permission changes, plugin or theme install, and server-side command execution.

Apply the strictest controls (stronger authentication, re-confirmation, network restrictions, least-privilege admin roles) to the highest-blast-radius operations, and treat admin session cookies as the most sensitive credential in the store.
Remember the attacker need not read the response; a successful state change is enough, so log and alert on anomalous admin-level state changes rather than only on errors.
caveats: The source's damage examples come from a classroom bank and WordPress-admin scenario, not from a measured ecommerce incident; treat them as illustrations of blast radius, not benchmarks.

The source assumes the attacker knows the target endpoint path and that the victim is logged in; attacks fail if the user is not authenticated, which does not reduce the need to protect active sessions.

cards.title: Short Expiry With Rolling Renewal for Session Cookies
cards.summary: Set a modest cookie lifetime and renew it on each visit so legitimate users stay logged in while a stolen session has a bounded useful window.
cards.use_when: Choosing session and persistent-login cookie lifetimes for a storefront, balancing shopper convenience against the exposure window if a session is compromised.
steps: Use the source's heuristic of roughly 30 days for a persistent login cookie, refreshed on each visit, so the expiry is 30 days from the most recent activity rather than from first login.
Refresh the cookie by sending a new Set-Cookie header with the same name and updated Max-Age whenever the returning user makes a request.
Keep very short lifetimes on sensitive, less convenience-dependent sessions, and reserve the long rolling cookie for ordinary shopper convenience.
When implementing expiry, express the lifetime in milliseconds and multiply out the days, hours, minutes and seconds consistently; the source writes 30 days as 30*24*60*60*1000.
Ensure the same attributes are used on renewal and on clearing so the cookie is updated or removed rather than duplicated.
caveats: The source presents 30 days as a rule of thumb, not a measured optimum; adjust to your own risk tolerance and regulatory requirements.
Long-lived rolling sessions widen the window in which a stolen cookie remains valid, so pair them with the other cookie attributes and origin checks.

cards.title: Inspect Request Origin with Security Headers During Testing
cards.summary: Use browser-provided request origin metadata to confirm how a request was triggered, so you can validate defences like SameSite against your actual attacker surface.
cards.use_when: Debugging why a SameSite or CSRF defence appears not to work, and confirming whether the browser is classifying a request as same-site or cross-site for your store.
steps: When a defence such as SameSite appears ineffective, inspect the incoming request headers that browsers and proxies add to describe where the request came from and how it was triggered.

Reproduce the test with a realistic hostname rather than a raw IP: the source found the attack still succeeded while the attacker site was addressed by localhost IP and the cookie was re-sent, then behaved correctly once the attacker site was addressed by a real hostname mapped to the same machine.

Note the source's explanation: cookies scope by domain only and ignore IP-versus-hostname distinctions, while the same-origin policy also considers protocol and port, so a same-IP setup can behave differently from a same-host setup.
Re-run the cross-site scenario after each change to cookie attributes and confirm whether the cookie is actually being attached to the outgoing request, rather than assuming the setting took effect.
Keep this validation on systems you own, using your own test domains, and do not treat a passing test on one hostname as proof of protection on another.
caveats: The source's live debugging was inconclusive at the time and the presenter deferred the explanation to a later session, only confirming the fix after switching to a hostname; do not treat the IP-versus-hostname behaviour as universally guaranteed.
