Verify the current header names and browser interface, since request-origin metadata and browser defaults change over time.

cards.title: Never Use document.domain to Relax Same-Origin Policy
cards.summary: document.domain opt-in lets any attacker page on the same registrable domain cross origin boundaries, so treat it as a forbidden pattern.
cards.use_when: Auditing storefront or admin front-end code for cross-subdomain communication (e.g. shop.example.com talking to checkout.example.com) and deciding whether document.domain is acceptable.
steps: Understand the mechanism: pages can opt in to a common registrable domain by setting document.domain, which relaxes the same-origin check for iframes or popups that also opted in. Protocol and port cannot be relaxed, only the host component.

Recognise the vulnerability condition: once a legitimate subdomain opts in, any other page on that same registrable domain can also opt in and then read or manipulate the first page's content and cookies. On a store, an attacker-controlled or third-party-hosted subdomain or any XSS on any sibling subdomain gains access to the checkout or account subdomain.
Prefer per-subdomain isolation: keep authentication, checkout and account pages on their own origins and communicate only via postMessage with strict origin checks, or use a shared backend endpoint.
If document.domain already exists in the codebase, flag it for removal during review and replace the cross-frame access with postMessage, same-origin API calls, or a server-side session check.
Verify in the current browser's documentation what the current status of document.domain is; behaviour and deprecation plans have changed over time.
caveats: The source states this is a bad idea and instructs never to use it.
Relaxation applies only to the host component; you cannot bridge different protocols or ports this way.

cards.title: Use postMessage for Cross-Origin Page Communication
cards.summary: The postMessage API is the sanctioned way for cooperating origins to exchange messages, replacing the old fragment-identifier hack.
cards.use_when: Building or reviewing legitimate cross-origin communication in an ecommerce flow, e.g. a checkout iframe talking to the parent storefront, an embedded payment widget, or a third-party upsell frame.
steps: From the sender: obtain a handle to the target window (an iframe's contentWindow, or a window you opened), then call targetWindow.postMessage(message, targetOrigin).
From the receiver: register a listener with addEventListener('message', handler) and update your UI from the event's data.
The message can be a structured object (arrays, nested properties, even cyclic references) but cannot include functions, DOM nodes or live object instances.
For very large payloads such as graphics buffers, use transferable objects so ownership moves to the other page without copying, at the cost of losing your reference.
Avoid the historical workaround of encoding messages into a child iframe's URL fragment and polling location.hash every fraction of a second; it is slow, fragile and only relevant as history.
Confirm the current API surface in MDN or the browser vendor docs before implementing, as supported options evolve.
caveats: postMessage only works when at least one page holds a reference to the other, typically via an iframe or a window opened by script.
Without origin validation on both ends the channel is open to any page that can obtain a reference.

cards.title: Always Specify targetOrigin When Posting Messages
cards.summary: Omitting the destination origin in postMessage leaks data to any page that manages to embed or reference your window.
cards.use_when: Reviewing any code on an account page, login helper or checkout frame that posts user data such as a name or session detail to a parent window.
steps: Identify every postMessage call in store code and its third-party widgets.
Ensure the call passes an explicit targetOrigin string (e.g. 'https://shop.example.com') rather than '*' or an omitted argument.
The browser then refuses to deliver the message if the receiving window's origin does not match, which removes the need to hand-roll origin checks that are easy to get wrong.
If multiple legitimate destinations exist, some APIs accept an array of origins; verify current browser support before relying on it.
Treat the destination list as a security boundary and update it deliberately when adding new frames or partners.
caveats: A recipient you correctly trust may still mishandle the data it receives; the source notes that once information is handed to a cooperative but incompetent site, the sender cannot retrieve or revoke it.
Trusting a site to handle data responsibly is a business decision, not a technical control.

cards.title: Validate event.origin on Every Message Listener
cards.summary: A message listener without an origin check accepts forged data from any page that holds a window reference, enabling spoofed user data.
cards.use_when: Hardening storefront frames that receive data such as logged-in status, cart contents, coupon codes or shipping details from a parent or sibling origin.
steps: Locate every addEventListener('message', ...) callback in the storefront and embedded widgets.
At the top of the handler, compare event.origin against the exact expected origin and return early on mismatch, before reading or acting on event.data.
Assume the event object does not identify the sender beyond origin, so untrusted sources cannot be distinguished by any other property.
Consider window references cheap for an attacker: a page can open a popup or new tab and immediately hold a reference, so any window that does not verify the sender is reachable.
If a frame may navigate between being legitimate and hostile, re-check origin on each message rather than caching trust at setup time.
caveats: postMessage makes the origin check easy to omit because it is a runtime property, unlike the sender-side targetOrigin parameter which the API can enforce at call time.
The source treats failure to validate origin as a real vulnerability class, not merely a nicety.

cards.title: Prevent Clickjacking on Checkout and Account Pages
cards.summary: If your site can be framed, an attacker overlays invisible elements and turns a visitor's click into a purchase, bid or account action.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether a checkout, buy-now, one-click order, subscription cancel or account settings page should refuse to render inside a third-party frame.
steps: Understand the attack class: the attacker frames your page, positions it with CSS, sets the frame's opacity to zero, and places their own visible button exactly over a sensitive control such as Buy Now. The visitor sees one button and clicks another.
The framed action executes with the visitor's ambient session, so the usual outcome is whatever would have happened had they clicked normally, including completing a purchase or bid.
Compare to what reduces risk: blocking framing on sensitive pages, and using SameSite cookies so a cross-site framed request arrives logged out and cannot complete an authenticated action.
Evaluate whether a clickjacking defence header or frame-ancestors policy is appropriate for the specific pages, and confirm the current syntax and browser behaviour in vendor documentation.
Note that HTTPS alone does not stop clickjacking; the source says the same attack works over secure connections.
caveats: Any site that allows itself to be framed is exposed; the source frames this as the site permitting framing, not as a transport problem.
SameSite cookies mitigate the authenticated outcome but are described by the source as a complementary fix, not a complete clickjacking solution.

cards.title: Set SameSite on Session Cookies to Stop Ambient Cross-Site Requests
cards.summary: Cross-site image, form and frame requests silently carry a visitor's cookies unless the session cookie is scoped with SameSite.
cards.use_when: Configuring authentication and cart-session cookies so cross-site requests from third-party pages cannot act as the logged-in shopper.
steps: Recognise the ambient-authority problem: the browser attaches cookies automatically to cross-site requests such as an embedded image or a submitted form, so the receiving server may treat the request as coming from the logged-in user.

One illustrated case: an attacker page can embed an image URL that maps to the logged-in user's avatar, confirming login status or making a page look more convincing, because the browser supplies the target site's cookies.

Apply SameSite to session and authentication cookies so they are only attached on requests originating from your own site; the source describes strict and lax modes and notes you should check the slides or current documentation for exact semantics.
Test the chosen mode against real flows, because stricter settings affect links clicked from external sites, embedded payments and OAuth redirects.
Treat this as the preferred fix rather than trying to infer identity from the Referer header.
caveats: The source describes two modes, strict and lax, and refers to details outside the transcript; verify current cookie attribute names and browser behaviour before shipping.
A framed request from your own site to your own site is still within scope, so framing your own pages can reintroduce exposure.

cards.title: Do Not Rely on the Referer Header for Access Control
cards.summary: Referer-based defences break under caching, referrer-policy opt-outs and legitimate unknown referrers.
cards.use_when: Considering blocking requests to product images, downloads, coupon pages or account resources based on where the request appears to come from.
steps: Note the intent: the browser sends a Referer header telling the server which page generated the request, and some sites use it to reject or vary responses.

Identify failure mode one: browsers cache responses. If an image or asset was already fetched legitimately, an attacker's later request can be served from the local HTTP cache without contacting your server, so your check never runs.

Identify failure mode two: sites can opt out of sending the referrer entirely for privacy reasons, for example documents that embed secret URLs. Google Docs is cited as a case where outgoing links deliberately omit or reduce the referrer.

Identify failure mode three: referrer policy has several levels from full URL, to origin-only, to nothing, and the modern default already strips the referrer on secure-to-insecure downgrades. The linking site chooses this, not you.
Where caching is unavoidable, the source mentions a cache-varying header as a partial workaround, but presents SameSite cookies as the better answer; confirm current header names before implementing.
caveats: A site owner cannot prevent another site from linking to them; the source says there is no real answer for that and Referer inspection is only the best available partial tactic.
Referrer policy is set by the page containing the link, so an adversarial linker controls whether you receive the header.

cards.title: Treat Referrer Policy Settings as a Store-Level Trade-off
cards.summary: Choosing a referrer policy balances analytics, partner attribution and leaking private URLs.
cards.use_when: Setting or reviewing the referrer policy on storefront pages, order confirmations, customer dashboards or shared cart links.
steps: Enumerate what you lose with each level: no-referrer hides everything from destinations but also blocks you from seeing inbound referral sources for your own analytics.
Origin-only reference tells a destination that traffic came from your site, which preserves attribution credit, without exposing the specific page path.
Full-URL reference supports your own flow analysis across your pages but reveals individual page URLs to any destination you link to.

Consider the sensitive-URL case: if one of your pages is protected only by an unguessable URL, such as an order status or shared wishlist link, a referrer can leak that URL to whatever the customer clicks next.

Choose a policy that still allows the analytics and partner crediting you genuinely need, and re-check the currently supported policy values in browser documentation because the defaults have changed over time.
caveats: The source characterises Google Docs' policy as a bundle covering full URL for same-origin and stripping down to origin or nothing across origins; treat that as an illustration of the trade-off rather than a recommendation for stores.
Referrer policy is a blunt instrument and cannot be relied on as a security boundary.

cards.title: Treat Cross-Origin Script and Style Embeds as Full Trust
cards.summary: Scripts, stylesheets, images and fonts from other origins can be embedded by default, but an embedded script executes with your page's authority.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to load third-party JavaScript, CSS, fonts or pixels on product pages, checkout or account pages.
steps: List the automatic exceptions to the same-origin policy: pages may embed images, stylesheets, scripts, fonts and other resources from other origins, link to them, and submit forms to them, but cannot read data back from another origin.

Recognise that an embedded script runs in your page's context, exactly as if you had pasted the code into your page. It can therefore read and act on everything your page can, including form fields and session-dependent behaviour.
Apply this to tag managers, chat widgets, reviews, A/B testing tools and analytics on checkout: each is a script with full page authority, not a sandboxed component.
Prefer self-hosting or reviewing critical libraries, and keep third-party scripts off the most sensitive pages where possible.
Remember that cross-origin stylesheet and font embeds are common and generally lower risk than scripts, since they carry layout and font data rather than executable code.
caveats: The source notes these embed permissions predate the same-origin policy and were effectively grandfathered in; that is why they feel inconsistent with origin isolation.
There are minor edge cases around content-type sniffing that the source declines to cover in detail.

cards.title: Prevent Cross-Site Script Inclusion Leakage of JSON Endpoints
cards.summary: Endpoints that return JSON as a script-compatible response can be read cross-origin when loaded via a script tag.
cards.use_when: Reviewing API or data endpoints on a store that return buyer data, pricing tiers, inventory or account details and may be fetchable as scripts.
steps: Understand that a script loaded from another origin runs in the loading page's context, so an attacker page can include a script tag pointing at your data endpoint and receive whatever the browser parses as JavaScript.

When you inspect JSON-returning endpoints in a live store, look for an unusual leading sequence of characters before the data; the source points to such a prefix in a major webmail response as a deliberate defence against this class of inclusion attack.
Treat a syntactically invalid prefix as the defensive idea: the payload then fails to parse as a script in a foreign page while remaining parseable by a careful legitimate consumer.

Add an equivalent prefix only together with verifying that existing legit clients still parse the response, and that the endpoint does not leak session-scoped data solely because cookies were attached.
Pair this with SameSite cookies and origin checks on the endpoint so inclusion alone does not reach authenticated data.
caveats: The source presents the prefix observation as a motivating puzzle rather than a fully specified recipe; do not copy an exact hard-coded prefix without testing your own parsers.
JSON is not generally valid JavaScript in all cases, but the source treats script-compatible responses as the live risk.

cards.title: Do Not Trust Cookie Path Scoping as an Origin Boundary
cards.summary: Cookies and the same-origin policy are different, mismatched models, so path scoping and subdomain scoping are weaker than they look.
cards.use_when: Designing cookie scope for a store with several subdomains, such as www, account and checkout, or auditing an existing cookie configuration.
steps: Note that cookies are more specific than origins in one direction, allowing a path restriction, but that path scoping is ineffective as isolation because pages on the same origin can frame each other and read the sibling's cookies.

Note that cookies are less specific in the other direction: a page on one subdomain can set cookies for the broader registrable domain, and a DNS-hijacked or otherwise hostile response on that domain can read and set cookies for the whole domain.

Illustrate the risk with the invalid-domain case: if an ISP hijacks a nonexistent domain and serves an ad page, JavaScript on that page can read and set cookies for that domain, so an insecure or malicious ad is enough to compromise it.
Choose your session cookie's domain deliberately, prefer host-only cookies where subdomains do not need to share the session, and avoid broadly scoped cookies for authentication.
Combine with SameSite and HTTPS on the whole site, since the source notes that mandating HTTPS addresses the network-interception leg of this scenario.
caveats: The source stresses that cookies were designed before the same-origin policy and were never retrofitted to match it.
HTTPS fixes interception; it does not by itself fix scoping mistakes or same-domain hostility between subdomains.

cards.title: Bound Validation of Cross-Origin Flows to Owned Environments
cards.summary: Hands-on verification of frame and message behaviour belongs in local test setups with two controlled origins, not on live third-party sites.
cards.use_when: Prototyping or regression-testing cross-origin communication in a store's checkout or account flow before shipping postMessage or frame changes.
steps: Reproduce the environment safely: run two local servers on different ports so that the pages count as distinct origins under the origin tuple rule, and load one inside an iframe of the other.
Instrument what you need to see, for example rendering the received message string into a visible element so you can confirm delivery and timing.
Verify sender-side enforcement by setting targetOrigin to the exact expected origin and confirming the browser drops messages when the frame points elsewhere.
Verify receiver-side enforcement by checking event.origin and returning early on mismatch, then attempting a message from a deliberately wrong origin to confirm it is ignored.
Keep the harness to systems you own or are authorised to test, and never point these techniques at production third-party sites or real customer sessions.
caveats: The source demonstrates these techniques in a classroom with two local servers; the localhost ports are a teaching setup, not a deployment recommendation.
Origin equality includes scheme and port, so a same-host page on a different port is a distinct origin for these checks.

cards.title: Prevent Clickjacking with Frame-Ancestors Header
cards.summary: Use the Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive (or legacy X-Frame-Options) to stop competitors and attackers embedding your storefront in a frame and overlaying invisible buttons.
cards.use_when: Hardening your storefront or admin dashboard against clickjacking, e.g. when a third party could overlay a hidden add-to-cart or account action over an enticing button.
steps: Understand the attack: if your site allows framing, an attacker page can embed your site in a full-page iframe and transform/zoom it so a click lands on your real button (e.g. a social like button or an authenticated account action) while the user thinks they clicked something else.

Serverside, send the frame-ancestors directive in the response: 'none' to forbid all framing, or "'self'" to allow only your own origin to frame you. This is the reliable defense the source recommends over JS frame-busting.
Set the policy on every page or at the site-wide header level; do not assume you can detect at request time that a request is a framing attempt, since the server often cannot see it.
Verify on your own staging site by embedding your page in a test iframe and confirming the browser refuses to load it.
If you must support very old browsers, note the source says this header is long-supported and pervasive, but for other defensive headers check current browser support before relying on them.
caveats: Legacy X-Frame-Options with ALLOW-FROM is inconsistently supported; prefer frame-ancestors.
Frame-busting JavaScript is not a reliable defense per the cited Stanford research on busting frame busting.
Recently, browsers correctly require the entire embed chain to be same-origin; older behavior allowed an A->B->A chain. Verify with current browser behavior before relying on edge cases.

cards.title: Reject Cross-Site Form Submissions Using Origin Header
cards.summary: Check the Origin header against an allow list to block form POSTs from other sites; this does not stop request forgery but prevents the request from being accepted.
cards.use_when: Protecting storefront or checkout endpoints that accept form POSTs, such as changing an account email, applying a promo code, or placing an order, from being forged by a third-party page.
steps: Recognize that SameSite cookies only strip cookies from cross-site requests; they do not prevent the form submission itself, so the POST still arrives.
Serverside, read the Origin header on incoming POST requests and compare it against an allow list of origins you expect (e.g. your own storefront domain).
Reject requests whose Origin is missing or not on the allow list.

Note that GET requests are treated as CORS-simple and may not carry an Origin header for image/script/style loads; rely on the POST check for state-changing actions rather than expecting Origin everywhere.
Do not rely on the Referer header as a primary control; the source says it can be manipulated and is not reliable.
caveats: The browser sets and protects the Origin header; a site making the request cannot forge it, which is why it is trustworthy for this check.
You cannot truly stop a determined client (e.g. a script) from sending a request; the goal is to make your server reject requests it did not originate.

cards.title: Protect private ecommerce media with authorization or scoped links
cards.summary: Distinguish private customer assets from public assets whose bandwidth needs protection.
cards.use_when: Serving images such as user avatars, customer-uploaded photos, downloadable receipts, or paid content where hotlinking or leaking would cost bandwidth or expose private data.
steps: Classify the asset: public product media, customer upload, invoice or private support attachment.
Enforce server-side authorization for private assets or issue appropriately scoped, expiring signed links after authorization.
Treat a shared link as a bearer capability that can leak through logs or forwarding; avoid unnecessary exposure.
Use caching, rate limits and delivery controls for public-media hotlinking without confusing them with customer-data access control.
caveats: A random path alone does not establish the requester's identity or permission.

cards.title: Choose the Right Tool for Each Cross-Site Boundary Question
cards.summary: A decision framework mapping the same-origin questions (can A link to B, embed B, read B's data, submit forms, steal images/scripts) to reliable vs unreliable defenses.
cards.use_when: Architecting storefront integrations, embedded widgets, third-party scripts, or any cross-origin data sharing and needing to know which control actually holds.
steps: Can site A link to or embed site B? By default yes; block it with the frame-ancestors header if you don't want to be embedded, and the source says this works reliably.
Can site A embed B and modify B's DOM? No; the same-origin policy is strong here and there is no way to relax it, so this stays a safe default.
Can a site submit a form to you? You can reject cross-origin submissions by checking the Origin header, which the source says works quite reliably.
Do you want forms allowed but without cookies attached? Use SameSite cookies for that middle ground.
Can another site read the bytes of your response? No; strengthening this is not foolproof, and the source treats 'images and scripts' defenses as best-effort only.
When you need to intentionally allow cross-origin reads (e.g. collaborating with a partner API), plan to relax the policy explicitly rather than weakening defaults.
caveats: Only the frame-ancestors and Origin-allow-list controls are described as reliable; Referer-based and similar tricks are explicitly not foolproof.
Verify current browser behavior for any relaxation mechanism before shipping, since these details change.

cards.title: Kill Cross-Site Scripting by Escaping User Data at Output
cards.summary: Treat all user-supplied strings as data by HTML-escaping them before inserting them into your page, and consider the limits of blacklists.
cards.use_when: Building any storefront page that reflects user input, such as a search results page, a personalized welcome based on a URL parameter, or a product review display.
steps: Identify the pattern that causes the bug: server code concatenating a hard-coded HTML template with untrusted user input, so the browser cannot tell the user's string from your markup.

Understand the impact: an attacker who gets their text parsed as code can run script in your origin's context, taking actions as your logged-in customer (e.g. reading document.cookie and exfiltrating it, or submitting requests).
Fix it by escaping the untrusted value so angle brackets and other significant characters become inert HTML entities (e.g. < becomes <), so the browser displays the text instead of executing it.
Escape only the specific values that are user-supplied, not the entire page; escaping everything would turn your own tags into visible text.
Prefer your web framework's built-in output-escaping for inserting data over hand-rolled functions where possible.
Do not rely on a blocklist of 'bad words' (like banning usernames containing 'script' or 'select') as your primary defense; per the source, missing a single entry defeats it.
caveats: The source's example demonstrates this all with a same-tab self-test (alerting your own cookie); a real attack requires the victim to be logged in and to click a link, which is why 'don't click suspicious links' is not sufficient protection.
Note the distinction between escaping for HTML text context versus other contexts; the source only demonstrates HTML escaping.

cards.title: Why Cross-Site Scripting Is Worse Than Clickjacking for Your Store
cards.summary: Understand the attacker's goal — running code in your origin so they act as a logged-in customer — before choosing defenses.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing remediation when you discover a stored or reflected input vulnerability on a customer-facing page like a profile, review, or search results page.
steps: Recognize that the same-origin policy blocks an attacker from framing your site and reaching into the login form to read a password; XSS is the workaround that gets their code into your page.
Trace what an attacker can then do: take any action as the customer (submit requests with the victim's cookies), or read document.cookie and send it to an attacker server to hijack the session.

Treat any page that mixes attacker-controlled text with your code as a potential injection point, whether it is reflected (in a URL parameter) or stored (saved to your database and shown to other users).

Prioritize fixes for stored injection on pages other customers view, since that enables self-propagating worms (the source's MySpace example added the attacker as a friend and copied the payload into victims' profiles, causing exponential growth and an outage).
When reviewing your store, test your own pages with a harmless proof payload (e.g. alerting the current document cookie) so you confirm the vulnerability without attacking anyone else.
caveats: The source stresses that clients cannot be trusted at all; server-side defenses must hold even if a client is a hacked browser or script.
Worm-style exponential spread is a described historical case study, not a prediction of outcomes for any specific store.

cards.title: Avoid JSONP for Partner Data; Prefer Headers or Proxy
cards.summary: JSONP lets a cooperating server hand you cross-origin data wrapped in a callback, but it grants that origin execution context on your page — consider safer alternatives.
cards.use_when: Deciding how a storefront should read JSON from a partner or internal API that lives on a different origin, especially when the data varies per logged-in user.
steps: Understand the trick: a script tag bypasses the same-origin policy, and JSONP asks the server to wrap its JSON in a caller-specified function name (callback parameter) so the returned script calls your function with the data.

Recognize the dangers: the server must write extra code to support it, some valid JSON is not valid JavaScript (whitespace issues), and the caller controls the callback name, which opens a reflected-file-download / injection class of bug if not sanitized.
From the consuming site's view, including a script from another origin gives that origin remote execution in your page if their response is ever compromised.

Consider alternatives before adopting JSONP: a serverside proxy on your own domain (which also lets you keep the request authenticated to your own session), or a proper CORS-style header that the other server sends to permit your origin to read the response.
If you must relax the boundary intentionally, restrict it narrowly rather than granting full script execution.
caveats: The source describes JSONP as a 'clever hack' that works but is a bad idea for untrusted or unstable partners.
A serverside proxy changes where the request originates and won't reflect per-user logged-in responses the way a browser-side call would.

cards.title: Layer CSRF defenses on authenticated store actions
cards.summary: Use framework CSRF protection, origin checks and appropriate cookies together for state-changing requests.
cards.use_when: Configuring session cookie attributes for a storefront so cross-site pages can't trigger authenticated actions like account changes or a placed order against a logged-in customer.
steps: Keep state changes out of safe read methods such as GET.
Use maintained framework CSRF protections and validate the expected token for relevant authenticated actions.
Validate request origin as appropriate and set Secure, HttpOnly and a suitable SameSite policy on session cookies.
Test cross-site login, payment redirects and embeds; Lax, Strict and None have different behavior.
Recognize that same-site sibling origins and XSS can undermine assumptions; keep authorization and output safety independent.
caveats: SameSite is defense in depth, not a universal guarantee that every cross-origin request is unauthenticated.

cards.title: Treat Script and Image Inclusion as Best-Effort, Not Secure
cards.summary: Blocking hotlinked scripts and images is about bandwidth, not confidentiality, and Referer-based blocking is explicitly unreliable.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether and how to stop other sites embedding your images, stylesheets or JavaScript (e.g. a signature animation or theme asset they are stealing).
steps: Clarify the goal: for a static image, script or CSS asset, the concern is bandwidth theft (hotlinking), not data leakage, because the asset holds no private data.
Recognize that a hotlinked script runs in the embedding site's page, not yours, so it does not threaten your origin directly.
Use Referer-based checks to reduce casual hotlinking, but accept that the source calls this not foolproof because the header can be manipulated.
For private or per-user assets, prefer unguessable URLs or SameSite-gated responses rather than Referer rules.
Use a CDN (the source cites Google's CDN serving the d3 graphics library) as normal practice for serving such libraries, separate from the hotlinking question.
caveats: The source explicitly lists image/script protection as best-effort; do not treat it as a security boundary.
Origin headers are not sent for simple image/script/style loads, so an Origin allow list won't cover this case.

cards.title: Make Store Input Fields Untrusted by Default
cards.summary: The root condition for both XSS and SQL injection is mixing untrusted customer input with code, so treat every input field as a potential injection vector.
cards.use_when: Reviewing storefront and back-office features that accept customer text — signup fields, search boxes, review forms, support messages, profile/bio fields — before launch.
steps: For every place customer data is combined with code, name the code context: HTML output, a SQL command, a URL, or JavaScript.
Apply the correct neutralization for that context (HTML escaping for HTML, parameterized queries for SQL) rather than one generic sanitizer.
Prefer frameworks and ORMs that parameterize queries and escape output by default, and confirm they are actually enabled rather than bypassed for convenience.
When the user's data modifies a SQL command, the risk is reading different data or running a second command — the same class of bug as XSS applied to the database.
Include stored fields (bios, reviews, display names) in your review, since stored injection can spread to every visitor's page.
caveats: The source notes the SQL-injection parallel briefly; the detailed lecture focus is XSS.
Blacklisting programmer-sounding usernames is called out as an inadequate defense on its own.

cards.title: Automate Defensive Controls Across All Store Pages
cards.summary: Anti-framing and output-escaping controls should be applied consistently at the site or framework level, not page-by-page where gaps appear.
cards.use_when: Rolling out security headers and escaping after an audit reveals inconsistent coverage across your storefront's templates.
steps: Set frame-ancestors (or the legacy X-Frame-Options header) as a site-wide response header so every page — product, cart, account, admin — refuses untrusted framing.
Enable your web framework's automatic output escaping by default and audit for places where developers disabled or bypassed it.
For each reflected input (URL parameters driving page text), confirm the untrusted value is escaped before it reaches the HTML string.
Add the Origin allow list to your shared POST-handling middleware so new endpoints inherit the check.
Re-test after rollout with self-directed proof payloads on staging to confirm controls fire on every template.
caveats: Retrofitting a site-wide header is easy; retrofitting escaping may require touching many templates and finding old bypasses.
Verify header and attribute support in the browsers your customers actually use before assuming blanket protection.

cards.title: Treat all client-supplied data as untrusted input
cards.summary: Any value from URLs, form fields, headers or profile data must be escaped before insertion into HTML or JavaScript, because client data can never be trusted.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing any storefront feature that echoes user input — search terms, review text, profile names, wishlist labels, coupon codes, or URL parameters — back into the page.
steps: Assume every value originating from the browser (query string, form field, header, stored profile field) is suspect regardless of how mundane it looks.
Identify every place that value is inserted into HTML, an attribute, or inline JavaScript — each insertion point needs its own correct escaping.
Prefer the escaping mechanism built into your framework or templating language (e.g. ejs, Jade) over hand-rolled concatenation of HTML strings with user data.
Read the framework docs to find the safe insertion helper and the explicitly dangerous opt-out; treat the opt-out as requiring justification, not convenience.
For high-power attributes (src, href, style, event handlers), do not rely on generic escaping; validate the value separately (see related cards).
Log where untrusted data enters your stack so future features inherit the same discipline.
caveats: The source cites research (a WhiteHat Security report circa 2015-2016) that roughly half of sites had XSS issues; this is a historical statistic, not a current benchmark.
Framework behaviour and default escaping change over time — verify the current interface and defaults for whatever framework you use.

cards.title: Escape user data inside HTML element contexts
cards.summary: When inserting untrusted data between HTML tags, escape the left angle bracket, ampersand, and both quote characters to neutralize injected markup.
cards.use_when: Rendering user-supplied text into normal page regions such as review bodies, collection descriptions, order notes, or any block that is not a script, style, comment or tag name.
steps: Replace left angle brackets (<) with the HTML entity (<) so the browser shows the character instead of starting a tag.
Also replace ampersands (&) with the entity (&) — otherwise a user typing the literal sequence '<' would be rendered as a real '<' and could re-open an injection.
For attribute values, additionally convert both single and double quotes to their HTML entities, so it does not matter which quote character surrounds the attribute.
Do not apply HTML entity escaping to the whole page — that would show every legitimate tag as visible text; only escape the specific untrusted variables.
Where possible delegate this to your framework's safe-insertion helper, but understand what it does so you can audit it.
caveats: This rule covers ordinary element text and quoted attribute values only; script and style blocks have completely different rules.
Escaping entities inside a script block does not work because the JavaScript parser does not understand HTML entities.
Over-escaping is generally harmless to display (any character can be turned into an entity), but it breaks contexts where the parser expects raw characters.

cards.title: Always quote HTML attribute values you build
cards.summary: Unquoted attributes let browsers treat many characters as ending the value, so never build storefront attributes without surrounding quotes.
cards.use_when: Generating HTML snippets for product images, alt text, srcsets, data attributes, or any element whose attribute values include dynamic store data.
steps: Always wrap dynamic attribute values in quotes in your templates; do not emit attributes like alt=userText with no quotes.
Recognise that an unquoted value cannot safely contain a space, and browsers also treat many other characters as ending the value, not just spaces.
Treat unquoted attributes as effectively impossible to escape correctly, because you would need to block a long and browser-dependent list of characters.
When reviewing templates or generated markup, flag any attribute whose value is unquoted and dynamic.
Rely on the framework's templating, which quotes attributes for you, rather than manual string concatenation.
caveats: Historically browsers disagreed on which characters terminated unquoted values; behaviour is more standardised now but still a poor practice.
This is defence-in-depth: quoting alone does not make high-power attributes safe.

cards.title: High-power attributes need value validation, not just escaping
cards.summary: Attributes like src and href can execute or load attacker-controlled content even when quotes are correctly escaped, so validate the URL itself.
cards.use_when: Any storefront flow that lets a user or merchant supply a URL for an image, link, iframe, or script — user avatars, custom collection banners, affiliate links, or rich-text product descriptions.
steps: Do not assume that escaping quotes is sufficient for src or href; even a well-contained value can cause a script to load or a page to navigate somewhere dangerous.
Validate that the supplied value is a well-formed, expected URL (correct scheme and shape) in addition to quoting and escaping it.
Explicitly reject the data: and javascript: schemes, which are legitimate URL forms but enable script execution and page injection.
For iframe or script sources specifically, restrict to trusted origins you control or explicitly allow.
When writing validation regexes, test them against data: and javascript: payloads, since these are easy to overlook and cause serious outcomes.
caveats: Data URLs have legitimate uses (see the data-URL card); the risk depends on where the value is inserted.
The source notes uncertainty about how some data-URL iframes are treated origin-wise; do not rely on iframe origin isolation without verifying.

cards.title: Reject data: and javascript: URLs in user-supplied links
cards.summary: data: and javascript: URLs can execute arbitrary code, so block them wherever users can supply a link or source.
cards.use_when: Building any feature that accepts a user-submitted link or image source — user-generated content, curated wishlists, third-party product feeds, or rich product description editors.
steps: Understand that a data: URL is a synthetic response from a non-existent server: the browser pretends to fetch it and treats the contents after the comma as the document.
Understand that a javascript: URL runs code in the current page; browsers such as Chrome may strip the javascript: prefix on paste, but users can re-add it, so do not rely on that.
Whitelist accepted schemes for user links (typically https) and reject everything else, rather than blacklisting only the two known-bad schemes.
For images, restrict to image data URLs or a controlled CDN origin if you must permit them at all.
Re-test after any change to link handling, and log rejected scheme attempts to spot abuse.
caveats: Chrome, Firefox and Safari handle pasted javascript: URLs differently (stripping the scheme or requiring a setting), so browser behaviour is not a reliable control.
Even if a data-URL iframe is isolated by origin, a heavy or blocking script inside it can still lock up the page in the shared event loop (a denial-of-service concern).

cards.title: Escaping alone fails inside inline event handlers and JS strings
cards.summary: When user data sits inside an inline handler (onclick) or a script string, you need JavaScript-level escaping in addition to HTML escaping, or break out is possible.
cards.use_when: Generating trigger text, analytics labels, or inline event handlers that embed store data, or embedding a user string inside a <script> variable.
steps: Recognise that data inside an onclick or script variable is in a JavaScript context nested inside an HTML context — one layer of escaping is not enough.
For strings inside JavaScript, escape quotes by prefixing with a backslash, and also escape backslashes themselves, otherwise a supplied backslash can neutralise your escape.
For values inserted into script variables, consider hex-encoding the data (using only 0-9 and A-F) so it cannot contain quotes, closing script tags or other breakout characters; decode it at runtime.
Alternatively use the HTML <template> tag as inert storage: put the escaped user data between tags (only < and & need escaping), then read it via JavaScript when needed.
Write tests with inputs containing quotes, backslashes, closing script tags and mixed contexts.
caveats: Pure HTML entity escaping inside a script produces garbage because the JavaScript parser has no concept of entities, so the user sees the wrong text.
The source notes some edge cases (e.g. double-backslash handling) were uncertain in the lecture — validate against your own parser and runtime.

cards.title: Avoid pages where user data passes through nested parsers
cards.summary: Layered contexts (HTML attribute to JavaScript string to eval-like call) require multiple correctly-ordered escapes and are extremely error-prone, so avoid the pattern.
cards.use_when: Designing features where store data flows through an HTML attribute, then a JavaScript string, then a dynamic execution call (e.g. rich-text widgets, custom button scripts, or analytics configuration).
steps: Identify nesting when a single value must be escaped at multiple levels — e.g. user data inside a string inside an onclick attribute, which the browser parses as HTML, then as JavaScript, then as a string argument.
Count the escapes required: each nested context adds its own layer, and getting the order or characters wrong breaks security.
Prefer architectures that avoid inline scripting and multi-layer embedding: pass data as escaped HTML between tags and read it via a script, rather than rebuilding scripts from strings.
If you cannot avoid nesting, write explicit tests that inject breakout characters at each layer and confirm nothing escapes.
Document the escaping contract wherever developers must remember multiple layers.
caveats: The source describes such nesting as surprisingly common in real code, but its recommended remedy is to avoid it rather than perfect the escaping.
No numeric guidance is given; the rule is architectural, not a formula.

cards.title: Only HTML element text and quoted attributes are reliably escapable
cards.summary: Several HTML contexts (comments, tag names, script bodies as plain text) cannot be escaped safely, so refuse to insert user data there.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or designing any template or editor where store or customer data could land in a comment, in a tag name, or directly in a script body.
steps: Refuse to insert user data into HTML comments — they do not affect rendering, so there is no legitimate need, and the parser rules are difficult to get right.
Refuse to build tag names from user input; even a blacklist of dangerous tags (script, style) will miss new tags and browser-specific interpretations.
Never place raw user data in an unquoted script position; use the hex-encoding or template-tag approaches described elsewhere.
Reserve the escapable contexts — ordinary element text and quoted attribute values — for any user-dependent content.
When a feature seems to require a non-escapable context, redesign the feature rather than attempting clever escaping.
caveats: The source states the comment-parsing rules were hard to pin down, which is itself a reason to avoid, not to improvise.
Blacklist approaches fail as browsers evolve and add new elements.

cards.title: Recognise reflected versus stored XSS and prioritise accordingly
cards.summary: Reflected XSS lives in the request, while stored XSS persists in your data and reaches every visitor regardless of the URL they use.
cards.use_when: Triageing vulnerability findings or designing storefront features: deciding where user data is stored (reviews, profiles, messages) versus only reflected in a response (search, filters).
steps: Classify a potential issue as reflected if the payload must be carried in a link the victim clicks (URL path or query).
Classify it as stored if the payload is persisted server-side — in a database, cache, or any durable field — and rendered for other visitors.
Treat stored issues as higher impact because the delivery route is irrelevant: the victim need not click anything from the attacker, so the whole user base is exposed.
Accept that the entry route for stored payloads can be obscure — an HTTP header, an API import, or a bribed insider — because any route to the data store suffices.
Prioritise fixes for stored flows: user profiles, uploaded content, review text, and anything that imports external data.
caveats: This is a classification framework, not a numeric severity scale; actual risk depends on the page and audience.
Stored XSS can be reached by means that would be impractical for reflected XSS, so do not use 'the attacker could not get them to click it' as a rejection reason.

cards.title: Escaping cannot defeat breakouts caused by a closing script tag
cards.summary: The HTML parser locates script tag boundaries before JavaScript parsing, so a literal closing script tag anywhere in a script breaks out regardless of string escaping.
cards.use_when: Reviewing any storefront or checkout page where user data or third-party content is embedded in a script, or when evaluating page-builder widgets that inject sequences into scripts.
steps: Understand the parser order: the HTML parser runs first and identifies script boundaries, then a separate JavaScript parser runs on each script body.

Recognise that including the literal characters for a closing script tag inside a string or comment in JavaScript still terminates the script element and can let an attacker resume HTML context, executing code.
Do not rely on escape sequences for quotes or backslashes to prevent this, because the boundary is determined before those sequences are interpreted.
Fix the embedding pattern: hex-encode the data so no breakout characters exist, or keep the data out of script bodies entirely.
Prefer loading third-party scripts by src from a trusted destination, which avoids this class of problem.
caveats: The source notes a syntax error in one script generally does not prevent other script elements from running, but the breakout itself is the security concern.
This applies wherever user data reaches a script body, including dynamically generated widgets.

cards.title: Blacklist filtering of tag names fails against forgiving HTML parsers
cards.summary: HTML parsers are deliberately lenient, accepting many syntax variations that bypass tag-name blacklists.
cards.use_when: Evaluating any input sanitisation that tries to block specific tags or words in customer reviews, product descriptions, or rich-text fields.
steps: Treat blacklists of tag names (script, style, etc.) as unreliable, because browsers accept unusual whitespace, slashes and other characters between a tag name and its attributes.
Assume new elements and browser-specific quirks will appear after your blacklist is written.
Where possible, work from an allowlist of the exact, minimal markup and attributes you intend to support, and escape everything else.
Understand the robustness principle ('be conservative in what you send, forgiving in what you accept') is why parsers are lenient — that leniency is a security liability for filters.
Validate changes against real browsers rather than assuming a filter behaves as written, and treat consistency across browsers as unproven.
caveats: The source notes older browsers differed significantly in how they interpreted unusual characters; modern behaviour is more consistent but still not safe to filter against.
This is a validation caution, not a recommendation to write your own full sanitiser.

cards.title: Beware DOM-injected globals via user-controlled element IDs
cards.summary: The DOM exposes elements with IDs as global JavaScript variables, so letting users choose an ID can let them inject or override variables your script depends on.
cards.use_when: Designing features that assign element IDs from user input, such as personalised widgets, review anchors, or per-customer page components.
steps: Recognise that the DOM creates a global JavaScript variable automatically for each element with an ID — this is a DOM behaviour, not a JavaScript feature.
If a script references a variable that is normally undefined and a user can set an element ID to that name, the condition can flip to truthy and divert the script's logic.
Do not let users control element IDs or form field names; generate IDs server-side from a safe pattern (e.g. a numeric token) instead.
Also avoid letting users control form field 'name' attributes, since forms rely on them.
When reviewing templates, treat any user-controlled identifier as a potential variable-injection point.
caveats: The source was uncertain how duplicate IDs are resolved, but notes duplicates can change which element JavaScript selects.
This is an indirect attack that depends on what your script does with the variable; not every case is exploitable.

cards.title: Use data URLs for small inline assets, not large ones
cards.summary: Data URLs can inline small images or stylesheets into a page to save an HTTP round trip, but they cannot be cached and bloat the document.
cards.use_when: Choosing whether to inline small storefront assets such as icons or logos into the page or CSS, versus serving them as separate requests.
steps: Understand that an inlined data URL travels with the HTML or CSS, so the browser shows the asset on the first response instead of making an extra request, then waiting.
Inline only genuinely small assets; the source suggests a tiny icon may be worth it while a multi-megabyte image is not.
Recognise that inlined assets cannot be cached separately, so a large or repeat-viewed asset re-downloads with every page load.
Use the same technique inside CSS to avoid an extra HTTP request for small background images.
Weigh the round-trip saved against the added page weight before deciding.
caveats: The source gives no specific size threshold, only the principle that small is suitable and multi-megabyte is not.
Separately, data URLs are a security risk when users can supply them as link or source values — context determines whether they are helpful or dangerous.

cards.title: Fix XSS with Context-Aware Output Encoding
cards.summary: Encode untrusted values separately for each output context (HTML body, attribute, JavaScript string, URL) rather than escaping once at input.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or briefing developers on your storefront's product review fields, search results pages, or any template that echoes customer-supplied content.
steps: Identify every place customer-controlled data is echoed: product reviews, search query display, cart notes, custom engraving text, account names.

For each output location, apply the encoding matching that context: HTML-entity encoding in HTML body, attribute encoding inside attributes, JavaScript-string escaping inside script blocks, URL encoding inside hrefs.
Do not encode only at input or only once: a value written into a JavaScript string and then injected into HTML needs a second round of context-appropriate encoding.

Avoid deeply nested encoding chains where the same value passes through several languages or contexts; if a value must cross contexts, isolate it into a data attribute or JSON blob rather than embedding it inline.
Add a review step or linting rule so new template code that echoes user input gets a context check before release.
caveats: Encode at output, not just input; input filtering alone does not cover stored XSS in reviews or legacy data.
The source presenter calls deep nested encoding fragile and advises against it.

cards.title: Treat XSS Filtering Browser Features as Unreliable
cards.summary: Built-in reflected-XSS filters can be bypassed and even aid attackers, so do not count on them as your storefront's XSS defense.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether browser-level XSS filtering removes the need for server-side sanitization on your storefront's reflected input pages.
steps: Assume the browser's reflected-XSS filter may decide not to block an attack, or may be absent entirely, and that some bypasses can degrade into new attack classes.
Keep reflected XSS prevention on the server and in templates: encode output by context and validate input, rather than relying on the browser to strip script from URLs.
When testing your own storefront, use your own staging copy, not third-party sites.
Verify the current state of any named browser filter before relying on descriptions of it, since browser behavior and availability change.
caveats: The source describes this as a historical browser feature; verify its current status before citing it.
No filter, header, or browser feature alone guarantees XSS protection.

cards.title: Choose Between Content-Matched and Person-Targeted Ads
cards.summary: Content-based ad placement ties ad revenue to page quality; person-level tracking decouples ad value from content and shifts spend toward cheap, low-quality pages.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether your store should buy content-matched placements (relevant publishers, category pages) or behavioral audiences, and understanding why cheap inventory may outperform contextually relevant inventory on cost.
steps: For each campaign, state whether the targeting is against content (site, category, article context) or against the person (retargeting pools, lookalikes, cross-site profiles).
If using person-level targeting, compare effective cost per acquisition on premium publishers versus low-cost long-tail inventory, since the same user may be reachable much more cheaply elsewhere.

If you are the publisher or content site, recognize that person-level buying reduces the marginal value of quality content and pushes ad revenue toward cheap inventory; budget for this when forecasting content-driven revenue.

For sensitive product categories (e.g. health, fertility, baby, debt), suppress or exclude person-level audiences where downstream disclosure could harm the customer; the source cites a case where pregnancy-related targeting revealed a pregnancy to a family member.
caveats: The source's ad-economics discussion is the presenter's analysis, not a measured benchmark for your account.
Historical claims about which ad companies were profitable are dated; verify current figures.

cards.title: Plan for Third-Party Tags as Tracking Surfaces
cards.summary: A typical page loads around twenty third-party resources with tracking vantage, and roughly 70-80% of first-party URLs may be observable by one large analytics provider, per the cited census.
cards.use_when: Auditing your store's third-party script footprint or preparing a privacy review before adding another analytics, personalization or ad tag.
steps: Build an inventory of every third-party resource loaded on home, category, product, cart and checkout templates: analytics, pixels, chat, reviews, A/B tools, payment SDKs.
For each tag, record what data it can observe (URL, referrer, cookies, form contents) and whether it operates in the first-party context.
Prefer tags that make explicit contractual privacy commitments and avoid others; the source notes some CDNs publish such guarantees, though a published promise is not enforcement.
On checkout and account pages, minimize third-party scripts because those paths carry payment and identity data.
Re-audit after each new tool ships, since tags accumulate.
caveats: The census figures cited are several years old; treat the ~20 third parties and ~70-80% reach as directional, not current measurements.
A vendor privacy promise is a legal commitment, not a technical control.

cards.title: Understand Cookies and Third-Party Cookie Exposure
cards.summary: Cookies store a server-issued identifier returned on subsequent requests; the decision to send them on third-party image and iframe requests is what enabled cross-site tracking.
cards.use_when: Reviewing how your store's session, cart persistence and embedded third-party content handle cookies.
steps: Distinguish first-party cookies (set and read by your own domain) from third-party cookies (set by embedded resources); cart and login typically depend on first-party cookies.
Audit embedded third-party elements (images, iframes, widgets) and whether they receive cookies on your pages.
Set session cookies with HttpOnly and Secure attributes where applicable, and scope cookie domains narrowly, so attached third-party resources do not inherit your identifiers.

Recognize that third-party request cookie behavior has been restricted by several major browsers; verify current behavior in the specific browsers your customers use before assuming a cookie will or will not be sent.
caveats: Browser cookie policy changes frequently; treat any specific current restriction as subject to change.
Secure cookies prevent interception over plaintext, not tracking via other identifiers.

cards.title: Treat HSTS as a Security Feature That Can Be Repurposed
cards.summary: HSTS tells browsers to refuse plaintext requests to a domain, but subdomain-level rules can be abused to encode per-user bits.
cards.use_when: Reviewing domain and subdomain configuration for your store, especially if you control or delegate many subdomains.
steps: Deploy HSTS on your storefront domains deliberately, with care about preload and long max-age, since the setting is effectively sticky for returning visitors.
Inventory subdomains: because HSTS rules can be set per subdomain, a large delegated subdomain space becomes a tracking surface.
Restrict who can create subdomains and which parties can set headers on them, and retire unused subdomains.
Treat HSTS as transport protection only; it is not an anti-tracking or XSS control.
caveats: The subdomain encoding technique is discussed in the source as an observed abuse; do not rely on HSTS to prevent tracking.
HSTS configuration mistakes can lock users out of plaintext access; test before preloading.

cards.title: Assess Fingerprinting Risk on Your Storefront Analytics
cards.summary: Fingerprinting identifies a browser by combining many semi-unique attributes without storing anything, so it survives cookie clearing and third-party cookie blocking.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether removing third-party cookies actually reduces cross-site tracking of your store's visitors, or choosing an analytics approach for privacy-sensitive audiences.
steps: List the attributes your site or its tags can read: user-agent string, installed fonts, screen and window dimensions, canvas rendering output, audio rendering output, hardware concurrency, device memory, WebGL parameters, network type.
Treat any single attribute as non-identifying but the combination as highly identifying, and measure the combined entropy using a tool like the EFF's Panopticlick-style test against your own site.
If you are the publisher or merchant, note that fingerprinting continues working after cookies are cleared, so cookie-consent banners alone do not stop cross-site identification.
If you are evaluating privacy tooling, prefer approaches that address the combined fingerprint set rather than any single attribute.
caveats: Fingerprinting libraries and browser countermeasures change; check current implementations before acting.
The source discusses defensive countermeasures and open problems, not guaranteed solutions.

cards.title: Recognize Font Enumeration and Why It Is Hard to Fix
cards.summary: Pages infer installed local fonts by measuring whether applying a candidate font changes an element's size, giving one entropy bit per unusual font.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a privacy-preserving analytics or anti-tracking approach that claims to neutralize fingerprinting, to check whether font enumeration is addressed.
steps: Understand the mechanism: a page iterates a long list of font names, applies each to a test element, and checks if the rendered size changed; changed size implies the font is installed.
Accept that you cannot block reading element dimensions without breaking page layout, so a simple blocker is not the answer.

Consider the tradeoffs used in practice: treating local fonts as unavailable is acceptable for many Western sites but breaks some sites, especially in Asian-language contexts where local fonts are commonly required because system fonts are poor.
Alternative mitigations include mapping a language to a small permitted font set (trading privacy-set size for compatibility) and gating font access behind a permission prompt.
If you are auditing your own store, note that you almost certainly do not need local font enumeration for legitimate function.
caveats: The source notes defenses here are unsatisfying and standards work is contested.
Permission prompts help only when users decline; network traffic can still reveal font loading.

cards.title: Treat Canvas and Audio Fingerprinting as Unpredictable APIs
cards.summary: Canvas and audio rendering produce slightly different output across hardware and drivers, which can be hashed into an identifier the user never sees.
cards.use_when: Understanding what browser-based fingerprinting can extract from visitors to your store, or assessing what a privacy tool must suppress.
steps: Recognize that drawing operations rendered to a canvas can be read back as a blob or data URL and hashed; harmless uses exist (e.g. checking emoji support) but the same API serves fingerprinting.
Note that audio processing can be fingerprinted either by querying capability information or by generating a waveform and hashing subtle device-specific differences.
Treat these as hard-to-lie-about signals, since the rendering difference is inherent to the hardware and usually imperceptible to users.
When evaluating fingerprinting protections, check whether canvas and audio outputs are perturbed or blocked and whether that breaks legitimate functionality.
caveats: The source describes these techniques as observed in a widely used fingerprinting library; it does not claim they cover every device or browser.
Perturbing rendering can break legitimate canvas applications, so blanket blocking is a tradeoff.

cards.title: Audit Permissionless Hardware and Network APIs
cards.summary: Several APIs expose hardware and network characteristics without any permission prompt, giving every script on the page identifying data.
cards.use_when: Auditing third-party scripts on your store or judging how much identifying data your pages already leak by default.
steps: Enumerate what scripts on your pages can read without asking: hardware concurrency (CPU cores), Web Audio channel configuration, WebGL shader capabilities, an approximate device memory value, and network-touching APIs that reveal connection type and IP-adjacent details.
Treat these as available to every script on every page; there is no user-facing consent gate for them in the browsers described.
When adding a new script or SDK, include these APIs in the review of what that vendor can observe.
For privacy-sensitive storefronts, consider which scripts genuinely need hardware or network information and remove those that do not.
Verify the current standardization and browser support for each API before relying on any specific one.
caveats: Standardization status varies; some APIs are non-standard or Chromium-only per the source.
These APIs are not the only identifying sources; they are a subset.

cards.title: Treat Viewport Size as the Hardest Fingerprint to Fake
cards.summary: True visible window dimensions are difficult to spoof without breaking layout, making them among the most identifying browser attributes.
cards.use_when: Assessing how much identifying information your responsive storefront design indirectly exposes, or evaluating anti-fingerprinting tooling.
steps: Distinguish between querying window dimensions via JavaScript (easy to override) and inferring them by measuring whether an image displays or how text flows (hard to override without breaking rendering).
Recognize that because the hard method cannot be faked without breaking pages, viewport size tends to be a strong identifying signal.
When designing responsive storefront layouts, be aware that layout APIs used to measure rendering can serve as fingerprinting side channels.
If evaluating privacy tooling, check whether it addresses dimension-based identification, not only JavaScript-visible values.
caveats: Countermeasures here are limited; the source calls it the hardest case.
Any specific tool's handling of viewport fingerprinting should be verified for the current version.

cards.title: Use Hashing Aggregation to Reason About Poisoning Fingerprints
cards.summary: Fingerprinting implementations typically hash many inputs into one combined value; corrupting one input can invalidate the whole fingerprint.
cards.use_when: Evaluating anti-fingerprinting approaches or deciding which single signal a protection should target when full masking is impractical.
steps: Understand the implementation pattern: each input (font set, viewport, canvas output) is separately hashed, then all hashes are combined into one stored value.
Recognize the implication: altering any one contributing input changes the combined output, so you do not necessarily need to neutralize every signal.
Treat this as a reason to prioritize which signal is cheapest to randomize reliably without breaking functionality, rather than trying to mask all signals.
Do not assume this always works: the source notes it is often, not universally, true, and sophisticated implementations may be resilient.
caveats: The source explicitly qualifies this as 'not always true', so treat it as a heuristic.
Randomizing an input may degrade legitimate functionality such as localization or rendering.

cards.title: Account for Cookie Syncing Across Identifiers
cards.summary: Tracking consolidates multiple cookie identifiers into one person by matching them with fingerprint data when a cookie is new or unrecognized.
cards.use_when: Understanding why clearing cookies or blocking third-party cookies alone does not sever an existing cross-site profile of your store's visitors.
steps: Understand the pattern: when a tracker sees a recognized cookie, it stops; when it sees an unrecognized cookie, it fingerprints the browser and links the new cookie to the existing profile.
Recognize that this makes cookie clearing insufficient on its own to prevent identity linking across sites.
For analytics and personalization on your store, avoid embedding tracking vendors whose linking behavior you cannot inspect, since identifiers you set may be joined to external profiles.
Prefer first-party measurement where practical, and document which identifiers (cookies, local storage) your own stack writes so you can reason about linkage risk.
caveats: The source describes this as an extremely difficult problem to work around; do not present a simple fix as guaranteed.
Specific tracker behavior changes; verify current practices of any vendor you use.

cards.title: Check New Tags for Identity-Linking Risk Before Adding
cards.summary: Any script with broad page access may join your visitors' identifiers to external profiles; review new store tools for this before shipping.
cards.use_when: Before adding a personalization, reviews, chat, A/B testing, or attribution vendor to your storefront.
steps: Ask what identifiers the tool reads and writes, and whether it operates across other sites where it already has a foothold.
Check whether the vendor claims to fingerprint or sync cookies with other data; independent value does not require cross-site identity linkage.
Prefer tools that operate with limited page access and explicit privacy commitments, and confirm whether those commitments are contractual.
For account and checkout pages, restrict script access to data beyond what the tool needs to function.
Re-check after vendor updates, since a tool's data collection can change post-integration.
caveats: Vendor claims and practices change; verify rather than assuming.
Independent functionality does not guarantee no cross-site linkage.

cards.title: Set Up a Repeatable External Script Review
cards.summary: Consistent periodic review of embedded scripts, APIs used, and identifiers collected keeps tracking exposure from quietly expanding as the store changes.
cards.use_when: Scheduling a recurring privacy and security review of your ecommerce site, or onboarding a new developer to review standards.
steps: Establish a checklist that covers every template: home, category, product, search results, cart, checkout, account, order confirmation.
For each template, record the third-party resources loaded, what data they can read (URL, cookies, form fields, hardware signals), and whether they require permission.
Note which screens reveal sensitive product interest (health, fertility, baby, financial) where person-level targeting could create downstream disclosure harms.
Review on a recurring cadence and after each release that adds a tag, script, or integration.
Spot-check against an available fingerprint-testing tool to see how identifying your own site's configuration makes an average visitor, without assuming any single tool covers all signals.
caveats: Specific testing tools and their signal coverage change; verify current versions.
Automated tests reveal what your own rendering exposes, not what external trackers can infer from elsewhere.

cards.title: Browser API permission tiers for storefront feature planning
cards.summary: Browser APIs sit in tiers from unrestricted (DOM, downloads) through user-gesture-gated to permission-prompt and engagement-gated, and knowing the tier tells you what a storefront can do on page load versus after a user interaction.
cards.use_when: Deciding when a storefront can trigger clips, sound, fullscreen, vibration, clipboard or camera during PDP video, spin-to-win, or promotional widgets.
steps: Treat level 0 APIs (DOM manipulation, moving windows, triggering file downloads, hiding the mouse cursor) as callable the moment a visitor lands — no interaction required. Level 0 downloads are the surprising one: a page can deposit a file in a visitor's downloads folder on load, though browsers prompt before a second simultaneous download.

Treat level 1 APIs (window.open pop-ups, clipboard write, picture-in-picture, vibration) as requiring a user gesture — a click, tap or key press. Scrolling does not count; the call must be made directly inside the event handler for the gesture.
Treat level 2 APIs (geolocation, camera, microphone, torch/flash) as requiring an explicit permission prompt; a visitor must click Allow before the storefront gets the capability.
Treat the engagement-gated tier (autoplay with sound) as browser-decided: sites a visitor engages with repeatedly may autoplay audio, others will not.
Design promotional and video features so their required capability maps to a tier you can realistically reach on first visit, not one that only long-term returning visitors get.
Verify the current tier assignments in the browsers you support before shipping — several capabilities have moved up a tier over time and the exact list changes.
caveats: Tier assignments are not contractual and vary by browser and over time; the source's list is a snapshot.
Engagement-gated behavior is opaque and unpredictable for developers, so don't build critical functionality on it.

cards.title: UI denial-of-service patterns that can lock down a storefront session
cards.summary: A malicious or compromised page can override ordinary browser escape routes — back button, close-window shortcuts, context menus — and a commerce operator should know these exist as scareware and annoyance vectors, not as legitimate merchandising behavior.
cards.use_when: Auditing suspect third-party scripts, promo takeovers, or scareware landing pages that trap shoppers, and deciding what to add to a monitoring or content-review checklist.
steps: Understand the mechanism set: intercepting keyboard events so Cmd/Ctrl-W does not close the tab (partly mitigated by triggering an alert/prompt between the Cmd and W keystrokes), pushing extra history entries so the back button cannot escape the page, spawning windows from every captured user event and refocusing them, hiding the cursor via a CSS property, and stacking dialogs on a timer.
Recognize the commerce-relevant abuse case: scareware pages that claim the device is infected and lock the visitor in to make a purchase pitch more convincing, especially to non-technical shoppers.

Defend by policy and process rather than by building the same tricks: restrict which third-party scripts run on your checkout and PDP, and screen any purchased traffic destinations for trapping behavior.
Note the modern mitigation: multi-process browsers can kill a tab stuck in an infinite loop without freezing the whole browser, and file-download prompts limit bulk silent downloads.
Do not use these techniques on your own storefront — the source frames them as attacks, and trapping visitors is a legal and trust risk, not a conversion tactic.
caveats: The source describes these as attack patterns demonstrated in a classroom setting; the card converts them into vulnerability recognition and prevention, not reproduction instructions.
Some mitigations described are historical and browser-specific; verify current behavior.

cards.title: GET-request and CSRF exposure in storefront logout and account actions
cards.summary: State-changing actions reachable by a GET request can be triggered by any site embedding a matching image or link, so a storefront should keep logout, prefetch and account mutations behind POST plus SameSite cookies.
cards.use_when: Reviewing storefront endpoints for logout, cart mutation, wishlist, subscription pause, and account actions before launch or a security audit.
steps: Inventory every endpoint that changes server state: log out, add/remove cart line, apply coupon, pause subscription, change email. Flag any that answer to GET.

Reason about exposure: because any page can cause a GET by embedding an image whose URL points at your endpoint, a visitor to a third-party site can be logged out of your store or have cart state altered without noticing.
Require POST (with CSRF token) for state-changing operations, and set SameSite on session cookies so a cross-site request cannot carry the shopper's authenticated cookie.
Check whether your platform already does this and whether legacy endpoints slipped through — the source notes even large providers have left logout-style GET endpoints working.
When evaluating a third-party integration, ask whether its callbacks to your store use POST with CSRF protection or whether they silently rely on GET.
Retest after any framework upgrade, since fetch/prefetch behavior and cookie defaults change between versions.
caveats: The source's Gmail/Google logout example is a case observation, not a claim that any particular store is currently vulnerable; verify your own endpoints.
SameSite cookie support and defaults have changed over browser versions; confirm current browser handling.

cards.title: Client-side fingerprinting surfaces to audit on a storefront
cards.summary: Audio, WebRTC, plugin and font surfaces can identify a visitor across sessions even without cookies, so a store owner should know which of these their analytics and anti-fraud vendors touch.
cards.use_when: Reviewing analytics, anti-fraud, or ad-fraud scripts on a PDP or checkout for covert device-based identification, and preparing a data-privacy disclosure.
steps: Know the surface list: canvas rendering differences, audio via AudioContext capability probing or generated waveform hashing, WebRTC enumeration of device names or IDs (labels or IDs depending on granted permission), installed plugins or unusual Java versions, and font enumeration.
Expect these to be hard for a shopper to fake — the source notes several are effectively impossible for a normal user to spoof, so relying on them implies persistent identification.
When evaluating anti-fraud or attribution tools, ask whether they use any of these surfaces and whether that use is disclosed in your privacy notice.

Watch for the false-security trap: a browser extension that lies inconsistently across surfaces (for example reporting one region on one endpoint and a different preferred language on another) can make a visitor MORE identifiable, not less.
Plan disclosure and consent around this: aggressive fingerprint-based tracking is a compliance and trust exposure for a store, separate from its effectiveness.
caveats: The source calls this a representative, not complete, list of fingerprinting methods.
