Fingerprinting guidance from the lecture includes opinion about tools and is not a legal opinion about what your store must disclose.

cards.title: Choosing a client-side anti-tracking approach for a storefront's third parties
cards.summary: The source lays out five high-level counter-measures to fingerprinting and rates them, which is useful when deciding how aggressively a store blocks or degrades third-party scripts.
cards.use_when: Choosing how a store handles third-party analytics, tag managers and ad pixels — whether to strip capabilities, standardize, scope by origin, add noise, or adopt a privacy-budget style limiter.
steps: Option 1 — remove the functionality (disable canvas reads, font enumeration, and similar). Works because benign uses are rarer than abusive ones, but it breaks legitimate use cases and is a losing long-term strategy for a product that wants broad site compatibility.
Option 2 — standardize the value across browsers so everyone reports the same thing. Conceptually different from removal but functionally close — you have effectively broken the functionality anyway.

Option 3 — scope access by origin, letting first-party code do more and third-party frames less. The source notes this is a useful primitive but you still need a concrete mechanism to block each specific endpoint, not just a policy about who may use it.

Option 4 — inject noise via steganography (subtly perturbing high-entropy values so readings are unusable for identification while remaining imperceptible). The speaker rates this as the most promising current approach, with the caveat that a determined fingerprinter can detect and discard the noised values.

Option 5 — privacy budgets (Google's proposal): enumerate endpoints, assign identifying bits, and stop granting access past a precision threshold. The speaker calls this a bad idea with unresolved scope, lifetime and third-party budget questions.
Apply to your store by asking which option each vendor actually implements before trusting it; a 'privacy-friendly' label does not tell you which approach is behind it.
caveats: The ratings (option 4 promising, option 5 bad) are the speaker's opinions, not settled consensus; the privacy-budget proposal is described as an early proposal likely to change.
Permission-prompt strategies suffer from well-documented prompt fatigue — visitors reflexively accept, so don't treat prompts as reliable user consent for heavy device access.
Engagement-derived permission decisions are hard for developers to reason about and change unpredictably.

cards.title: Drawing the line between store conveniences and visitor harm
cards.summary: A concise framing for evaluating storefront growth mechanics: an anti-tracking approach that continuously degrades other sites is itself an abuse pattern, and privacy harms are a fail state, not a feature.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a growth hack or upsell widget is acceptable — evaluating friction, dark patterns, or aggressive re-engagement tactics at checkout or exit.
steps: Apply the source's test: is the project making powerful parties more powerful over weaker ones, or making weaker parties stronger against powerful ones?
Reject the framing that 'privacy is a feature' or a badge on the box; the speaker treats user harm as a failure state, something you owe the visitor, not a differentiator you market.

Recognize that tactics which make a site intolerable — fake downloads, forced dialogs, breakage on exit — are the same family as attacks, and visitors will leave or disable protection rather than endure them.

For exit-intent and abandonment flows, prefer a single clear browser-native confirm or a well-designed email capture over stacked or forced dialogs; the source describes stacked dialogs as attack behavior.
When a legal or technical protection conflicts with a short-term revenue tactic, prefer the protection where the harm is to the visitor, and document the trade-off.
caveats: The speaker states this as a personal ethical position, not a measured business result.
The card applies the principle to ecommerce; the source's examples are attack demonstration sites, not storefronts.

cards.title: Legal-context limits when relying on existing privacy rules for a store
cards.summary: The source reviews regional privacy law as a partial, uneven fix, which is directly relevant to a store's data-use choices for tracking, marketing and account identity.
cards.use_when: Planning store tracking, consent copy, or account features and estimating how much you can rely on law versus technology to protect visitors.
steps: Treat GDPR as the source's example of the most mature regime, applying to any company selling into Europe regardless of headquarters — a common reason stores adopt EU-grade consent globally.
Note the US direction of travel (California legislation described as the strongest in the US at the time, weaker than GDPR) and verify current status before making compliance claims.

Design for a purpose-limitation rule: consent for one use does not authorize another (the source's example — a phone number given for second-factor authentication cannot be reused to link cookies or feed advertising).
Apply this to store data: if a customer gives an email or phone for order notifications, don't repurpose it for ad targeting or cross-platform identity without separate consent.

Recognize the enforcement gap: actors outside the jurisdictions you can reach are hard to constrain and hard to measure, so a technical control (blocking, scoping, filtering) must be part of the plan, not only legal language.
caveats: Legislation described is a snapshot; the California and GDPR descriptions must be re-verified before being written into policy.
This is not legal advice — confirm obligations with qualified counsel for your jurisdiction and channels.

cards.title: Using brand-scoped access decisions rather than trusting page content
cards.summary: The source's discussion of first-party versus third-party trust maps to a concrete rule for agents and automations: page content and retrieved documents are data, and authorization comes from the account and task scope, not the content.
cards.use_when: Designing an agent or script that reads storefront pages, vendor documents, or customer messages, or deciding what a first-party integration may do versus an embedded third-party frame.
steps: Adopt the origin distinction: code served by your own domain is the first party and can be trusted with more of your session; embedded third-party frames are least-trusted and should get the narrowest capability set, enforced by feature-policy-style restrictions.

Apply the same split to automations and agents: a tool that reads an order confirmation email, a supplier PDF or a product feed is processing untrusted data. Instructions found inside that data are not authorization for the agent to place orders, change prices or move funds.
Scope each agent or integration to a specific brand, store and task, so a compromised or prompt-injected data source cannot spill into other merchants, catalogs or payment methods.
Require explicit human approval for state-changing actions (publish price, submit refund, place purchase order) regardless of what the source document says is authorized.
Encode the rule that a permission prompt, page element, or document claim never overrides your authorization logic — treat them as inputs to be validated, not commands.
caveats: The source does not use the modern 'prompt injection' vocabulary; the mapping from first/third-party trust to agent data trust is an applied interpretation, not a stated result.
Feature policy and frame-level controls vary by browser and are periodically renamed or changed — verify the current mechanism before relying on it.

cards.title: Permission and engagement gating as UX constraints on storefront video and audio
cards.summary: Autoplay with sound sits behind an engagement gate, so a PDP or landing page should not expect sound to play on a first visit, and should design video merchandising accordingly.
cards.use_when: Planning PDP video, hero autoplay, or promotional overlays that include audio, and deciding whether to mute by default or gate playback behind a click.
steps: Assume audio cannot autoplay on a visitor's first arrival; browsers gate it behind a user gesture and may relax that based on engagement.
Capturing the gesture is the realistic path: attach a click listener and call play inside the handler — the call must be made directly in response to the event, not from a deferred callback.
Expect returning, engaged visitors to behave differently — the source notes sites like YouTube start playing immediately because those users have a history of triggering audio and staying.

Choose a default: the source notes a well-known demo defaults its video to muted, which sidesteps the gate; a product page promoting a video with sound should either mute by default or use a clear play button.
Do not build a core purchase path that depends on a capability you may not get on first visit; keep the fallback (poster image, muted loop) as the primary experience.
caveats: Engagement gating is browser-specific, undocumented at the rule level, and changes over time.
The requirement that the call happen inside the gesture handler is a technical constraint that breaks subtle deferred implementations.

cards.title: When clipboard and download APIs are acceptable on a storefront
cards.summary: Clipboard read and multi-file download are gated or restricted for good reason, and a store can use clipboard write and single downloads in legitimate flows when triggered by a real user action.
cards.use_when: Implementing coupon copy buttons, share links, invoice or label downloads, or a 'your download is starting' page after purchase.
steps: Keep clipboard writes tied to a user gesture; a write on any captured interaction can silently replace the visitor's clipboard, and the source describes the abuse of injecting promotional content.
Never expect clipboard reads without a permission prompt — the source lists this as intentionally gated so a site cannot read what the visitor has copied.

Use single-programmatic downloads freely: a post-purchase or thank-you page that starts a file download without an extra click is an accepted pattern, and the source identifies that pattern as the reason the capability stays ungated.
Plan for the multi-download prompt: a second simultaneous file download triggers a browser prompt, so bundle or multi-file downloads need a user click or a zip.

Consider the version gap: if you want a shopper to trigger actions in a privileged context (local tool, hardware button, permission prompt), note that this space was once Flash territory and verify the modern browser route before building.
caveats: Browser gating for downloads and clipboard has changed repeatedly; verify current behavior on target browsers.
The source's examples are demonstrations, not measurements of storefront conversion effects.

cards.title: Standardizing error and edge behavior to reduce identifying signal
cards.summary: Browsers respond differently to errors and edge cases, so a site's error behavior itself can reveal browser and version — relevant when you worry about bot detection or anti-fraud false positives.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why anti-fraud or analytics flags certain customer segments, or when configuring a storefront so error responses don't become an identifying signal.
steps: Understand the mechanism: if a visitor spoofs a user agent, a fingerprinter can break them out by making the browser throw and reading the subtly different error response across browsers and versions.

Expect the same idea applied to HTML parsing: the source cites a body of work enumerating malformed-HTML cases that both enable code execution and act as fingerprinting surfaces, with standardization of error conditions as the proposed remediation.
For a store: standardize your own error pages and API error responses so they don't reveal stack details, framework versions or platform identities to scanners and fraudsters.
Reduce reliance in anti-fraud scoring on browser-version tells that can be spoofed, since a determined actor can and does falsify them.
Test error behavior across the browsers your shoppers actually use before drawing conclusions from a bot score, since the same visitor may look different from different environments.
caveats: The source presents this as an area of active research with no complete solution; the error-case work is cited as a paper reference, not a shipped product.
Do not treat error standardization as sufficient bot detection or blocking on its own.

cards.title: Budgeting identifying bits across third parties before adding another script
cards.summary: Every tracking script and third-party tag adds identifying precision, and privacy-budget-style schemes raise unresolved scope and lifetime questions that a store owner should understand before adopting a vendor that claims to solve them.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing which analytics, chat, personalization and ad scripts to keep on a checkout or PDP, and evaluating a vendor's 'privacy budget' claim.
steps: Start from the observation that fingerprinting endpoints vary widely in how much they identify — the source's illustrative attribution is roughly a bit for one endpoint up to about 13 bits for a strong one, and those add up.

Ask three questions of any budget-style or scoring scheme before trusting it: what happens when the budget is exhausted (do features break?), what is the lifetime of the budget (a fresh allowance per page view makes the scheme meaningless), and does the scope reset per third party?

Recognize the third-party problem: if each embedded third party gets its own budget, identifiers can be traded across parties; if the budget is shared page-wide, one third party can exhaust the first party's allowance — the source calls both outcomes a game-changer.
For your store, count the third-party scripts actually running on checkout and PDP and remove any whose marginal value does not justify the added identification.
Treat privacy-budget proposals as early-stage and likely to change; don't build contractual promises on them.
caveats: The source states that this proposal likely will not ship in its stated form and calls it a bad idea; that is the speaker's prediction, not a settled outcome.
Bit-count attributions in the source are illustrative of the approach, not measured effectiveness for any actual deployment.

cards.title: Privacy-preserving measurement for store analytics
cards.summary: Differential-privacy-style methods (the source's 'analyzed' approach, mixing survey-like results through secret-sharing and noise) can offer privacy guarantees for aggregate reporting, which is a realistic fit for store dashboards.
cards.use_when: Choosing a privacy-preserving analytics approach for store performance reporting, cohorts or vendor-shared benchmarks.
steps: Understand the model at a high level: it treats a transaction as if it were a survey result and mixes data across a secret-sharing scheme with clustering and timing before reporting, producing privacy guarantees in aggregate.
Apply it where a store needs aggregate numbers (conversion by cohort, category performance) but does not need per-customer granularity to make the decision.
Do not expect it to replace operational data you need per-order — privacy-preserving aggregation is for reporting, not fulfillment or customer service.
Treat specific mechanism details as the source does: presented briefly, complex, and requiring separate study before adoption.
When a vendor claims differential privacy, ask for the guarantee's parameters and scope, since guarantees are only meaningful with their epsilon-style budget and the population they cover.
caveats: The source explicitly declines to explain the mechanism in detail and calls it sophisticated and hard to summarize in the time available; don't over-claim what it does.
This is a research direction described by a speaker, not a documented storefront result.

cards.title: Defend storefront links against tab nabbing (reverse tabnabbing)
cards.summary: Any outbound link that opens in a new tab can let the destination site navigate your customer's original store tab to a fake page, so add rel=noopener to external links.
cards.use_when: Auditing or building outbound links on a storefront, PDP, blog, help center, or email/chat share flow that opens partner, review, ad, or supplier links in a new tab.
steps: Understand the vulnerability condition: if a link uses target="_blank", the newly opened page receives window.opener pointing back at your store tab and can navigate that tab to an attacker-controlled clone (e.g. a fake login). This is a demonstrated classroom result, not a live incident report.
As the linking site, add rel="noopener" to every external link that opens a new tab. The source frames this as the standard defense on the linking site.
In a component-based storefront, add the attribute once in the shared link component so every rendered link inherits it, rather than hunting links manually.

Confirm your framework versions and current browser behavior before assuming a default; the source notes browser vendors have discussed changing defaults, so verify current behavior rather than assuming target=_blank is safe or unsafe today.
Do not rely on CAPTCHA, HTTPS, or a WAF for this class of issue; those controls address different problems. HTTPS alone never guarantees the destination is trustworthy.
caveats: The source presents this as an unsettled area; browser defaults and mitigations (and a proposed isolation header) may change, so verify against current browser documentation.
This card is about links your store produces outward, not about fixing a third party's site.

cards.title: Use SameSite cookies to block cross-site state-changing requests
cards.summary: SameSite cookie attributes stop another origin from triggering requests that carry a logged-in customer's cookies, defending against cross-site request forgery.
cards.use_when: Configuring session cookies for customer login, cart, or admin accounts, or reviewing whether an authenticated action (e.g. cart change, address update, admin mutation) can be triggered from a third-party page.
steps: Recognize the CSRF conflict: an attacker page can point an image, form action, or similar request at your store and the browser may attach the victim's cookies to it. The source notes some large providers have historically appeared vulnerable to this pattern.
State-changing operations should use POST (or equivalent), not GET-through-an-; a GET URL that logs a user out or mutates state is inherently abusable.

Set SameSite on session/auth cookies. Strict sends cookies only on top-level navigations from your own site and withholds them on cross-site requests; Lax sends them for normal navigations but blocks them from cross-site subrequests. Treat Lax/Strict as the source's two documented modes and choose per flow.

Test the tradeoff: Strict can break legitimate cross-site return flows (e.g. returning from a payment or identity provider). Lax is the source's practical compromise for flows that need a normal navigation with cookies.
Independently verify your CSRF token strategy; SameSite reduces but does not by itself guarantee protection for every browser or legacy flow.
caveats: The source explicitly says it is uncertain why some major sites appeared to remain vulnerable, so do not treat SameSite as a proven universal fix.
Strict can break payment/SSO return journeys; validate your checkout flow before switching.

cards.title: Recognize IDN homograph attacks against lookalike domains
cards.summary: Unicode look-alike characters let an attacker register a domain that renders identically to a brand domain, so verify the true host and prefer password managers on high-risk flows.
cards.use_when: Training support teams, reviewing brand-domain monitoring, or designing login and admin flows where a customer or staff member might be steered to a lookalike domain via a link in a chat, ad, or email.
steps: Vulnerability condition: a hostname can be built from non-ASCII Unicode letters (e.g. Cyrillic) that are visually identical to Latin letters, so the rendered URL looks like the real brand while the bytes differ. This is a demonstrated condition, not a claim about your store.

Know browser rendering heuristics: browsers may show a domain in 'punycode' (the xn-- form) instead of the Unicode characters when the domain mixes scripts or contains look-alike characters against a non-international TLD. The exact rule differs by browser and version, so verify current behavior rather than trusting a screenshot.

Note the known weakness: if the whole domain is composed of one non-Latin script, browsers have historically displayed it as normal text and the look-alike can pass unchecked. The source says some browsers still had not fixed this at the time of the recording.

Practical controls: use a password manager for staff/admin accounts so credentials are never auto-filled on an unrecognized origin; use hardware security keys where possible; keep an eye on brand lookalike registrations.

Communicate simply: teach staff to read the registrable domain (the part just before the first single slash, roughly the last two dot-separated labels), not the full URL from the left, because attacker-controlled subdomains are prepended.
caveats: Browser URL rendering changes over time; the 2017-era examples may not match current interfaces.
The source notes HTTPS padlock and extended-validation UI do not reliably signal trust and historically did not prevent this attack.

cards.title: Be skeptical of HTTPS padlock and EV badges as trust signals
cards.summary: A padlock proves encrypted transport to some server, not that the operator is legitimate, and attackers can obtain certificates freely.
cards.use_when: Deciding which trust indicators to display on a storefront or checkout, or explaining to customers and staff why a padlock is not a legitimacy guarantee.
steps: Understand the distinction: a secure connection means you are talking to the server named in the certificate over encryption. It does not establish that the operator is who they claim.

Recognize the incentive: certificate authorities are automated and commercial, and free issuance (e.g. the source's mention of Let's Encrypt era behavior) means anyone controlling a domain can obtain a certificate with no human review. Treat certificate issuance as evidence of domain control only.

For storefront design: do not present a padlock or 'secure' badge as proof of legitimacy in your own UI; that reflects your site, and the customer's browser UI is a separate, attacker-spoofable surface.
Keep real controls on the sensitive paths instead: password managers, hardware security keys, and verifying the registrable domain.
Do not claim HTTPS, hashing, CAPTCHA, a WAF, or prompt filtering alone guarantees security in policy or marketing copy.
caveats: Certificate issuance policies and browser UI (e.g. EV treatment) change; verify current practice before citing specifics.
This covers why padlocks are insufficient, not how to configure TLS.

cards.title: Defend against clickjacking that overlays fake trusted UI
cards.summary: Attackers can hide or overlay interfaces so store actions (buttons, consent, downloads) get clicked under a misleading visual, and the durable defense is framing/isolation control on your own pages.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether your checkout, login, admin, or consent pages can be embedded by third parties, and hardening framing headers for sensitive store surfaces.
steps: Vulnerability condition: an attacker page embeds or overlays your interface under a decoy visual so the user clicks the real hidden control (the source calls this clickjacking and notes cookie-drag variants). The demonstration is a classroom result; treat it as a vulnerability pattern.
As the framed site, send an anti-framing header (the source references X-Frame-Options) on sensitive pages so browsers refuse to render them in third-party frames.

Understand the relevant cookie-mode distinction the source notes: with Strict SameSite, a cross-site request that relies on navigation may not carry cookies, which reduces some overlay utility, but this is a partial layer, not a complete frame defense.
Test in an owned staging environment whether your checkout, login, and admin pages can be embedded from a different origin you control; document the result rather than assuming.
Combine with password managers and hardware keys for authentication so a mis-clicked overlay cannot yield reusable credentials.
caveats: The source's demonstrations are historical and some attacks were later blocked by browser changes; verify current browser support for framing headers.
Frame headers alone do not stop all overlay tricks on other surfaces.

cards.title: Manipulated browser history and UI-suppression tricks are perception attacks
cards.summary: Attackers can add embarrassing or misleading entries to a visitor's history and hide the browser UI on scroll, so trust decisions should not rest on ambient browser chrome.
cards.use_when: Assessing how a visitor could be convinced a phishing page is a trusted store (e.g. a fake bank or brand login reached from an ad, chat link, or QR code) and choosing defenses that do not rely on browser chrome.
steps: Vulnerability condition: a page can cause top-level navigations that appear in the visitor's history (the source describes opening a popup to a search and navigating a window it holds a reference to). Frames do not add history entries because they are not top-level navigations.

Recognize the UI-hiding variant: the source shows a page embedding an inner scroll region so the browser hides and never restores its own chrome, letting the page draw a fake URL bar. This is a demonstrated technique, not a claim about current browsers.
Treat all of this as an attack on human perception, per the source: there is often nothing wrong with the code being attacked, only with the UI cues people rely on.

Better defenses: password managers (which bind credentials to a known origin and will not autofill on an unfamiliar one) and hardware security keys (which will not release the secret to the wrong site).
Assume a segment of users will end up on a sketchy page and layer in reputation warnings (safe-browsing-style) rather than expecting users to read the URL bar accurately.
caveats: These specific demonstrations are historical and reported as fixed or dependent on access to another site's window reference; verify current browser behavior.
The source explicitly says there is no easy way to defend a site against a picture-in-picture fake-browser attack.

cards.title: Verify what your URL bar actually shows before trusting subdomains
cards.summary: Browsers render long attacker-controlled subdomains inconsistently, and shrinking the window can hide which domain is real, so teach customers and staff the registrable-domain rule.
cards.use_when: Writing security education for staff or customers, and evaluating whether a URL in a support ticket, ad, or partner link is a real brand domain versus a lookalike subdomain.
steps: Vulnerability condition: subdomains are free to create, so an attacker can register any domain they control and prefix it with a brand name (e.g. brand.com.webapps.example-attacker.com). The registrable domain is the part before the first single slash, roughly the last two dot-separated labels.

Know that browsers differ: the source observed Chrome and Safari rendering the whole hostname in black and greying only the path, while Firefox greyed out the subdomain to highlight the registrable domain. Verify the current behavior in your target browsers.

Test the shrinking case: when the window narrows, browsers may show only part of the hostname, and the source shows a lookalike subdomain can appear safe ('looks like PayPal'). Do not trust a truncated URL bar.
Operationalize for ecommerce: in support and staff training, tell people to locate the first single slash and read left to the registrable domain rather than reading the URL left to right.
Additionally, monitor for and file takedowns of brand-prefixed lookalike subdomains and typo-squatted domains, and use password managers/hardware keys on seller and admin logins.
caveats: URL bar rendering is browser-specific and changes over time; treat the described behaviors as observations at the time of recording.
The registrar/domain-attribution rule is a heuristic for reading URLs, not a security control.

cards.title: Treat browser UI/API features as a security-vs-capability tradeoff with fingerprinting cost
cards.summary: Powerful browser APIs enable richer shops but expand attack surface and fingerprinting vectors, and the cost/benefit is judged by how often disabling a feature breaks real sites versus how often it is implicated in exploits.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add a browser-capability-dependent storefront or checkout feature (device APIs, media capture, sandbox/iframe isolation requirements) and judging the customer-risk tradeoff.
steps: Apply the source's rough usefulness metric: if a feature were disabled, how many real sites break? Widely used capabilities (e.g. video/voice calling in the source's example) carry high benefit; rarely used ones (the source's example: vibration) are harder to justify.
Apply the rough cost metric: how much code does the feature add and how often has it been implicated in browser vulnerabilities? More code and more exploit history mean higher risk.

For an ecommerce feature decision, ask whether the capability is on a customer-trust-critical path (checkout, login, payment, account) or a low-stakes path; be more conservative on trust-critical paths.

Prefer build defaults that do the right thing rather than a prompt for every capability. The source cites research that users click through prompts heavily (fewer than a quarter of Chrome malware/phishing warnings and a third of Firefox SSL warnings were clicked through, versus about 70% on older, poorly designed Chrome SSL warnings), so prompt design and frequency matter.

Do not rely on security prompts as your only control; combine defaults with isolation and authentication controls. Note the source's counterintuitive finding that early-adopter/beta users clicked through phishing warnings at higher rates than average.
caveats: The usefulness metric is explicitly described as rough; it is a judgment aid, not a benchmark you can cite as fact.
The prompt click-through figures are from a 2010-era research context and should be treated as historical, not current browser behavior.

cards.title: Check URLs against a safe-browsing list without leaking full browsing history
cards.summary: Safe-browsing style protection queries a reputation list using hash prefixes downloaded locally, so a store or browser can warn on known-bad URLs without sending each full URL to the provider.
cards.use_when: Evaluating or implementing URL reputation/abuse-warning tooling for a storefront, link shortener, or marketplace, and deciding between real-time URL submission and a downloaded prefix list.
steps: Recognize the naive approach and its two costs: sending each URL in the clear to the reputation service leaks the full request (and by extension browsing behavior) and adds latency because the check must complete before loading.
Alternative: download a large list of suspicious URLs locally to avoid latency, but accept that the list is constantly changing and enormous. The source frames both as workable but inferior.

A better model: the provider hashes suspicious URLs, keeps a list of hash prefixes, and distributes only the prefixes to clients. The client hashes each URL it inspects the same way, takes the prefix, and checks membership locally.
Consequence of prefix matching: a match means the URL may be unsafe, not that it definitely is; treat a hit as a candidate for a fuller check rather than a verdict.

Apply the principle to ecommerce tooling: prefer local/prefix-based reputation checks over submitting every customer or staff destination URL to a third party, and log which tool used which data source.
caveats: The source describes the protocol at a high level and defers detailed mechanics to a later session; verify current provider documentation before implementing.
Hashing obscures the URL but prefix lists are an approximation and produce false positives.

cards.title: Design browser security around an assumed-sketchy-site layer
cards.summary: Rather than handicapping the browser with endless prompts, assume users will reach malicious sites and add a separate reputation/warning layer that protects them there.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much friction to add to storefront security prompts (login, payment, download, permission requests) and where to invest instead.
steps: Adopt the source's framing: UI security is an attack on human perception, so plan for the case where the visitor is on a sketchy page rather than trying to prevent every such visit through warnings.
Keep tasteful, well-worded prompts in specific high-value places where research shows they work, per the source's reading of the prompt-effectiveness paper; avoid showing prompts constantly.
Add an independent protective layer (browser/store warnings, password managers, hardware keys) that works even when the page's own UI is misleading.
For your own store, keep prompts on sensitive flows specific and actionable, and test whether a prompt is understood rather than assuming more warnings equals more safety.

Recognize the underlying tension the source describes between the browser as a simple document viewer and as a powerful app platform; this tradeoff does not go away and should be acknowledged rather than claimed solved.
caveats: Presented as an ongoing design tension with no settled solution; do not present prompt counts or warning text as a guaranteed control.
Click-through statistics cited are historical research figures, not current benchmarks.

cards.title: Scope untrusted content and tool output as data, not authority
cards.summary: Pages, documents, and agent/tool output can be attacker-influenced and must not be treated as authorization for privileged store actions.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing ecommerce automation (order bots, support agents, listing tools, integrations) that reads external content or tool output and can take store actions.
steps: Treat any retrieved document, web page, email, review, or tool response as untrusted data. Do not let it authorize actions such as refunds, price changes, credential changes, or fulfillment edits.
Bind permissions to the brand and the task: an agent that manages listings should not hold payment or customer-account credentials, even if a retrieved document asks it to act.
Require explicit human approval for irreversible or financially material actions, and log which actor, tool, and source triggered each action.
Keep secrets out of retrieved content and tool output where possible; store credentials in a scoped secret store and reference them by role rather than pasting them into prompts or configs.

Rely on authentication/authorization, encryption, hashing, and signing as distinct controls: authentication proves the caller, authorization scopes what they may do, and no reputation list or prompt filter substitutes for either.
caveats: No single control (HTTPS, hashing, CAPTCHA, WAF, prompt filtering) guarantees security; layer controls and verify against current platform documentation.
This card transfers the source's phishing/untrusted-content principle to agent tooling; the source itself did not test agent permission models.

cards.title: Convert an embarrassing-history or fake-UI trick into a customer-protection test
cards.summary: Use the source's demonstrated browser-abuse techniques as vulnerability conditions to test your own store's exposure rather than as offensive recipes.
cards.use_when: Running a defensive review of storefront pages, popups, and iframes that could be repurposed by an attacker, or training support staff to recognize manipulated browser UI.
steps: Frame each technique as a condition to check on owned systems: can a third-party page cause a top-level navigation from my store, can my checkout be framed, can an overlay hide my own controls, and does my session cookie ride along on cross-site requests.
Test only in owned staging environments and with accounts you control; do not attempt these techniques against third-party sites.
Record findings as concrete controls to add (rel=noopener on outbound links, anti-framing headers on sensitive pages, SameSite cookie mode, POST for state changes) rather than as payloads.
For each control added, note the residual risk: frame headers do not stop every overlay, and SameSite strict can break legitimate cross-site returns such as payment provider redirects.
Re-verify after browser or framework upgrades, since the source's own examples were fixed by vendors over time.
caveats: Omit or avoid reproducing payload recipes; this card deliberately describes conditions and defenses only.
The source's demonstrations are classroom and historical; do not present them as current live exploitable behavior without verification.

cards.title: Use Safe Browsing hash-prefix lookups to block malware/phishing destinations
cards.summary: How browser-style local hash-prefix matching lets you flag malicious URLs without sending full URLs to a third party, and its limits.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to screen outbound links, user-submitted content or redirect URLs (e.g. affiliate links, UGC product listings) against known malicious destinations without leaking every URL to a reputation service.
steps: Understand the mechanism: a reputation service hashes reported malicious URLs (e.g. SHA-256), keeps the full hashes, and distributes only truncated hash prefixes to clients so the download stays small.
On the client, hash a candidate URL the same way and compare its prefix to the downloaded list. If the prefix is absent, the URL is guaranteed not to be in the known-malicious set (a clean pass).

If the prefix matches, treat it as 'maybe malicious' only, because chopping the hash introduces collisions. Send the prefix (not the full URL) to the service to fetch the full hashes sharing that prefix, then confirm an exact match.

Account for evasion: attackers can randomize query strings, so the lookup should test multiple URL variants — e.g. the full path, progressively trimmed paths, and the site home page — rather than one exact URL. A hit on the home page blocks the whole site.
As an ecommerce operator, apply this to any place you accept or forward third-party URLs (user reviews, affiliate feeds, image/link uploads) and to protecting your own checkout redirect chain.
Treat the list as one layer of defense-in-depth; it will always miss fresh or never-reported URLs.
Note the privacy trade-off: even prefix-only queries leak that a user visited some URL sharing that prefix, and repeated queries from one IP can be correlated over time.
caveats: Hash-prefix checking is a blacklist approach and is guaranteed to miss unseen or newly created malicious URLs.
Truncated-prefix collisions mean a prefix hit is not proof of malice — always confirm with the full hash.
A whitelist-only approach is impractical for dynamic URLs (query strings, unique document keys) since it blocks anything the service has not seen.
If you implement this yourself, verify the current Safe Browsing API behavior and rate/format requirements before relying on it.

cards.title: Why hashing is used for integrity and lookup, and what its properties guarantee
cards.summary: The five properties of cryptographic hash functions that make them useful for URL reputation, integrity checks and lookups.
cards.use_when: Choosing or reviewing a hashing scheme for things like URL/entity reputation lists, file-integrity checks on uploaded assets, or tokenizing customer data for lookups.
steps: Pick a hash function that is one-way: given the output you cannot feasibly recover the input, so a leaked hash list does not directly expose the original URLs or IDs.
Confirm determinism: hashing the same value twice yields the same output, which is what makes prefix/equality lookups possible across many clients.
Confirm speed: the function must be fast enough to run on every candidate URL or request, since lookups happen frequently.
Confirm collision resistance: it should be infeasible to craft an input that produces a chosen hash value — important if a passing hash is treated as authorization for a safe/valid object.
Confirm avalanche behavior: a tiny change to the input (e.g. one query parameter) should drastically change the output, which is what stops trivial near-duplicate evasion of a hash-based blocklist.
Distinguish this from encryption and signing: hashing is for compact comparison and integrity, not for confidentiality of recoverable data or for proving authenticity by itself.
caveats: Truncating a hash (as with hash prefixes) deliberately weakens it — collisions become expected, so a truncated match is a candidate, not a verdict.
Hashing does not make an input safe or authenticated; it only lets you compare values without storing the raw values.

cards.title: Model side channels on your storefront: a correct system can still leak data
cards.summary: Side-channel attacks reveal information through timing, size or sensor differences even when no code bug exists, which matters for how much you expose cross-site.
cards.use_when: Threat-modeling your storefront or admin pages for what a third-party script or an embedded attacker page could infer about logged-in customers, cart state or history.
steps: Recognize the definition: a side channel is leakage from a correctly implemented system, via timing, layout, power, size or sensor readings, not from a logic bug.
Inventory the observable differences your pages create for logged-in vs logged-out users: response sizes, layout width shifts, redirect targets, timing of protected vs public responses.
Assume any state that changes rendered output (button labels, banner widths, item counts) can be measured by a third-party page that embeds a request to your origin.

Reduce precision and observability: make protected and public code paths take similar time, keep response sizes consistent, and avoid conditionally rendering elements whose dimensions reveal account state.
Treat repeated embedding of your URLs in untrusted pages as a fingerprinting channel; limit what cross-origin embeds can trigger on your domain.
Operate under the source's framing: side channels are everywhere and very hard to fully prevent, so prioritize the ones that reveal account status, payment state or order contents.
caveats: Most demonstrated attacks (reading QR codes via ambient-light sensor, recovering speech via gyroscope) are proof-of-concept and may be impractical in real conditions.
Fully eliminating side channels is not achievable; mitigations reduce precision or rate rather than guaranteeing elimination.

cards.title: Fix visited-link and history leaks: browser whitelists, timing and lying APIs
cards.summary: How browsers mitigated CSS-based browsing-history leaks and why the fix is intentionally incomplete, with lessons for styling untrusted links.
cards.use_when: Handling links to third-party or user-submitted destinations on product pages and deciding which link styling is safe to let influence layout or resource loading.
steps: Understand the leak: browsers render :visited links differently, and a page can read style or trigger resource loads to learn whether a visitor has been to a URL, exposing browsing history at scale.

Whitelist CSS properties for visited links so styling cannot cause layout, size or resource-loading side effects — restrict visited styling to color, underline, weight and similar non-layout properties.
Make the browser's internal handling of visited vs unvisited links take equal time, so timing the href change or redraw does not reveal state.
Have the browser report unvisited styles when script queries computed styles of visited links, so direct inspection lies rather than leaks.

Accept that the fix is incomplete: rendering-time differences (e.g. expensive text-shadow on visited links) can still be measured with requestAnimationFrame timing, especially with many links and large shadow radii.
For your own store, avoid relying on :visited for anything functional and be cautious about heavyweight visual effects on link-heavy pages if you handle untrusted links.
caveats: The source presents the 2010 browser mitigation as partial — later timing-based demonstrations still recovered visited history.
Some listed attacks require specific browser implementation details that may have changed; verify current behavior rather than assuming it still holds.

cards.title: Prevent cross-origin state leaks via embedded images and layouts
cards.summary: Images embedded from another origin attach that origin's cookies and can reveal logged-in state through size or layout differences.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing any partner widgets, tracking pixels or third-party scripts that embed requests to your logged-in domains on a storefront or admin panel.
steps: Recognize the mechanism: when a page requests an image from another origin, the browser automatically attaches that origin's cookies, so the returned asset can be conditioned on the victim's login state.
Understand the leak channel: if a logged-in response (e.g. a 'Log out' button) differs in width from the logged-out response, an attacker page can detect the layout shift and infer account state.
Apply the fix: use SameSite cookies so that cross-site requests do not carry session cookies, causing the embedded resource to always render as logged-out.
Audit any images, pixels or embeds that hit your authenticated origins and can be included from arbitrary third-party pages.
Treat distinguishing logged-in vs logged-out as valuable to phishers, since it lets them pick which brand to impersonate.
Combine with consistent asset sizing so conditional states do not also leak via width or height differences.
caveats: This is described as an inherent leak from how same-origin policy interacts with image embedding rather than a single implementation bug.
SameSite is the principal mitigation; without it, correctly implemented pages still leak login state.

cards.title: Decide how to handle ambient-light and sensor APIs on your storefront
cards.summary: Sensor APIs (ambient light, gyroscope) can leak information through measurable screen or device changes, which shaped whether browsers expose them.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to use device-sensor APIs (light, motion, orientation) in responsive storefront features and how to bound the risk of the data they expose.
steps: Recognize the risk pattern: if a page can show or hide white/black or colored content and then read an ambient-light sensor, it can confirm which of two visual states it caused, leaking visited-link status, browser state or image contents.
Note that the same pattern was shown to extract a QR code: zoom into one square, read the light value to determine black vs white, and iterate to reconstruct sensitive content.
Treat motion/gyroscope access as a similar channel — high-precision readings can capture acoustic vibration, effectively bypassing microphone permission if exposed without restriction.
Mitigations browsers considered or shipped include putting the sensor behind a permission, limiting the frequency of sensor readings, and quantizing (reducing) the precision of sensor output.

For your own store, prefer explicit user-granted permissions rather than silent sensor access, and do not build features that depend on reading sensor data while showing attacker-controllable content.
Verify current browser vendor and OS behavior before relying on any sensor API — availability and permission requirements have changed over time.
caveats: The source notes these attacks are often impractical (full-screen, slow, visible) but were serious enough to make browsers reconsider shipping sensor APIs.
Sensor permission and precision behavior is browser- and OS-version-specific and changes; do not assume a current configuration.

cards.title: Prevent command injection in server-side features like file or report generators
cards.summary: Never concatenate untrusted request data into shell commands; use argument-array process APIs that escape inputs.
cards.use_when: Building or reviewing any server-side feature that shells out — file viewers, image converters, PDF/CSV exporters, backup scripts — triggered by storefront or admin input.
steps: Identify the vulnerability: concatenating untrusted input (URL params, form fields, cookies, headers) into a string passed to a shell interpreter lets attackers append commands using shell syntax like semicolons.
Verify the impact: injected input can execute arbitrary OS commands on the server — listing directories, reading files, creating or deleting files, or worse.

Fix the root cause: do not build a command string from program name plus user data. Use an API that takes the program and an argument array (in Node, spawnSync with ['cat', ...args] instead of execSync with a concatenated string) and escapes arguments for you.
Run the child process with least privilege and validate/allowlist expected arguments (e.g. permitted filenames or extensions) rather than trusting the raw value.
Keep the server bound to a restricted interface during development/testing so you do not expose a vulnerable demo to the network.
Understand that error handling and output should not echo raw command output back to the client if it can reveal filesystem contents.
caveats: The escaping function differs by language and framework; verify the safe API for your stack rather than assuming one exists.
Escaping arguments protects against shell metacharacter injection but does not make an arbitrary file viewer safe by itself — still restrict which files or operations are allowed.

cards.title: Recognize code injection as the parent category behind XSS and similar bugs
cards.summary: Code injection mixes untrusted user data with interpreter code so the interpreter misreads data as commands.
cards.use_when: Reviewing how any user-supplied value reaches an interpreter (HTML, SQL, shell, template) on your storefront, checkout or admin tooling.
steps: Define the pattern: code injection occurs when the interpreter processes a mixture of programmer-written code and untrusted user-supplied data.
Understand the failure mode: the interpreter cannot distinguish user data from programmer commands, so attacker input is executed as instructions.
Note the escape technique: attackers break out of the data context using a special character (a quote, semicolon, or similar syntax) and start writing code.
Treat XSS as one concrete instance of this broader category, alongside command injection, SQL injection and template injection.
Apply the general fix principle: keep code and untrusted data strictly separate, and escape or parameterize user data before it reaches any interpreter.
Recognize that the client controls everything it sends — URL, body, cookies, headers — so all client-provided input must be treated as untrusted.
caveats: The correct escaping/parameterization mechanism is interpreter-specific; a fix for one context (e.g. HTML) does not protect another (e.g. SQL or shell).

cards.title: Prevent command injection with argument arrays, not string templates
cards.summary: Use language APIs that accept a program plus an argument list so escaping is handled by the runtime, and never build shell strings from user input.
cards.use_when: You are building storefront features that shell out to a tool — image resizing, PDF generation, label printing, inventory export scripts, or any admin automation that runs a program on user-supplied values.
steps: Identify every place in the store backend where a user-controlled value (filename, SKU, uploaded asset name, search term) is concatenated into a command string.

Replace string concatenation with the API that takes the program name plus an array of arguments; in Node-style runtimes the source used spawnSync with an argument array, and equivalent functions exist in Python, Ruby and other languages — verify the current API for your runtime version.
Rely on the runtime to escape each argument so quotes, semicolons and other attacker-controlled characters are treated as literal data, not shell syntax.
Confirm the semantics: the call should run exactly the named program with those arguments and nothing else, and should reject attempts to append a second command.

Check the return shape — the source found the API returns a child-process object rather than stdout, so inspect the exit status and read the captured stdout on success and stderr on failure, and surface the failure to the operator instead of silently continuing.

Treat escaping as only one control: if the command itself is dangerous because the user can choose any file, path or target, fix that separately with an allowlist of permitted files/directories and an authorization check on the requesting account.
Validate on your own staging environment with benign but tricky inputs such as a filename containing a semicolon and a filename containing quote characters, and confirm no second process runs.

For admin or agent automation, require that the tool allowlist is defined by the brand, log every invocation with the requesting user, and treat any retrieved text or document as data that cannot expand the allowed command set.
caveats: Escaping alone does not make an inherently dangerous command safe — the source explicitly notes that if the produced command is one you don't want to run, nothing protects you.
The source presentation is a classroom demonstration on a deliberately vulnerable app; do not test injection strings against third-party or production systems you do not own.
Argument-array APIs and their exact behavior differ across languages and versions; verify the current interface rather than assuming.
Do not claim that using argument arrays guarantees security — it removes one class of injection but not path traversal, authorization gaps or bad command design.

cards.title: Recognize and close SQL injection in store login and lookup queries
cards.summary: Any query that concatenates user input into SQL can be manipulated to bypass login, enumerate the customer table, or delete data — parameterize queries and constrain what the query is allowed to return.
cards.use_when: You are reviewing or building store account login, order lookup, coupon validation, search filters, inventory reports or any admin query that embeds form input or URL parameters into SQL.
steps: Map every query that mixes a literal template with request values — login forms and any 'find by email/SKU/coupon' route are the highest-value targets.

Understand the failure modes you are defending against: an attacker who can change the query can read any table, modify rows, run administrative operations such as dropping tables, and in some database configurations execute operating-system commands, which is effectively full server takeover.
Replace string interpolation with parameterized queries or prepared statements that bind values separately from the query structure, so user input can never alter the query's shape.

Where the schema permits it, tighten the query's intent: the source's login example uses a get-style call intended to return at most one user row, which also rejects multiple statements in that API — but the source warns that other APIs in the same library (an exec-style call that supports multiple statements) do not give you that protection, so never rely on it.

Do not store or compare plaintext passwords; the classroom example kept them in plain text for demonstration only. Hash with a current password-hashing algorithm and verify credentials through the hash, and verify current recommended parameters for your platform.
Restrict database credentials so the application account cannot drop tables or run administrative statements, and separate read paths from write paths.

Log failed login and lookup attempts for anomaly detection, but write the log with a parameterized insert — the source shows a logging insert as an attack vector when it is built from string concatenation.
Validate on your own environment: submit a benign value containing a single quote to the login and search fields and confirm it is treated as ordinary text with no error page or behavioral change.
caveats: Single-quote testing is a diagnostic signal, not a proof of absence — a quote causing a different response suggests vulnerability, but a normal response does not by itself prove safety.

The source's examples are classroom demonstrations on an intentionally vulnerable bank app; do not run these strings against systems you do not own, and do not include working payload recipes in team documentation.
WAFs, input sanitizers or ORM usage do not by themselves guarantee safety; parameterization plus least-privilege database accounts is the durable control.
Verify current database driver and ORM behavior rather than assuming a specific API's protections.

cards.title: Understand and bound blind SQL injection as an operational risk
cards.summary: When an injection point does not echo query output, an attacker can still extract data by asking true/false questions through error behavior or response timing, so detection must not depend on visible output.
cards.use_when: You are assessing the risk profile of a store search, filter, order-status lookup or API endpoint that returns a generic success/failure response, and deciding how much effort detection and parameterization deserve.
steps: Accept that absence of echoed query results does not mean an injection point is low risk; the source describes two blind variants.

Variant one, boolean/error-based: the attacker constructs a condition and learns the answer because the page responds differently — for example a matched row returns an array where the code expected a single value and the handler crashes — so an observable difference between error and non-error states becomes a yes/no oracle.

Variant two, time-based: the attacker embeds an expression that deliberately runs slowly (the source's example builds a large blob, converts it to a hex string and uppercases it, costing roughly a third of a second) inside a conditional, so a slow response means true and an immediate response means false, and measurement of response time answers the question.

Recognize that the attacker can iterate character by character — the source's script tested each letter of a password by checking a substring condition and assembled the whole password regardless of password complexity, because only a timing difference was needed per character.

Defend by parameterizing queries so the injected condition never executes, by adding rate limiting and anomaly alerts on repeated near-identical requests or unusual response-time variance, and by keeping error pages generic so error/non-error is not a clean oracle.

Validate only on your own systems using timing measurement and error-message inspection to confirm parameterized queries produce uniform behavior; do not attempt randomized extraction against third parties.
Note that timing-based defenses are probabilistic — network jitter and load affect measurement, so treat timing anomalies as a signal for investigation, not as proof.
caveats: The timing values in the source are demonstration artifacts of a specific query on a specific machine, not a benchmark for detection thresholds.
Blind extraction is described as requiring creativity and patience; the source notes it is harder than visible-output injection, so prioritization should still weight visible-output endpoints higher.
Do not present error-page suppression or a WAF as a guarantee — both reduce signal for attackers but do not fix the underlying injection.
Time-based detection is noisy in real traffic; confirm before acting on alerts.

cards.title: Layer safe-browsing-style URL reputation using local hash prefixes
cards.summary: Download a locally cached list of hash prefixes for known-malicious URLs so most checks happen offline, then confirm only on prefix matches to limit what you disclose.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating or implementing a link-safety or phishing-warning feature for a storefront — for example scanning user-submitted review links, affiliate URLs, supplier links or outbound links in marketing content before they are shown or clicked.
steps: Understand the naive design and its two costs: querying a reputation service in real time for every URL sends your full browsing or link data to a third party and adds latency because nothing loads until the answer returns.
Downloading the entire malicious-URL list locally removes the latency and privacy problem but the list is constantly changing and very large, so a full download is impractical for repeated refresh.
Adopt the prefix approach: the provider hashes each known-malicious URL, truncates each hash to a prefix, and distributes only the prefix set, which the client caches locally.

To check a URL, hash it with the same algorithm (the source describes SHA-256) using the same transformations the provider uses, truncate to the same prefix length, and look the prefix up in the local set; a miss means the URL is safe with respect to that list and can proceed immediately with no network round trip.

On a prefix hit, the URL may or may not be malicious, so send only the prefix — not the full URL — to the service and receive the set of full hashes sharing that prefix, then compare your full hash against that returned set. If your full hash is present the URL is known-bad and you should warn; if not, it is safe.

Implement URL variant checking the way the provider's algorithm does, because attackers randomize query parameters: the source says roughly ten to twenty variants are checked, including progressively shortened paths and the site's home page. A reported malicious home page blocks the whole site and forces an attacker onto new domains that cost money to register.
Verify the current algorithm, prefix length and variant rules against the provider's live documentation before implementing, and log block events for review.
caveats: This is a blacklist approach and is guaranteed to miss cases — newly registered domains, unseen URLs with unique tokens such as private document links, and dynamic query parameters will not be listed. The source presents this as a trade-off: a whitelist would be unusable for the open web but may suit highly paranoid, narrow contexts.
Prefix truncation leaks some information: a provider can learn that you visited a URL matching a given prefix and could correlate requests over time by IP.
Always treat safe browsing as an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for browser protections or for your own link and content review.
List sources include user reports and automated crawling in sandboxed environments; coverage is not guaranteed and current behavior should be confirmed with the provider.

cards.title: Understand side-channel leakage as a class of risk to storefront logic
cards.summary: A system can behave exactly as designed and still leak secrets through timing, power or visual emissions, so security review must consider what observable differences reveal about hidden state.
cards.use_when: You are designing storefront or API logic that must not reveal whether a customer, coupon, account or inventory condition is true — for example email-enumeration checks in password reset, coupon validity endpoints, or stock lookups on a product page.
steps: Accept the definitional point from the source: a side channel exists when the implementation is correct — no code bug — yet an attacker can learn information they should not, because the system behaves observably differently between cases it is trying to hide.
Enumerate the observables in your own stack: response time, response size, error text, HTTP status, and the order in which your server performs work.

Identify secrets whose value is being compared or looked up: whether an email is registered, whether a password guess matched a prefix, whether a coupon code exists, whether a given SKU is in stock at a specific warehouse.

For each, design the response so the observable is identical in both cases — same status code, same generic message, same approximate duration — and where comparison itself is the secret, use constant-time comparison for secrets such as tokens and password-derived values rather than short-circuiting on the first mismatched character.
Rate-limit and monitor for repeated near-identical probing patterns, since side-channel extraction works by asking many small questions and observing answers over time.

Validate on your own environment by measuring response-time variance and comparing response bodies for the true case and false case of each question, then confirm the two distributions are not trivially separable.
Treat timing variance as noisy: network conditions and server load blur measurements, so a timing difference is a signal to investigate, not proof of exploitability.
caveats: The source's vivid examples — recovering speech from high-speed video of a chip bag or plant leaves, and extracting keys from power-line monitoring — are research results in physical settings; they illustrate the general principle, not a threat model for an online store.
Do not present constant-time comparison, uniform error messages or rate limiting as a guarantee against all side channels; they remove specific observables.
Measurement-based validation on shared infrastructure is approximate and should not be treated as a certified threshold.

cards.title: Browser history disclosure via CSS :visited and the whitelist trade-off
cards.summary: Links styled by :visited once let any page read a visitor's browsing history, and the durable fix is restricting which CSS properties can apply to visited links rather than trying to hide the difference.
cards.use_when: You are reviewing a storefront's CSS or third-party scripts embedded on PDP, checkout or content pages, and deciding whether any styling rule could reveal a visitor's prior browsing behavior to that page.
steps: Understand the historical vulnerability: browsers rendered visited links in a different default color than unvisited links, and scripts could read a link's rendered color to determine whether the visitor had been to a URL. Enumerating a large array of URLs would reveal the visitor's interests and history.

Recognize that the leak is not limited to color: the source notes CSS can also load a background image from an attacker's server when a link is visited, giving the attacker a server-side request as the signal, and can alter a visited link's position or size, which JavaScript can detect via layout changes.

Note the attempted alternatives and why they were rejected: only marking visited when the user clicked from that same site was considered but dropped for usability reasons because users would be confused by inconsistent styling, and simply making the color unreadable does not address the other CSS channels.

Apply the principle of the 2010-era mitigation: restrict the set of CSS properties that can apply to :visited links to a small whitelist of text-level changes such as color, underline, bold and italic, removing background images, positioning and sizing so layout-based detection is impossible.

Apply the accompanying performance-based defense: slow down the rate at which a page can probe history, making bulk enumeration impractically slow rather than impossible — the source frames this explicitly as accepting that the issue cannot be fully fixed and raising the attacker's cost instead.

For your own storefront, audit every third-party script and stylesheet on customer-facing pages for use of :visited selectors and layout-changing rules, and remove or isolate anything that reads computed styles of links.

Verify the current browser implementations rather than relying on the historical description — modern browsers continue to restrict :visited styling, so check current behavior before assuming a specific fix.
caveats: The source describes a 2010 change, attributed in the lecture to Mozilla/Firefox; browser behavior has evolved since, so treat the specific implementation as historical context and verify the current state.
This is a privacy leak of browsing history, not a data breach of your store's own records; the primary harm is to visitors.
Style restrictions do not make visited-link state invisible in principle — they reduce the channels through which it can be read.
Do not claim that removing a selector or a script guarantees no history disclosure, since other techniques may exist.

cards.title: Secure handling of retrieved documents and tool output in agent workflows
cards.summary: Text fetched from the web, uploaded by users, or returned by a tool is untrusted data and must never be treated as authorization to change an agent's targets or expand its permissions.
cards.use_when: You are deploying an ecommerce automation agent that reads supplier pages, review content, uploaded CSVs, order notes or API responses and then acts — for example updating prices, drafting replies, creating orders or running scripts.
steps: Classify every input the agent processes into trusted configuration versus untrusted content, where untrusted includes scraped pages, user-uploaded files, email bodies, third-party API responses and any tool output that carries external text.
Define the agent's permitted scope explicitly by brand and task — which store, which tables, which tools, which files — as configuration the model cannot alter from content it reads.

Never let instructions found inside retrieved content change the target, destination, data range or command that will be executed; if a document appears to contain directives, treat that as content to report, not to obey.

Restrict tool permissions to the minimum needed for the task: read-only query access where writes are not required, an allowlist of programs the automation may run, and no shell string construction from fetched values.

Require human approval for irreversible or high-impact actions such as bulk price changes, refunds, order cancellations, credential changes or any operation that deletes data, and log the approval with the actor identity.

Handle secrets outside of content: keep API keys and database credentials in a secret store that the agent can use through a scoped interface but cannot read back into its context or write into a file, and rotate them on a schedule.
Log every tool invocation with the requesting identity, the exact parameters, the retrieved content hash and the outcome, so an anomalous action can be traced and replayed.
Validate on a staging store by feeding a document containing injected directive-like text and confirming the agent takes no action outside its configured scope and instead surfaces the anomaly.
caveats: Do not claim that prompt filtering, a WAF or content sanitization alone guarantees safety against injected instructions in retrieved content.
Distinguish authorization from data handling: seeing a credential or an instruction is not permission to use it, and encryption protects data at rest or in transit, not the decision to act.
This card adapts the source's injection principle to agent inputs; the source does not present an agent-specific benchmark or outcome.

cards.title: Visited-Link History Leaks and Storefront Fingerprinting Risk
cards.summary: Browsers mitigate visited-link sniffing with CSS whitelists, timing equalization and style lying, but rendering-timing side channels still leak which URLs a user has visited.
cards.use_when: Auditing storefront or marketing-site third-party scripts and ad pixels for the risk that they fingerprint visitors' browsing history, or advising engineering on what a page's own rendering performance reveals about customer behavior.
steps: Understand the core vulnerability: browsers apply a 'visited' style to links a user has clicked before, and though the page cannot read the true computed color of a visited link, it can measure how long the browser takes to render or reflow when a link's state changes.

Recognize that browsers restricted visited-link styling to a small whitelist (color, underline, bold/italic), equalized internal code-path timing, and made style-querying APIs lie (return the unvisited color) — but these are incomplete, so don't assume visited-state is fully protected.

Treat any third-party script on your PDP, category, or landing pages as a potential timing side-channel: a script can swap an anchor's href between a never-visited made-up URL and a target URL and time the redraw via requestAnimationFrame, using a large text-shadow and thousands of links to amplify the signal.

Assess the practical risk for a store: leaking which product, category, or competitor URLs a visitor has seen enables cross-site behavioral profiling and targeted phishing; weigh it against the ad/analytics value of the script.
For your own first-party pages, keep third-party JS minimal and audited in checkout and account flows, where a history leak plus a credential-capture page is most damaging.
Verify current browser mitigations before acting: behavior described here is implementation-specific (notably Chrome) and changes over time, so re-test rather than relying on a fixed rule.
caveats: The timing technique is unreliable — the source's demo had false negatives (a visited link measured below threshold) though no false positives; enlarging the shadow was only a hypothesis for improvement.
This is a fundamental, hard-to-fully-fix client-side problem; there is no complete mitigation, so scope decisions to risk reduction, not elimination.
Do not assume any single browser mitigation (CSS whitelist, timing equalization, lying APIs) prevents all leaks — the source explicitly calls the solution incomplete.

cards.title: Cross-Site Image Requests and Cookie-Bearing Side Channels
cards.summary: Images embedded on any site send the target origin's cookies automatically, so an attacker can infer login state or read sensitive images via layout and rendering side channels.
cards.use_when: Reviewing cookie attributes, third-party image embeds and account-state endpoints on a storefront, or threat-modeling how a competitor or attacker page could learn whether a customer is logged into your store or payment/email accounts.
steps: Understand the mechanism: when a page loads an image from another origin, the browser automatically attaches cookies for that origin, and the response can vary (e.g. a 'log in' vs 'log out' button of slightly different width) based on those cookies.

Recognize that the embedding page cannot read the foreign image's pixels or cross-origin state, but can still infer it: differences in image dimensions can shift layout, which attacker JavaScript detects; the attacker can also just observe the rendered size.

Prevent it for your own store by setting same-site cookies (SameSite) on session and authentication cookies so they are not attached to requests initiated from other origins, which forces the cross-site request to look signed-out.

Audit any state-dependent images or endpoints (login buttons, feature flags, personalized banners) that return different content for logged-in users and are embeddable cross-site, since these are the exploitable surfaces.

Also treat sensitive images (e.g. QR codes containing keys) as leakable via side channels: because image dimensions/position are observable, avoid serving secrets as embeddable images without origin restrictions and auth checks.
Verify the current cookie defaults and SameSite behavior in target browsers before assuming protection, since defaults have changed over time.
caveats: There is no general way around the underlying information leak from image size/layout; SameSite cookies solve the cookie-attachment variant but not all size-based inference.
This is described as an unintentional leak violating the spirit of the same-origin policy, not a designed feature to rely on.
Exact browser cookie-default behavior is version- and vendor-dependent; confirm rather than assume.

cards.title: Ambient-Light Sensor as a Browser-History and Image-Reading Side Channel
cards.summary: An unpermissioned ambient-light API can be abused to infer visited links and even read sensitive images pixel-by-pixel by correlating screen output with room brightness.
cards.use_when: Deciding which browser sensor/permission APIs to allow or request on a storefront or PWA, or assessing privacy exposure of device-sensor features used for theming, games or interactive PDP experiences.
steps: Understand the attack: a page can render content (e.g. a link with a black background if unvisited, white if visited, or a QR code region) and read the ambient-light sensor value (0–1) to infer what is on screen.

Calibrate first by showing a fully white page then a fully black page and reading the sensor each time; then render the target and infer its color from the sensor value against those two reference readings.

Recognize the image-reading variant: because a QR code (or any sensitive image) loads cross-origin with cookies but cannot be read as pixels, an attacker can zoom the display into one cell at a time and read black vs white via the sensor, reconstructing the whole image.
For your store, avoid using sensor-gated features that could be repurposed; if you add light-adaptive theming, know that fine-grained ambient-light access can silently expose on-screen content.
Mitigations to consider: request sensor access behind a permission prompt, limit the frequency of sensor reads, and quantize sensor precision so a site cannot extract high-resolution signal.
Check your target browsers: this API's shipping status and permission model were under reconsideration at the time of the source, so verify the current interface before building on it.
caveats: The demonstrated attacks are described as technically real but low-practicality (they occupy the screen and are visible to the user); practicality doesn't remove the policy violation.
Browser vendors were reconsidering whether to ship the ambient-light API unpermissioned — availability and protection status must be verified and may differ per browser.
Restricting these APIs also breaks legitimate demos and features; treat this as a security-vs-capability tradeoff, not a free win.

cards.title: Gyroscope API Eavesdropping and Sensor Permission Tradeoffs
cards.summary: Highly precise, unpermissioned motion sensors can pick up acoustic signals and infer speech, illustrating why sensor APIs belong behind permission prompts.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a storefront, web game or interactive product experience should request motion/orientation sensor access, and auditing which sensitive device-permission APIs your site invokes.
steps: Understand the 2014 Stanford finding: the gyroscope API could be precise enough to pick up acoustic signals so a site without microphone permission could infer what was being said near the device.
Recognize the general pattern — any unpermissioned, high-precision sensor (motion, ambient light, etc.) can be repurposed as a covert input channel and a privacy leak.
