For your store, avoid requesting motion/orientation access unless a specific interactive feature genuinely needs it, and explain why when you do; users who grant access for a game are also granting whatever else the site does with the data.

Accept that once a user has granted a permission, you cannot reliably control how the data is subsequently used — the same concern applies to native apps that use granted navigation/location data for ad targeting.
Mitigations for platforms/your own features: gate sensors behind permissions, limit reading frequency and quantize precision to reduce the extractable signal.
Verify current platform state: iOS moved the gyro API behind a permission flag (reported around iOS 12/13), so check the present OS/browser behavior before relying on it.
caveats: Locking down sensor APIs breaks legitimate orientation-based experiences; this is an explicit security-vs-capability tradeoff.
The eavesdropping demonstration was a research result, not a promise that arbitrary sites will succeed against modern devices — precision and OS gating affect feasibility.
Permission prompts do not fully solve the problem, because users may grant access for one purpose and the data may be used for another.

cards.title: Why Side Channels and Phishing Resist Full Mitigation
cards.summary: Side channels are pervasive and hard to eliminate, phishing is fundamentally a human problem, and browser security controls always trade off against web capabilities.
cards.use_when: Setting realistic security expectations for a storefront — deciding how much engineering effort to spend on browser-level hardening versus user education, monitoring and account controls.
steps: Treat side channels as an inherent, ongoing class of leak rather than a single bug: timing, layout, image-size and sensor channels each need separate analysis, and fixing one doesn't close the others.

Treat phishing as a human problem: a phishing page becomes more effective when it first learns (via a side channel) which service the victim uses, so reducing pre-click information leaks also reduces phishing success — but no single control eliminates phishing.

Accept the security-vs-capability tension: every restriction that closes a side channel (banning link styling, gating sensor APIs) also breaks legitimate features, so design controls to target the highest-risk leaks rather than blanket bans.
For a store, combine layered defenses: minimal third-party scripts, SameSite session cookies, MFA and login-anomaly monitoring, and clear customer communication about how your store contacts them.

Distinguish login/session security from data-leak concerns when prioritizing, and don't expect any one mitigation (HTTPS, CAPTCHA, a WAF or prompt filtering) to guarantee safety against these classes.
Re-verify browser mitigations over time, since vendor behavior is implementation-specific and changes as standards evolve.
caveats: Side channels are described as fundamentally hard, if not impossible, to fully prevent — plan for risk reduction, not elimination.
Phishing success depends on user behavior and cannot be fully engineered away.
Do not assume any single control guarantees security; treat each as one layer among several.

cards.title: Command Injection in Store Backends and the Argument-Array Fix
cards.summary: Combining untrusted user input into a shell command string lets attackers run OS commands on the server; use argument-array APIs that escape input instead of string concatenation.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or writing any store backend code or admin/integration feature that shells out — file viewers, image/asset processing, export tools, report generators or third-party CLI wrappers.
steps: Understand the vulnerability condition: whenever code concatenates untrusted input (URL params, form fields, cookies, headers) into a shell command string, a special character such as a semicolon can terminate the intended command and start a new one the attacker controls.
Recognize that untrusted data reaches the shell wherever the client can influence a value — query strings, form bodies, cookies — so treat all of it as attacker-controlled.

Fix it by using a spawn-style API (e.g. Node's spawnSync, with equivalents in Python, Ruby and others) that takes the program name and an explicit array of arguments, so the library escapes each argument and guarantees only the intended program runs.

Avoid the insecure pattern (e.g. exec with a concatenated string); the safe pattern passes arguments as a list and returns a child-process object, so read stdout on success and stderr on non-zero status.

Note that escaping user input fixes command injection but does not fix other flaws: a file viewer that lets users choose any path still allows path traversal (e.g. ../../etc/passwd), so also restrict which files are accessible.
Verify the exact function signatures and return shapes in your language, since the API details differ and may change across versions.
caveats: Escaping input prevents adding commands to your program but does not prevent the program itself doing something dangerous with a valid-looking input (e.g. reading arbitrary files).
The source's live demo ran on the presenter's local interface only; do not reproduce injection tests against systems you don't own or have written authorization to test.
Exact function behavior (return value, escaping rules) is language- and version-specific — confirm against current docs.

cards.title: Review store database queries for SQL injection
cards.summary: Find data/code mixing in login, order lookup and catalog queries and replace it with parameter binding.
cards.use_when: Reviewing authentication, search or account-lookup endpoints on a store for SQL injection, or testing whether an input field safely parameterizes queries.
steps: Trace customer input and imported data into database query construction.
Use parameterized queries for values and allowlisted mappings for dynamic identifiers; avoid concatenation.
Use harmless fixtures in an owned test environment to confirm unusual input is treated as data.
Inspect query errors without interpreting every syntax error as proof of injection.
Apply least-privilege database access and review adjacent endpoints using the same query helper.
caveats: No visible error does not prove a query is safe; code review and bounded validation are complementary.

cards.title: Stacked SQL Injection via APIs That Allow Multiple Statements
cards.summary: Some database APIs permit multiple semicolon-separated statements, letting an attacker with an injection point run additional queries such as changing passwords or dropping tables.
cards.use_when: Choosing database query APIs for a store backend and reviewing existing endpoints that run SQL for login, logging or admin operations.
steps: Understand the condition: if the injection point sits in code that uses an API allowing multiple statements (e.g. an exec-style call), an attacker can terminate the intended query with a semicolon and append a second one.

Recognize the impact: an appended query can update another user's password (then log in as them), insert attacker data, or drop an entire table — the source demonstrated both password takeover and dropping the users table.

Note that some APIs (e.g. a get-style single-row fetch) reject multiple statements, so a payload that fails there may still succeed elsewhere in the same app — audit every query call site, not just one.

Watch realistic second-statement surfaces: any feature that runs an extra query on the same code path (such as inserting a login-attempt log row) can become the vector that enables stacked statements.
Remediate by using parameterized queries everywhere and by selecting database APIs that disallow multiple statements in a single call where possible; never concatenate user input into query strings.
Verify current behavior of your specific driver/library, since multi-statement support and defaults vary by engine, driver and version.
caveats: Protection against stacked queries depends on the API and database; a fix in one call path does not protect another.
The demonstrated password change and table drop are examples of impact, not guarantees that every injection yields them.
Do not test destructive payloads against systems you don't own or lack written authorization to test.

cards.title: Recognize blind SQL injection signals without exposing customer data
cards.summary: Response and timing differences can reveal unsafe queries even when the application hides database output.
cards.use_when: Assessing whether a store endpoint that accepts search/filter input and gives only success/failure or timing feedback could leak database contents, and prioritizing remediation for such endpoints.
steps: Review repeated unusual parameter probes, response differences and timing anomalies affecting store data endpoints.
Trace suspect inputs to query construction and parameterize the underlying values.
Use synthetic records and bounded tests in an owned test environment to validate the fix; do not extract real customer records.
Keep error messages generic while retaining useful restricted diagnostic logs.
Use least privilege and query/resource limits as additional containment, not a replacement for parameterization.
caveats: Timing differences can have benign causes; confirm the root cause before declaring exploitation.

cards.title: HSTS: force browsers to HTTPS and rewrite HTTP requests
cards.summary: Deploy Strict-Transport-Security so browsers internally upgrade HTTP requests to HTTPS and block certificate-error bypass for your store domain.
cards.use_when: You are hardening checkout, login and account pages against network interception, and deciding an HSTS rollout plan for your storefront domain.
steps: Serve the Strict-Transport-Security response header from your store; browsers will then internally rewrite HTTP requests for that host to HTTPS before they hit the network, and will not offer users a click-through on certificate errors for that site.
Set the max-age directive to the cache lifetime. When first testing, use a very low max-age so you can back out; mature deployments move to long values (the speaker cites around a year as a cap).
Use includeSubDomains only after auditing every subdomain, because it applies to all of them — the source notes large organizations get stuck when one vendor-operated subdomain lacks HTTPS.

Because a subdomain cannot set HSTS for the whole registered domain, if users land on www.example.com, load an invisible first-party resource from example.com that carries the includeSubDomains header.
Submit to the preload list only when you are committed long-term: preloading fixes the vulnerable first-visit gap but removals are slow and bottlenecked on browser release cycles.
caveats: HSTS is effectively irreversible once cached by real users — there is no undo, which is why gradual max-age increases are recommended.
The first visit is still unprotected unless your domain is on the browser preload list.
HSTS state can be abused as a tracking/supercookie vector in third-party contexts; HTTPS and HSTS do not guarantee safety on their own.

cards.title: Recognize HSTS as a persistent third-party tracking vector
cards.summary: An ad-network script can set and read HSTS state across subdomains to build a supercookie that survives normal cookie clearing.
cards.use_when: You are assessing third-party scripts, pixels or ad-network embeds on product and checkout pages for privacy and tracking exposure, or responding to a data-subject request to clear tracking state.
steps: Understand the mechanism: a third-party script sets HSTS on many unique subdomains to encode an identifier in bits, then reads it on other sites by detecting which sub-resource loads are upgraded to HTTPS.
Treat any persistent per-browser state that can be set and read in third-party contexts as a potential tracking vector, not only cookies.
Recall that HSTS state is not cleared by clearing cookies — a user (or your own QA) may believe they started fresh while persistent state remains.
Audit which third parties load sub-resources on your store templates and reduce the number of distinct third-party origins, especially on payment and login flows.

When evaluating browser protections, prefer the stable principle (limit third-party state) over current vendor-specific rules, which change; verify the current behavior in each target browser before relying on it.
caveats: The source describes Apple/Safari and Chrome mitigations as evolving and states Chrome's plan was not final at the time; do not treat any specific vendor rule as a permanent guarantee.
Prevention is described as a trade-off between security and privacy, not a solved problem.

cards.title: Treat HTTPS as baseline, not a proof of trustworthiness
cards.summary: HTTPS provides confidentiality, integrity and server authentication, but only as strong as the certificate chain behind it, so it must not be treated as a standalone safety guarantee.
cards.use_when: You are deciding what security claims to make on your storefront landing page or checkout (badges, trust copy) and which protections to actually implement.
steps: State the real properties HTTPS gives: confidentiality, integrity and authentication of the server over TLS — and that it does not by itself validate the merchant, the content, or the product.
Account for the certificate bottleneck: any certificate authority can issue for any domain, so a compromised or fraudulent CA can impersonate your store to users on the attack path.
Do not stop at redirecting HTTP to HTTPS: an attacker on the network can strip the redirect and inject content, so serve HSTS rather than relying on redirects.
Prefer controls that are checkable and auditable (CAA DNS records, certificate transparency monitoring) over claims that cannot be verified, and describe them accurately.
If you use a hosted platform (hosted CMS, cloud web server), confirm whether it enables HTTPS/HSTS for you by default and what you still need to configure yourself.
caveats: Positive security indicators such as lock icons were found by research cited in the source to be unreliable — users generally do not notice a missing indicator.
The source notes HTTPS adoption lagged in some regions historically and migrating large existing sites remains technically challenging.

cards.title: Use CAA DNS records to constrain who may issue certificates for your domain
cards.summary: Certificate Authority Authorization is an advisory DNS record that tells CAs which issuers are allowed for your domain, reducing rogue issuance without the unreliability of key pinning.
cards.use_when: You are setting up or reviewing domain-level certificate management for your storefront and want an implementable control against mis-issuance.
steps: Publish a CAA DNS record listing the CA(s) you actually use, so a CA checking before issuance sees it is not authorized and should stop.
Treat CAA as advisory enforcement: it relies on CAs behaving correctly, and remediation is after the fact (revocation, escalation) rather than runtime prevention.

Understand the gap: DNS itself was not integrity-protected or authenticated at the time of the source, so an on-path attacker between CA and your DNS could tamper with the response; the source treats it as better than nothing, not a guarantee.
Pair CAA with certificate transparency monitoring to detect issuance you did not request.
Keep records current when you change issuers, since a stale CAA record can block legitimate renewal.
caveats: CAA does not stop a determined or compromised CA from mis-issuing.
CAs generally do adhere, but this is behavioral, not cryptographic enforcement.

cards.title: Treat browser certificate pinning as deprecated and use the alternatives
cards.summary: Dynamic public-key pinning (HPKP) was removed from Chrome because chain-building differences, unrecoverable errors and hostile-pinning risk made it too unreliable; CAA, static pinning and certificate transparency replace it for most needs.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating whether to implement HPKP or certificate pinning on your storefront or deciding how to respond to pinning advice from a vendor or agency.
steps: Do not plan new adoption of dynamic HPKP: the source states Chrome unshipped it years after launch because server operators could not reliably predict the chain a client would build, and failures were unrecoverable and non-actionable for users.
If you still have HPKP configured, remove it and rely on safer mechanisms; a wrong pin with a long max-age can lock users out of your site even after you recover from an incident.
Make sure any pinning you do pin public keys, not serial numbers or other certificate fields — the source calls non-key pinning forgeable and incorrect.
Prefer CAA records plus certificate-transparency monitoring as your primary mis-issuance defense; understand both are after-the-fact/audit-based rather than runtime prevention.
Recognize hostile pinning as a risk: an attacker who compromises your server could set pins that brick access to your domain.
caveats: The source notes some operators were unhappy to lose pinning's safety benefits and were using hostile pinning as a feature; removal was a deliberate trade-off, not a claim pinning never helps.
Static preloaded pins still exist in Chrome for a curated set of high-value sites, but are not something a typical merchant can self-serve quickly.

cards.title: Plan HSTS preload carefully: it fixes the first-visit gap but is slow to reverse
cards.summary: Preload lists bake HSTS opt-in into browsers so the first visit is protected, but removal requires waiting on release cycles and getting off the list is difficult.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to submit your storefront domain to the HSTS preload list and how to sequence that decision.
steps: First recognize the gap you would be closing: without preload, the very first visit to your site is unprotected because the browser has not yet received your HSTS header.
To prove domain control for preload, serve the HSTS header with the preload directive on the site — that is the ownership proof mechanism described.

Meet the list's automated requirements, then submit via the public preload site; note that Chromium maintains the list and other browsers apply their own policies on top, so removal may take even longer.
Know the reversal cost before committing: removal could require waiting on a release cycle for Chrome and potentially longer for other browsers.
Do not submit expecting to check the site's ongoing health: the source says entries were not pruned for liveness at the time.
Weigh the binary-size cost context: on Android, larger browser binaries can mean a percentage of users do not get updates, and users may pay for the download data.
caveats: The preload list was originally intended for a small set of high-value sites and grew into an unsustainable general list, per the source.
Verify the current preload submission and removal process, as the interface and policies may have changed.

cards.title: Track your HTTPS/HSTS adoption as a migration metric
cards.summary: Migration of a store from HTTP to HTTPS should be run as a measured rollout, not a one-step switch, using max-age ramps and breakage data.
cards.use_when: You are migrating a legacy or large storefront to HTTPS/HSTS and need to sequence the rollout without breaking customers.
steps: Start with short HSTS max-age values to test, then increase toward long values once confident; the source specifically warns against jumping straight to a one-year expiration.
Before enabling includeSubDomains, inventory subdomains and any vendor-hosted services; domains without HTTPS support will block you from enabling it across the whole domain.
To cover a registered domain from a www landing page, use the first-party sub-resource trick described (an invisible resource loaded from the apex carrying includeSubDomains).
Expect breakage when disabling insecure subresources: the source describes running experiments for an extended period and measuring breakage before phasing out mixed content.
Keep the old HTTP behavior available while measuring, then deprecate it deliberately — the source frames platform changes as breaking things carefully on the platform's terms.
caveats: The specific timelines in the source are historical and may not match current browser behavior; verify against current documentation.
Not all environments can migrate at once — hosted platforms may enable HTTPS for you, while large custom deployments remain harder.

cards.title: Harden mixed content by eliminating HTTP subresources on HTTPS pages
cards.summary: Removing HTTP subresources from HTTPS pages closes a class of tampering and tracking exposure, at the cost of breaking pages that still rely on them.
cards.use_when: You are auditing product, category and checkout templates for insecure subresource loads (images, scripts, fonts, pixels) and planning remediation.
steps: Inventory every subresource loaded by your templates and flag any absolute http:// URLs, hard-coded HTTP links and HTTP-scheme embeds.
Convert them to HTTPS or same-origin resources; verify the source actually serves HTTPS, and re-test after each batch rather than flipping everything at once.
Treat the known trade-off: the source states that when a page is already served over HTTP and loads an HTTP subresource, HSTS will not be applied — you lose the upgrade on those loads.

If you sponsor or operate vendors/ad networks, require HTTPS subresource delivery in your contracts and audit their scripts, since insecure third-party scripts can be replaced with malicious content (the source cites a real-world case of analytics scripts loaded over HTTP and swapped in transit).
Run the migration as a measured experiment: the source describes a multi-year measurement phase and a staged timeline rather than a single cutover.
caveats: Legitimate HTTP links will stop working, and the source acknowledges the change causes breakage.
Browser behavior around mixed content autoupgrading has evolved; verify current behavior in your target browsers before relying on it.

cards.title: Do not trust positive security indicators or geographic CA blocking
cards.summary: Lock icons and region-based blocking are unreliable defenses; the source argues both fail in practice and should not be the basis of a storefront security plan.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how to communicate security to shoppers or being asked to approve a 'block by country/region' style control for your store or infrastructure.
steps: Do not rely on users noticing a missing lock icon: research cited in the source shows positive security indicators are not a reliable signal, so treat visual trust badges as reassurance copy, not a control.

Reject 'just block a region or country' as a certificate mis-issuance defense; the source notes issuers serve customers globally and that mis-issuance has come from various geographies, and blocking is unenforceable and hard to define.
If a vendor proposes region blocking as a security or anti-fraud measure, ask what specific threat it addresses and what false-negative rate it creates for legitimate international customers.
Invest effort instead in controls that apply to all traffic: TLS/HSTS deployment, CAA records, certificate transparency monitoring and sane third-party script policies.
If you communicate security claims to shoppers, keep them factual and verifiable rather than relying on user vigilance.
caveats: The source's remarks on certificate authorities and geography are situated in web-PKI context; regional or IP blocking can still have legitimate, non-security uses such as regulatory controls.
This is a strong opinion from the presenter, supported with historical examples rather than a controlled study.

cards.title: Keep authentication, authorization, encryption, hashing and signing distinct in store design
cards.summary: Confusing encryption, hashing, signing and authentication leads to wrong security controls; each addresses a different property and the source's TLS discussion illustrates the distinction.
cards.use_when: You are specifying security requirements for storefront accounts, payment integrations, agent credentials or admin access and need to state each control precisely.
steps: Separate the properties: TLS/HTTPS provides confidentiality, integrity and authentication of the server; hashing (like the SHA-256 used for pinned keys) is one-way and verifies material, not identity by itself.
For server identity, the relevant control is certificate validation against a trusted chain — not the lock icon and not the mere presence of HTTPS.
For integrity of a DNS-based control such as CAA, note that DNS is not integrity-protected in the source's account, so the control is advisory.
Apply the same discipline to store accounts and bot defense: do not describe CAPTCHA, a WAF or a prompt filter as guaranteeing security — none of them alone is a guarantee.
Write requirements as testable statements (which property, which mechanism, which failure mode) so engineering and vendor claims can be checked.
caveats: The source's specifics about SHA-256 pinning and HPKP describe a deprecated mechanism; the general distinction between key pinning and certificate/serial pinning remains valid.
Current algorithm and protocol guidance changes; verify against current standards before implementing.

cards.title: Treat agents' retrieved documents and tool output as untrusted data
cards.summary: In an agentic storefront workflow, inbound documents, pages and tool responses are data to be evaluated, not authorization for actions.
cards.use_when: You are building or reviewing an ecommerce agent that reads supplier documents, product feeds, customer messages or web pages and can then call tools like price updates, refunds or order changes.
steps: Classify every inbound artifact — supplier PDFs, emails, catalog feeds, support tickets, scraped pages — as untrusted data; agent instructions come only from your own configuration and authorized operators.
Scope tool permissions to the specific store and task: an agent handling product descriptions should not hold refund or pricing-write credentials.
Require explicit human approval for irreversible or high-value actions (issuing refunds, changing prices, modifying fulfillment), with the approval recorded.
Keep secrets out of agent-visible context: inject credentials at the tool-call boundary rather than embedding them in prompts or documents the agent reads.
Log tool calls with inputs, outputs, the triggering untrusted source and the resulting action, so a malicious injection can be reconstructed and reverted.
When content instructs the agent to do something outside the task, treat it as a potential injection attempt and stop rather than comply.
caveats: No single control — prompt filtering, allowlists or retrieval hygiene — is claimed to guarantee safety; use layered controls.
Verify the current capabilities and limits of whichever agent framework you deploy against current vendor documentation.

cards.title: Bound validation of storefront attacks to systems you own
cards.summary: When verifying that a vulnerability actually affects your store, test only against your own properties and describe the vulnerability condition rather than weaponizing it.
cards.use_when: You are validating a suspected weakness (timing side channel, credential stuffing, insecure subresource, injection) in your own storefront before remediation.
steps: Establish written authorization over the exact assets in scope: your domains, staging environments, test accounts and test payment flows.

Convert observed behaviors into vulnerability conditions you can check — for example, whether an endpoint returns measurably different response times depending on whether a queried condition is true, or whether responses differ based on an attacker-controlled predicate.
Design validation to confirm the condition and the fix, then verify the fix; do not build reusable extraction tooling against third-party systems.
Involve engineering early to change the design where possible (constant-time or unconditioned responses) rather than trying to detect the probing.
Record the finding with timings, parameters and environment so a fix can be regression-tested.
caveats: Testing systems you do not own or are not authorized to test is out of scope and potentially unlawful.
A timing difference observed on your environment may not reproduce on production due to caching, load balancing and network variance.

cards.title: Assume any certificate authority can issue for your store domain
cards.summary: The web PKI lets any CA issue for any domain, so planning must assume impersonation is possible and rely on detection and authorization controls.
cards.use_when: You are threat-modeling domain impersonation of your storefront (phishing clones, fake checkout pages) and choosing which certificate controls to deploy.
steps: Accept the premise: any of the trust-store CAs can issue for your domain, which cuts both ways — you can buy cheap or free certificates from almost anyone, and so can an attacker.
Layer after-the-fact detection and authorization controls: publish CAA records, monitor certificate transparency logs for your domains, and keep an inventory of who can issue for you.
Understand the trade-off: after-the-fact controls (CAA, CT) reveal and remediate mis-issuance rather than prevent a certificate from being used at runtime.
Account for attackers inside the trust path: impersonation is most effective against users on the attacker's network path, so combine certificate controls with HSTS and mixed-content hardening.
Watch for fake-checkout clones as a business risk independent of your own server security, since a mis-issued certificate makes a clone look legitimate.
caveats: CAA is advisory and DNS was not integrity-protected at the time of the source, so on-path tampering of the CAA lookup is possible.
Certificate transparency is described as auditing, with enforcement handled socially/legally rather than automatically.

cards.title: Expect migration resistance and budget for it
cards.summary: Security migrations provoke strong resistance from some operators; plan ramp, measurement and deprecation rather than arguing about old costs.
cards.use_when: You are pushing an HTTPS/HSTS or mixed-content cleanup across a large store or multi-brand ecommerce organization with legacy systems.
steps: Anticipate the standard objections — cost of certificates, performance penalties, effort — and prepare current data; the source notes certificates are now often free or cheap and modern HTTPS can outperform HTTP.
Prioritize measurement over argument: track adoption percentages and page loads still using the old scheme so you can decide when the old path can be shut off.
Handle non-expert operators by making the safe option the default where possible — the source points to hosted platforms enabling HTTPS for large numbers of sites at once.
Plan phased timelines and expect to measure breakage before removing the legacy path rather than declaring a hard cutover.
Accept that some resistance will not be resolved by evidence and sequence the migration so holdouts do not block the security goal for the rest of the estate.
caveats: The source's remarks on adoption levels and regional patterns are historical observations, not current benchmarks.
Specific performance claims about modern protocols should be verified in your own environment before being used as a business case.

cards.title: Decide between CA-permissive convenience and stricter issuance assurance
cards.summary: There is no reliable way to validate an arbitrary CA's authority; controls must either reduce which CAs can issue for you or detect their failures.
cards.use_when: You are selecting a certificate-issuance strategy or vendor for your store and weighing convenience against assurance.
steps: Recognize the failed approaches: dynamic pinning was tried and removed because chain building, error recovery and hostile pinning made it unreliable; geographic blocking is unenforceable.
Choose a detect-and-constrain strategy: publish CAA records, monitor certificate transparency, and enroll in static preload or pin programs only where you can accept the release-cycle coupling.
If you pursue static pinning, include every issuer in your pin set and be aware that a key change you cannot migrate from can brick your site in Chrome until a new release ships.
For the storefront, prefer broad compatibility (any reputable issuer) with strong detection over narrow issuer restrictions that create operational fragility.
Review any agency recommendation to implement certificate pinning with skepticism, given the source's account that the web platform removed the feature.
caveats: The source presents pinning removal as a deliberate trade-off, noting that pinning works when everything is aligned.
Static preload pinning still exists for a curated set of high-value sites; eligibility and process are not self-serve.

cards.title: Certificate Transparency: Detection, Not Prevention, for Storefront TLS
cards.summary: CT makes mis-issued TLS certificates publicly discoverable rather than blocking them, so ecommerce operators should monitor logs for their own domains instead of treating CT as attack prevention.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to monitor for fraudulent or mistakenly issued TLS certificates on your store's customer-facing domains.
steps: Understand the distinction the source draws: CT is detection, not prevention (unlike certificate key pinning, which aimed to block malicious certs). There is a window where an attacker can use a mis-issued certificate before it surfaces in logs.

Because any certificate (issued intentionally, accidentally, or maliciously) can be submitted to CT logs by the CA, the site operator, or even crawlers like Googlebot, assume certificates for your domain may appear without your involvement.

Use CT monitoring as one layer of defense-in-depth: watch public logs for certificates on your domains that you did not request, and treat unexpected entries as a trigger to investigate your CAs and resellers/vendors.

Treat CT coverage as a noisy-attack deterrent and hygiene tool (the source notes Facebook discovered accidentally issued certs via CT, and CAs have been caught violating requirements) — not a guarantee that malicious certs are blocked.
Do not rely on CT as your only control; pair it with other transport and authentication protections.
caveats: CT does not provide the security properties of key pinning; mis-issued certs remain usable for a period.
A malicious log could delay or selectively omit certificates, and detection timing is unspecified.
The source describes CT deployments as still evolving, so verify current browser/log behavior before depending on it.

cards.title: Authentication vs Authorization: Keep Session Tokens Out of the Permission Business
cards.summary: Authentication verifies identity while authorization decides permissions; store session IDs that map to server-side authorization checks rather than embedding permissions in client tokens.
cards.use_when: Designing login, session, and admin-role handling for a storefront or its backend (customer accounts, staff/admin panels).
steps: Separate the two concepts: authentication answers 'who is this user'; authorization answers 'what is this user allowed to do' (the source notes NIST stresses authentication does not determine access privileges).
When you issue a session ID to a logged-in customer, issue an identifier only, then look up their current authorizations server-side on each protected request.
Avoid handing clients signed tokens that literally encode 'I am allowed to do X' — the source notes you cannot expire or update embedded permissions when rights change.
Model permissions with an ACL (user → allowed actions) or a capability token (a unique hard-to-guess URL token, like a Google Docs link) depending on the access pattern you need.
For store admin and fulfillment roles, re-check authorization on the server per request so revoking staff access takes effect immediately.
caveats: The source presents this as general guidance; exact mechanisms (ACL vs capability tokens) trade off revocation and simplicity.
Capability-style URL tokens remain valid as long as the URL leaks, so treat them as bearer credentials.

cards.title: Username Handling Rules: Case-Insensitive Uniqueness, Preserved Display Case
cards.summary: Store usernames case-insensitively with enforced uniqueness while preserving the user's preferred capitalization for display, to avoid duplicate accounts and impersonation collisions.
cards.use_when: Implementing customer account creation and login for a storefront where usernames or display handles are used.
steps: Enforce that usernames are unique so a second user cannot register an easily-confused variant of an existing account.
For lookup, normalize the typed username (e.g., lowercase it) and compare against a stored normalized column so logins are not case-sensitive in a way that creates duplicates.
Add a second stored column holding the user's preferred capitalization and render that version in the UI.
Reject registration attempts that collide after normalization, not just after exact match.
Apply the same normalization thinking to any account identifier your admin/fulfillment tooling keys on.
caveats: The source treats case-insensitive uniqueness as the goal; some systems deliberately allow case-sensitive identifiers — decide deliberately rather than by accident.

cards.title: Modern Password Policy: Length Over Complexity, Breach-List Checks, No Forced Rotation
cards.summary: The source's updated password guidance is to allow long passwords, enforce a minimum length, drop complexity/rotation rules, and screen new passwords against known breach data.
cards.use_when: Setting password rules for your store's customer accounts or admin logins.
steps: Stop requiring a mix of upper/lowercase, numbers, and symbols: the source argues 'complex is not necessarily strong' and such rules push users toward predictable patterns like trailing digits.
Stop forcing periodic password changes and password histories; the source calls three-month rotation outdated advice that yields trivial incrementing.
Encourage passphrases: multiple words from a large dictionary were shown by the source to yield more entropy than symbol substitution, and are easier to remember.
Allow long passwords (the source suggests permitting up to ~64 characters) but set a sensible maximum to avoid password-denial-of-service via slow hashing on huge inputs.
Enforce a minimum length (the source calls 8 characters the bare minimum, and notes even that is low).
Screen chosen passwords against known breach databases — the source cites this as NIST's current recommendation.
caveats: Breach-list blocking can reject a user's legitimate existing password if it has ever leaked — a usability/security tradeoff the source acknowledges, so weigh it against how sensitive the account is.
The source frames these numeric thresholds as heuristics, not universal law; the entropy claim depends on dictionary size and attacker assumptions.

cards.title: Password Handling Mistakes That Break Security and Usability
cards.summary: A catalog of password anti-patterns the source flags — silent truncation, blocked paste, weak hints, on-screen keyboards, and max-length caps — that weaken real security while annoying users.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a login/signup implementation before launch or when auditing an existing storefront's authentication.
steps: Do not silently truncate long passwords: the source notes bcrypt caps at 72 ASCII characters and requires only 72 bytes of input, so if you allow longer you must hash first or accept truncation ambiguity.
Do not disable cut-and-paste in password fields — this breaks password managers, which the source calls out as a real security loss.
Do not set low maximum password lengths for legacy reasons; the source describes banks capping at ~10 characters as an anti-pattern.
Avoid password hints with tiny answer sets (the source cites an airline whose hint answers were a dropdown of ~8 options, giving roughly a 1-in-8 guess).
Do not rely on on-screen click keyboards against keyloggers; the source notes screen recording and click interception defeat them while harming usability.
Allow arbitrary Unicode (including emoji) in passwords, then hash the password before feeding it to length-limited algorithms like bcrypt.
Never log passwords in plaintext — the source cites incidents where logs captured credentials; scrub auth fields from request logging.
caveats: The bcrypt 72-byte limit is a specific library behavior; verify your hashing library's limits rather than assuming.
Some of these patterns (e.g., max length) may be forced by legacy systems — the source treats them as mistakes to migrate away from.

cards.title: Defending Against Network-Based Guessing: Rate Limiting, Lockouts, CAPTCHA
cards.summary: Brute force, credential stuffing, and password spraying are distinct online guessing attacks; the source's defenses are rate limiting by username and IP, delays/rejections, and CAPTCHA as a human check.
cards.use_when: Hardening the login endpoint of a storefront or admin panel against automated credential guessing.
steps: Distinguish the three attacks: brute force iterates passwords against one account; credential stuffing replays username/password pairs from another site's breach (users reuse passwords); password spraying tries a few common weak passwords across many accounts.
Rate limit authentication attempts by username so no single account gets too many tries in a window.
Also rate limit by source IP so an attacker cannot spread attempts across accounts.
When a limit trips, either delay the response (hold the request) or reject with an HTTP error telling the client to slow down.
Optionally insert a human-verification step (e.g., CAPTCHA) and unblock the user once they pass.
Because credential-stuffing lists come from real breaches, pair rate limiting with breach-checked passwords and encourage a second factor.
caveats: The source cites a stress-test assumption of ~1,000 guesses/second as generous for an online attack, but notes it is an assumption, not a benchmark.
CAPTCHA is not a strong stand-alone control — the source describes solving farms and cheap solve APIs.

cards.title: CAPTCHA Limits: Why Human Checks Alone Won't Stop Bots
cards.summary: The source shows text CAPTCHAs were broken by automated solvers and that relay/outsourcing services and solver APIs defeat CAPTCHAs, so treat them as friction, not proof of humanity.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much to rely on CAPTCHA to protect signup, login, or high-abuse store actions (e.g., promo-code redemption, inventory hoarding).
steps: Assume text-based CAPTCHAs are defeatable: the source cites research solving real-world schemes with high accuracy (e.g., reCAPTCHA at 33%, CNN at 51%, Yahoo at 5%) and notes 'over 1% breakage' is considered broken.
Account for relay attacks, where an attacker forwards your CAPTCHA to other users (e.g., a free-content site) and returns the answer in real time.
Account for commercial solver APIs, which the source describes as inexpensive (it cites ~$0.50 per 1,000 solves).
Prefer risk-based/interactive verification that scores behavior (mouse, scroll, IP reputation) over static text challenges, but still treat it as one layer.
Layer CAPTCHA with rate limiting, anomaly detection, and (for sensitive flows) strong authentication.
caveats: CAPTCHA vendors and solvers evolve; verify current effectiveness rather than assuming these figures still hold.
Interactive/risk-based CAPTCHAs are harder but not proven impossible to bypass.

cards.title: Offline Cracking Realities Shape Password-Length Guidance
cards.summary: Password strength should be judged against three attack scenarios — online guessing (slow, network-bound) and offline cracking on a single machine or GPU array (fast) — which is why the source pushes for longer passwords.
cards.use_when: Choosing minimum password length and hash settings for customer or admin accounts based on how exposed your credential database is.
steps: Model three scenarios: online attacks (attacker sends login attempts over the network, limited by rate limits and detection), offline on one machine (attacker has a stolen hash database and cracks locally), and offline on a GPU array (the source cites a ~$20,000 rig as cheap for a determined attacker).
Because offline attacks are far faster than online, assume any leaked hash database will be worked on at high speed — so raise length requirements rather than relying on login throttling alone.
The source's mapping suggests passwords under roughly 12 characters are at high risk against a motivated offline attacker; treat that as a heuristic to justify longer minimums.
Note that exhaustive search isn't the only method: attackers also use known-password lists, which the source says can significantly shorten cracking time.
Since customers reuse passwords, combine length guidance with breach-list checks and a second factor for high-value accounts.
caveats: The source presents crack-time figures as illustrative assumptions about guessing rates and hardware, not fixed benchmarks.
Do not put real passwords into third-party strength/crack-time testing sites, even ones claiming not to transmit them.

cards.title: Multi-Factor Authentication: Knows, Has, Is — and Why Biometrics Stay on Device
cards.summary: Authentication factors fall into something you know, have, or are; combining factors raises assurance, and biometric data should be handled to avoid the 'can't reset a fingerprint' problem.
cards.use_when: Deciding which authentication factors to offer for customer logins and which to require for admin/staff or high-value store actions (e.g., payouts, price changes).
steps: Classify your factors: knowledge (password/PIN), possession (phone, badge, hardware key, passkey), and inherence (fingerprint, face).
Combine categories for two-factor authentication — the source uses the ATM example (card you have + PIN you know) — rather than stacking two of the same category.
Avoid depending on biometrics as transmittable secrets: the source stresses biometric data is not changeable, so if stolen you cannot reset it.
Follow the on-device pattern the source describes: use local biometrics only to unlock a cryptographic key store, then authenticate with a key, never sending the raw biometric to the server.
For sensitive store functions, require a second factor rather than merely encouraging it; for low-sensitivity accounts, encouraging it may be proportionate.
caveats: The source notes uncertainty about what can be extracted from devices with physical access — assume device compromise can threaten local keys.
WebAuthn support (the source mentions GitHub adopting it) is evolving; verify current browser and platform support.

cards.title: Fake Security Indicators: Anti-Phishing Images and Positive UI Cues Don't Work
cards.summary: Security images and other positive UI indicators are ignored or easily spoofed, so don't build phishing defense on customer-visible badges that attackers can replicate.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether any trust badge, security image, or pre-login indicator on your storefront actually protects customers from phishing lookalikes.
steps: Do not treat a user-selected security image as phishing protection: the source cites a study where ~72% of participants entered their password even when the security image and caption were removed.
Recognize that attackers can fetch the victim's image dynamically — the source describes looking up a victim's username on the real site and loading the returned image into a phishing page.
Recall the broader warning from the source: positive UI indicators are often ignored by users, so a badge appearing in a phishing clone doesn't reliably alert anyone.
Instead, invest in protections the attacker cannot copy: strong authentication (e.g., passkeys/WebAuthn-style origin-bound credentials), breach-checked passwords, and second factors.
If you run a brand that is frequently spoofed, treat customer education as a supplement, not a control.
caveats: The source describes these indicators as deprecated and ineffective, acknowledging they may once have helped; effectiveness studies are dated relative to current phishing tooling.

cards.title: Security-vs-Usability Tradeoffs: Match Friction to the Value at Risk
cards.summary: Password and authentication rules are balances between usability and security, so calibrate strictness to the sensitivity of the account rather than applying one policy everywhere.
cards.use_when: Deciding how strict login policy should be for different account tiers in a store (casual shopper accounts vs. accounts with stored payment, payout, or admin access).
steps: Ask what an attacker gains from the account: the source contrasts a low-stakes account (it cites streaming history) where heavy restriction may not be worth the friction against financial accounts where a second factor should be required.
Reserve strict controls — mandatory MFA, breach-list rejection, tighter rate limits — for high-consequence functions like payments, refunds, and admin panels.
Accept that some policies (for example, rejecting any breached password) will block some users who reuse passwords elsewhere; decide whether that tradeoff is right for your service.
Expect the attacker to know your scheme: the source says to assume the attacker knows your word list or policy, and to remain safe even then — so don't rely on secrecy of the rule for strength.
Document the policy per account tier so the tradeoff is a deliberate decision rather than an accident.
caveats: The source's examples of account sensitivity (streaming vs. financial) are its own illustrations, not measured outcomes for any named service.
Overly lax policy on accounts with saved payment methods shifts risk to customers and to you.

cards.title: Defense-in-Depth: Assume the Password Is Already Compromised
cards.summary: The source frames authentication design around building systems that stay secure even when an attacker holds the user's password, using layers rather than a single strong credential.
cards.use_when: Architecting login and account protection for a storefront where credentials commonly leak or get reused across sites.
steps: Adopt the source's working question — how can we build a system that stays secure when the attacker has the user's password? — as the frame for designing your login flow.
Layer controls: strong, length-based password policy, breach-list screening, rate limiting, a second factor, and monitoring for anomalous login behavior.

Because credential stuffing relies on reuse, verify login activity against indicators like new device/geography patterns rather than trusting the password alone (the source's broader security context emphasizes detecting failures rather than assuming none).
For sensitive actions (changing stored payment details, exporting customer data), require re-authentication or a fresh second factor even inside an active session.
Treat each layer as fallible on its own; the goal is that no single failure (e.g., a leaked password) becomes a full account compromise.
caveats: The source gives this as a design principle, not a specific product recommendation; pick concrete controls that match your stack and sensitivity.
No single control (password strength, MFA, CAPTCHA) is presented as sufficient alone.

cards.title: CAPTCHA strength is weaker than it looks — treat it as a speed bump
cards.summary: Published attack research showed solver accuracy against major CAPTCHA schemes ran far above the 1% 'broken' threshold, so CAPTCHA alone cannot be your bot defense.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much to rely on CAPTCHA/reCAPTCHA to protect storefront login, account creation, checkout, or admin actions.
steps: Assume automated solvers can pass a meaningful share of any given CAPTCHA scheme; treat it as one layer, not the gate.
Because a single widely-used scraper or solver can be pointed at many stores, do not assume your low profile protects you.

Layer CAPTCHA with server-side controls that do not depend on the puzzle being unsolvable: rate limits, device/IP reputation checks, behavioral signals, and step-up re-authentication for sensitive actions.
Log how often CAPTCHA is served and how often it fails. Treat spikes in challenge volume as attack traffic, not just as user friction.

Set your own tolerance: the source used, as an illustrative example, a 1% solver-success threshold for calling a CAPTCHA 'broken'. Do not copy that as a target — use it only to illustrate that low-looking success rates still matter.
caveats: Solver success rates quoted in the lecture are examples from a specific set of schemes and years, not current benchmarks for any vendor. Verify current vendor and third-party assessments before choosing a scheme.
CAPTCHA does not stop credential stuffing once an attacker holds a valid password; pair it with the login-side controls below.

cards.title: Reputation scoring and invisible challenges (modern reCAPTCHA-style)
cards.summary: Modern bot defense scores trust from behavior, session and IP reputation across many sites rather than from a visible puzzle, and increasingly runs with no UI at all.
cards.use_when: Choosing or configuring a bot-mitigation service for login, account creation, checkout, or coupon/inventory abuse on your storefront.
steps: Understand the model before you deploy: the vendor collects behavioral signals (mouse, scroll), session characteristics, and IP reputation across its whole customer network, then returns a trust score your site uses to allow, challenge, or block.
Feed the score into a decision, not just a boolean: define separate thresholds for low-risk (allow silently), medium-risk (challenge or step up), and high-risk (block or require re-auth) actions.
Apply the score to the specific action rather than the whole session — for example, allow browsing and cart edits but challenge at login, address change, and high-value coupon redemption.

Watch for false positives on privacy-preserving users. The source notes Tor and VPN-heavy traffic tends to look untrustworthy and gets challenged constantly; if you serve such users, expect and measure the friction.
Keep a fallback path so a vendor outage or an unscoreable client does not silently lock out legitimate customers. Verify current vendor APIs and consoles, which change.
Do not treat a trust score as proof of identity or as authorization for privileged actions; it is a risk signal only.
caveats: The lecture describes the general mechanism, not any specific current product. The exact signals, APIs, and no-UI behavior must be verified against the vendor's current documentation.
Cross-site reputation inherently penalizes some legitimate users and introduces dependence on a third party seeing your traffic.

cards.title: Step-up re-authentication for sensitive ecommerce actions (sudo mode)
cards.summary: Require the user to re-enter their password before a small set of high-impact account, payment, or address changes, as a defense-in-depth measure analogous to GitHub's sudo mode.
cards.use_when: Designing the admin/customer account flows where you allow changes to saved payment methods, shipping addresses, email/password, or payout/account details.
steps: Define a short, explicit list of 'sensitive actions' for your store: change password, change email, add/edit shipping address, add/remove a stored card, change payout/bank details, delete account, add an admin collaborator, generate API keys. Treat anything that redirects goods, money, or account recovery as sensitive.
Require the user to re-enter their password (or complete MFA) immediately before the sensitive action, then put the session into an elevated 'sudo' state.

Bound the elevation in time — expire the sudo state after a short window so a later request must re-enter. The source describes GitHub dropping the user back out after a while; set a window matching how long a real change takes, not hours.
Apply this on the server side per action, not just as a client-side modal, since the point is to require the secret even if an attacker already has session access.
Log every sensitive-action re-auth (who, when, from where) so you can review anomalies.

Note the secondary benefit documented in the source: this also protects against brief physical access to an unlocked device — someone who grabs a laptop cannot delete the account or change the payout bank without the password.
caveats: The source is explicit that this is 'not perfect' and does not cover every action — it is defense-in-depth, not a replacement for fixing XSS/CSRF or for MFA.
Adding re-auth adds friction; scope it narrowly to actions whose compromise is genuinely costly.

cards.title: Generic error messages to stop account enumeration on login, signup, and reset
cards.summary: Response discrepancies in login, password-reset, and signup flows let attackers learn which emails/accounts exist, so respond identically regardless of the underlying state.
cards.use_when: Writing the copy, logic, and status codes for storefront login, signup, guest-checkout account detection, and password-reset forms.
steps: Identify every place your store discloses account state: login ('no such user' vs 'wrong password' vs 'account disabled'), signup ('that email is already in use'), and reset ('no account with that email' vs 'we sent a link').

Return one generic message for all failure states: for login use something like a single 'we couldn't log you in' regardless of whether the user does not exist, the password is wrong, or the account is locked/disabled. For reset, use 'if this email exists, we'll send a link.'
Make sure the HTTP status code and any machine-readable response fields are also identical; the source calls out that differing status codes leak state even if the visible message is the same.
Apply the same genericization across all entry points — a common mistake is fixing login but leaving signup or reset revealing state, which lets an attacker bounce between them.

Consider who would benefit from enumerating your customer list. The source's example is a bank where confirmed customers make phishing far more effective; a specialty retailer's customer list can be similarly valuable.
Measure the trade-off: legendarily, generic messages confuse users who are unsure which email they registered with, so decide based on how sensitive your customer list is.
If you want the friendlier specific messages, use rate limiting as the primary control instead (see rate-limiting card) so attackers can't enumerate at scale.
caveats: The source presents this as a trade-off, not a rule: generic messages are worse UX, and some sites deliberately choose specific messages plus rate limiting.
Generic messages must be applied to every related flow or the fix is incomplete.

cards.title: Avoid timing side channels in authentication code paths
cards.summary: Early returns and skipped work in login handlers create measurable timing differences that reveal whether a user exists, so make both paths do equal work.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or writing login/password-check code where a database or service call only happens when the user exists.
steps: Watch for the anti-pattern: if the user lookup fails you return immediately, but if it succeeds you do extra work (hashing the submitted password and querying a slow remote service), the two responses take visibly different time.
Rewrite so both the 'user exists' and 'user does not exist' paths perform the same operations — hash the submitted password and run the lookup regardless, then decide validity only at the end.

Do not rely on thinking alone; the source recommends empirically testing your own system because you cannot assume the database takes identical time. If you measure a gap, add mitigation or eliminate the branch.
Treat this as a defense-in-depth detail alongside generic messages and rate limits, not as a substitute for them.

While addressing this, remember the broader point from the source: mitigation has trade-offs, so prioritize where enumeration actually matters (e.g., account recovery or payment flows) rather than over-engineering low-value paths.
caveats: The source itself admits it does not know how to guarantee a remote database takes identical time; treat timing mitigation as best-effort and validate.
Timing differences are only one of several enumeration channels (messages and status codes leak state more easily).

cards.title: Rate limiting authentication attempts — and the shared-IP caveat
cards.summary: Rate limit login and account-recovery attempts so credential stuffing and account enumeration can't be done at scale, while setting limits high enough for shared corporate/NAT IPs.
cards.use_when: Setting thresholds and locking policies for storefront login, password reset, and signup endpoints.
steps: Understand the trade-off: rate limiting lets you keep friendlier, more specific error messages while still preventing an attacker from enumerating thousands of accounts, because each attempt costs them time.

Set thresholds as a rule of thumb an order of magnitude above what you think the most extreme legitimate user would do — not a tight, theoretical limit. This protects users behind shared NAT, corporate networks, and households sharing one IP.

Account for IP sharing: too-low per-IP limits can block a hundred legitimate users behind one office IP. Prefer limits keyed on account/IP combinations or add per-account limits alongside per-IP ones.
Monitor for blocks that hit real customers and raise limits when you see them; the source recommends starting generously and adjusting based on observed friction.
Layer this with reputation and step-up controls so that a single successful credential-stuffing attempt still faces another checkpoint.
Verify current framework/library capabilities for layered rate keys (account, IP, device) in your storefront platform.
caveats: The 'order of magnitude above the extreme user' guidance is the source's personal rule of thumb, not a calibrated benchmark; you must test against your own traffic.
Rate limiting alone does not stop low-and-slow stuffing from many IPs; combine with reputation scoring and MFA.

cards.title: Check signup passwords against breach lists (Have I Been Pwned)
cards.summary: Because leaked-password corpora are public, reject/flag passwords your customers choose that appear in known breaches, and alert users whose credentials later surface.
cards.use_when: Choosing and enforcing password policy at account creation and password change on your storefront.
steps: Integrate a breached-password check into signup and password-change flows (the source names Have I Been Pwned as a service that aggregates leaked passwords; GitHub is cited as one site that refuses such passwords).
Decide the response: hard-reject the password and ask for another, or allow-with-warning. The source leans toward blocking because attackers already have the list.
Because leaked-password lists are large and attackers can try them against all accounts at once, treat 'is this password in a known breach' as a stronger signal than a simplistic strength meter.
Consider breach-alert monitoring for your own admin/staff emails so you know when a password they reused elsewhere is exposed.
Communicate the policy to users so rejected passwords don't feel arbitrary, and offer a password manager or generated passphrase guidance.
Verify the current API terms, rate limits, and privacy (k-anonymity) options of any breach-checking service before integrating.
caveats: This doesn't stop an attacker who already has a valid password; pair with MFA and rate limiting.
Breach coverage is imperfect — absence from a list is not proof the password is safe.

cards.title: Proactively lock or flag accounts after a breach you're tangentially involved with
cards.summary: If you learn a customer's credential is in a breach (yours or another service's), proactively force a reset or lock rather than waiting for stuffing to succeed.
cards.use_when: Incident response and ongoing account hygiene for a storefront whose customers reuse passwords across sites.
steps: Assume a large fraction of any customer base is already in someone's breach corpus; the source's framing is that 'probably yes' most users are affected by breaches somewhere.
When you discover credentials belonging to your users in a breach, identify impacted accounts and force a password reset or temporarily lock the account with a notification.
Make password reuse visible in your security stance: encourage unique credentials and make MFA easy to add, not just available.
Keep a documented process for the 'we got a breach dump' scenario so response is fast rather than improvised.

For customers calling about suspicious activity, have a recovery path that requires step-up verification (email + a second factor) rather than knowledge-based questions like 'first pet's name,' which the source ranks as weak, guessable factors.
caveats: Proactive locking creates friction and support load; scope it to accounts actually confirmed in a breach rather than guessing.
You will not have visibility into all breaches affecting your customers.

cards.title: Store passwords with a maintained adaptive password hasher
cards.summary: Use purpose-built password hashing with unique salts and tested cost settings rather than raw fast hashes or reversible encryption.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing how your storefront stores customer and admin credentials.
steps: Prefer the maintained identity system or framework password hasher over custom cryptography.
For new implementations evaluate current Argon2id guidance and platform support; retain a planned migration path for legacy bcrypt hashes.
Let the library manage salts and encoded parameters; a salted fast SHA hash is not a substitute for an adaptive password hasher.
Benchmark safe cost settings against login capacity, rate limits and current guidance.
Verify using the library API and rehash on successful login when the stored format needs upgrading.
caveats: Algorithm requirements can differ by platform or compliance context. Password hashing does not stop credential reuse, phishing or a compromised login endpoint.

cards.title: Why strong passwords alone fail — and what they actually protect
cards.summary: A strong password only blocks guessing and brute force; it does nothing against credential stuffing, phishing, MITM, or a malware-logged keystroke, so treat the password as one layer among several.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to require MFA on your storefront and explaining the value to stakeholders.
steps: Be precise about coverage: the source states a strong password protects against two things — password spraying/guessing and brute force. Everything else is out of its reach.
List what it does not stop: credential stuffing (password reused and already breached), phishing, man-in-the-middle, malware keylogging, extortion, and a physical post-it note.
Because attacker databases are cheap and lucrative — the source cites a paste claiming 32 million accounts for half a Bitcoin — assume leaked credentials will be tried against your store.
Therefore treat 'require MFA' as the primary control for accounts, and give users frictionless ways to enroll (TOTP, hardware keys, and WebAuthn-style device authentication where supported).
If requiring MFA for every login is too costly in UX, use the risk-based approach (next cards): require the second factor only for new devices, new locations, or suspicious behavior.
caveats: The source's framing ('passwords are broken', choose anything) is deliberately stark and comes from the cited Microsoft blog post — treat it as an argument for MFA, not a claim that password hygiene is pointless if MFA isn't available.
SMS-based codes are weaker than TOTP/hardware keys; the source uses TOTP as its worked example.

cards.title: Use risk-based step-up checks without weakening admin authentication
cards.summary: Use contextual signals to adjust customer authentication while maintaining stronger requirements for privileged actions.
cards.use_when: Designing when to add an MFA prompt in storefront login and account flows without hurting conversion.
steps: Set baseline authentication requirements by account and action sensitivity.
Use new-device, unusual-location and abuse signals as inputs to additional verification, not proof of legitimacy.
Do not let a remembered device or IP alone bypass required admin or sensitive-action authentication.
Measure false positives for shared networks, VPNs and traveling customers.
Maintain recovery, session revocation and rate limits alongside step-up checks.
caveats: The lecture's IP and volume thresholds are examples, not calibrated controls for the store.

cards.title: TOTP: implementing a two-factor second factor without SMS
cards.summary: Time-based one-time passwords authenticate a user by having the server and the user's authenticator app derive the same six-digit code from a shared secret and the current time, without any network call from the app.
cards.use_when: Choosing and implementing a second factor (TOTP/hardware key) for storefront customer and admin accounts.
steps: On account enrollment, generate a user-specific, cryptographically random secret on the server and store it in a column for that user.
Deliver the secret to the user's authenticator app — conventionally as a QR code the user scans with an app like Google Authenticator — so both sides share the same secret.

Code generation: derive a counter from the current time (the source's example uses current time divided by the 30-second interval), run the secret and counter through an HMAC-style function, then reduce the resulting hash to six digits (the source's approach takes a few bytes and mods by 10^6).
Rotation: the code changes roughly every 30 seconds as the counter increments; the app does this completely offline and never contacts the server.

Server verification: perform the same derivation using the counter corresponding to the current time and compare with the submitted code; allow a small clock-drift window in practice (verify current guidance from your library, which may differ from the source's raw description).
Combine with a password so the login requires something the user knows plus something the user has.
caveats: The shared secret stored on the phone and server is sensitive; losing the device means losing the factor, so provide recovery codes or a second enrolled factor.
The exact byte-extraction and drift-window details are implementation specifics — use a maintained TOTP library rather than hand-rolling.
TOTP is a second factor, not a replacement for a password, unless you deliberately architect it as a standalone mobile-app-based login (a different design).

cards.title: WebAuthn and passkeys: replacing passwords with device-based authentication
cards.summary: WebAuthn lets users authenticate with a device-bound key or biometric (something you have/are) instead of a phishable password, using public-key cryptography so the site never receives a reusable secret.
cards.use_when: Planning a passwordless or hardware-second-factor login option for customer and admin accounts on your storefront.
steps: Reduce the phishing problem: the source's core motivation is that passwords are 'terribly fishable' — anyone who convinces you to say your password can replay it exactly. A cryptographic device credential is not replayable this way.

Model it around a public key: the site holds a public key for the user, and authentication uses a private key that stays on the physical security key or in the device's secure hardware. If the security key is removed, the computer can no longer authenticate on the user's behalf.
Offer a hardware security key option for high-value/admin accounts, and passkey/biometric options for general customers where the platform supports it.
Explain to users that the security of 'something you have' rests on the key's hardware protections; a well-engineered hardware key resists even disassembly-style extraction for most threat models.
Support enrollment and a recovery path for lost keys, and keep a fallback factor so a lost device doesn't permanently lock a paying customer out.
Verify current browser/platform support and the WebAuthn/passkey implementation details against current documentation — the standard and vendor support have moved on since the source's August launch.
caveats: WebAuthn shifts trust to the device vendor and platform; it does not eliminate all account-recovery risk.
Passwordless isn't a universal fit — many users lack a suitable device or password manager, so the source treats it as an alternative rather than a replacement for everyone.
The source's discussion of factor categories is explicitly framed as a design abstraction, noting that not all authentication mechanisms fit neatly into know/have/are.

cards.title: Use modern, non-guessable factors instead of knowledge-based questions
cards.summary: Classic 'something you know' factors like security questions are guessable or publicly knowable, so prefer cryptographic device factors over knowledge-based verification for recovery and sensitive actions.
cards.use_when: Designing account recovery and verification for storefront customer accounts, billing support, and admin access.
steps: Recognize the weakness: the source notes that something you know traditionally includes security questions like a first pet's name, which are not tied to anything private and are often externally discoverable.
Replace knowledge-based recovery challenges with cryptographic factors: registered hardware keys, TOTP apps, or device-bound passkeys.

For the occasional case where a factor must be something you are — fingerprints, face unlock — recognize that these are device-bound and constrained; use them as the second factor inside WebAuthn rather than raw biometric data.

Think about threat models broadly: the source raises domestic-abuse scenarios where an attacker technically has the device but the trust boundary should still hold, which matters for recovery and access to sensitive account areas.
Design recovery so that resetting a factor requires the strongest available proof, not the weakest question, and log the recovery event for review.
caveats: The source's factor framework is presented as an abstraction that shouldn't be rigidly applied — you ultimately care about keeping the attacker out, not whether a mechanism matches a category.
Some users will not have modern device factors; provide a fallback path that is still stronger than a security question.

cards.title: Prevent data-breach exposure from common cloud misconfigurations
cards.summary: Breaches frequently stem from simple mistakes — publicly readable object storage, SQL injection, command injection, misconfigured servers — so audit these on your own storefront infra.
cards.use_when: Reviewing your store's storage buckets, servers, and database access for accidental public exposure.
steps: Treat public object storage as your first check: the source notes a common cause of large breaches is simply leaving an S3-style bucket accessible to anyone — anyone with the URL can download everything.
Assume that once an attacker reaches one application server, they can pivot to databases and other servers reachable from it, so limit network reachability from app servers to data stores.
Audit for injection classes named by the source (command injection, SQL injection) as entry points that lead to full data exfiltration.
Include breach response in your operational plan: assume you will be breached eventually, and design so the blast radius is small and detection is possible.
Because the source's lesson is 'even many well-known companies get breached', do not treat your own competence or obscurity as a reason to skip the audits.
caveats: This is a general reminder, not a complete audit checklist — many breach causes are out of scope of the source.
Assume your customers reuse passwords elsewhere, so even a non-financial breach on your store can enable attacks on other services.

cards.title: Audit your authentication implementation with HIBP and breach-awareness
cards.summary: Use Have I Been Pwned and similar resources to verify your own team's exposure, alert customers, and feed account-security decisions at signup and login.
cards.use_when: Standing up account-security review processes for a storefront, and checking your team's admin/ops accounts for exposure.
steps: Check admin and support staff emails against the Have I Been Pwned service to discover exposed credentials before attackers do (the source's lecturer demonstrates posting his own email publicly for illustration).
Subscribe to breach alerts for these emails so you learn about new exposure rather than finding out during an incident.
Incorporate the same service into your product at password-set time: reject or warn on passwords that appear in known breaches, as discussed elsewhere in these notes.
Be honest about coverage: the service can only know about breaches that have surfaced publicly, so absence from the list is not a clean bill of health.

Treat the customer-facing version of this as a way to protect users even when you cannot control their password habits; the source's closing advice is 'protect the user even when the attacker has their password'.
Encourage password managers so users can generate memorable, unique long passphrases (the source suggests four random words as a memorable, sufficiently random approach).
caveats: Do not expose or log checked passwords; use a k-anonymity/bulk-check approach and verify the current API's privacy model.
The source's 'four random words' advice is offered as an approach, not a formal benchmark.

cards.title: Model login security as credential-to-account binding, not factors
cards.summary: Stop enumerating knowledge/possession/biometric factor categories; instead inventory every thing that can bind a customer to an account and assess each one's interception and recovery risk.
cards.use_when: Deciding what login and account-recovery methods your storefront should accept, or auditing why a 'two-factor' customer account can still be taken over.
steps: List every method your checkout or account system actually accepts as proof of identity: password, email reset link, SMS code, authenticator app code, push notification, security key, biometric unlock, social login, support-desk challenge answers.

For each, ask the source's test question: if an attacker intercepts or relays that proof in real time, do they gain account access? Email reset links and SMS codes pass that proof along in full, so they collapse to 'as secure as the inbox' or 'as secure as the carrier's number-reassignment process'.

Note that classic 'something you know / have / are' categories break down (e.g., a security question, a credit-card last-4, an SSH key used only for recovery). Treat these as real factors anyway if your support flow accepts them.
Rank methods by how recoverable they are for a locked-out customer versus how interceptable they are, then choose a default and a documented fallback.
Do not convert source opinion (SMS 'really should' go away) into a blanket ban; weigh it against your customers' recovery needs and support cost.
